title: The Fathers on Job
rules: Larry Sanger's rules for Deep Dive Bible commentary editions (emails of 8 and 9 Nov 2026): comments of at most 6 adjacent verses (Selected at most 3); cuts marked with an ellipsis; square brackets for editorial additions only; paragraphs added; one-sentence capsule no longer than 40% of the comment. Every word outside brackets is Via Patrum's published translation, checked by script.
scope: Church Fathers (all died by 749) in works published on viapatrum.org as of 9 Nov 2026.

comments.capsule: Scripture records Job's goodness first, so the devil is seen to attack no negligent man but a great athlete.
comments.comment: And having announced also his pureness of soul, it shows how the devil did not seek a man who was negligent. For it was necessary before the struggle against the opponent to record the greatness of the athlete, to show that, abstaining from every evil thing, he had not been satisfied even unto this, but was also caring for perfection, which is a subversion of those saying that even children and irrational animals abstain from evil things. For this man was both righteous and blameless.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the book first records Job's goodness before the trial begins.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Abstaining from wickedness is praiseworthy when one who could be base does so out of hatred of evil, and 'true' means free of hypocrisy.
comments.comment:
… For praise has its place when one, being able to be base, abstains from wickedness through hatred of it. Not everyone who does not use wickedness is called to abstain from it; for infants, not using such things, no one would say they mainly abstain from wickedness, for the one doing this acts by judgment and word. …

For he is truly God-fearing, one honoring a life of reverence, whereas those honoring things not sacred are found impious.

And to the blessed one is added 'true' according to the theory of truth and the lack of hypocrisy in ethics; for one who seeks virtue through opportunism is not true.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Job abstained from every evil thing and was true and God-fearing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Uz is interpreted 'will', and in a higher sense Job's nobility comes from the sun of righteousness, not from men.
comments.comment: And it is also good that he dwelt in Uz, which is interpreted as 'will'; for the righteous man does nothing without purpose, but his house and city is pure will. 'And that man was noble from the rising of the sun' (Job 1:3). And this is possible regarding the sensible. But if one intended an ascent, it might be said that the righteous man acquires nobility, not from men, but from the light of the 'sun of righteousness' (Malachi 4:2)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the one spoken of is a son, 'he made' and 'he became' are used in place of 'he begot', as Scripture does of Job's sons and Hezekiah's children.
comments.comment:
Now when Scripture says, “And there were born to him seven sons” (Job 1:2), this will also help us against the Arians. They cling to what the Apostle says about the Only-begotten—“being faithful to him who made him” (Hebrews 3:2)—as a great support for their heresy, and they insist that the Son of God is a creature. But this support of theirs is a bruised reed. For when a substance is a creature and a created thing, then “he made” and “he created” are properly said of it, and they signify a creature.

But when a substance is an offspring and a son, then “he made,” “he became,” and “he created” are no longer properly applied to it, nor do they signify a creature; rather, a person uses “he made” without distinction in place of “he begot.” So the Arians will condemn themselves if they learn Scripture’s idiom. For even if parents speak of the children born from them as being made, becoming, and created, they do not thereby deny their nature. Hezekiah, for example, as it is written in Isaiah, prayed and said, “For from today I will make children” (Isaiah 38:19)—using “I will make” in place of “I will beget,” and speaking of the children born from him. And there is no difference. Here too it is said of Job, “And there were born to him seven sons” (Job 1:2), just as Moses also says in the law, “If they become” (Deuteronomy 25:5).
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's sons gathered among themselves, as brothers dwelling together in unity.
comments.comment: The sons of Job, being well-nourished, did not seek social pleasures with others, but among themselves, according to that which is said in the Psalms: "Behold, how good or how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity" (Psalm 133:1). … And it is also good to take along one's own sisters, which is a clear sign of temperance and grace.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the sons feasted together and what it shows about them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job rose in the morning to offer a sacrifice for each child, individually and in good order.
comments.comment: … the blessed Job rose in the morning not for some other work, but to present a sacrifice to God on behalf of the children "according to their number," which is to say, individually and in good order; for nothing is poured out in haste. But after this, he also presented the calf on their behalf in his own way, providing for the children's guidance. Thus, after the feasting was completed, he cleansed them, demonstrating both the sensory cleansing and the intellectual cleansings that complete the process.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job's morning sacrifice for his children was and how he did it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The calf offered for all the children may point to the Cross of the Savior.
comments.comment: If the "calf" offered on behalf of all signifies the "Cross" which remained for the sake of the human race as Savior, consider that He is also "fit for eating" in the parable of the Gospel, because of the nourishing nature of the divine teaching. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because no visible sin of the children was seen, the sacrifice was offered for hidden slips of the mind, and their death is not to be read as punishment for sins.
comments.comment:
"They thought my evils toward God." Great purity is shown in this of the children; for not seeing any perceptible sin of theirs, they offered the sacrifice regarding the intellect, considering that human weakness and softness in youth often have a slip. Therefore also the holy Paul said: "I do not even know within myself, but not in this have I been justified" (1 Corinthians 4:4), and the Psalmist: "From my hidden things cleanse me" (Psalm 19:12). Therefore it must be observed, not that they were struck down by such a death because of sins. "Thus Job did all the days of his life" (Job 1:5).

the steadfastness of the holy one's character is shown here … This also David says about himself, singing: "I will bless the Lord at all times" (Ps 34:1).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job offered sacrifices for sins his children might only have thought.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The angels stood before God to minister, and the devil stood among them, known to God even in the disguise of an angel of light.
comments.comment:
… providing their own ministry and their own labor toward God. While they were standing, the devil also stood by.

Even if he is manifold and many-sided, he does not escape God. … he himself is also known by the eye of God which oversees all things. And let the hypocrisy of the devil also reveal the explicit truth, "transforming" himself "into an angel of light" (2 Cor 11:14) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Created beings are in places and God alone is unbounded, so to 'stand before' him means to be formed by his will.
comments.comment: And the Lord said to the devil: “Where have you come from?” (Job 1:7). At the same time, this also establishes that all created things are in divided places—the lights in the firmament, the clouds in the air. And for human beings he fixed the boundaries of nations, while the angels are sent out for ministries, and they go up and down on the ladder. And here they came, it says, to stand before the Lord, and a question is put to the devil: “Where have you come from?” So they are in a place, and wherever they are sent, there they are present. But God alone is unbounded. Therefore they do not seek the one who is present everywhere as if he were in a place, so as to find the unbounded one enclosed in a region. Rather, to stand before him is this: to be formed by his will and to be stretched up wholly toward him. For every creature is before God, even the rebellious and most wicked one, in respect of the unbounded nature of that essence. But the angels are present to God in a special way, according to the insatiable longing of divine love.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that angels and the devil come to stand before the Lord.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Created beings, even the angels and the devil, are in a place and are sent, but God alone is unbounded, and to stand before Him is to be conformed to His will.
comments.comment:
And God said to the devil, “Where have you come from?” (Job 1:7). At the same time, in these words it is shown that all created things are in divided places—the lights in the firmament, the clouds in the air. And for human beings he fixed the boundaries of the nations; the angels are sent out for ministries, and they ascend and descend on the ladder. And here it says, “They came to stand before the Lord” (Job 1:6). And a question is put to the devil: “Where have you come from?” (Job 1:7). So they are in a place, and wherever they are sent, there they are present. But God alone is unbounded. They seek the one who is present everywhere, in order to find the unbounded one shut up in some region.

But “to stand before” means to be conformed to his will and to stretch oneself wholly toward him. For all creation is before God—even even that apostate and most wicked one—according to the unbounded nature of his being. But the angels are present to God in a special way, according to the insatiable longing of divine love.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that the angels and the devil came to stand before the Lord.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's question 'From where have you come?' rebukes the devil, who is not God's minister, just as God asked Adam 'where are you?'
comments.comment: … He said this to him so that hearing it, we might understand: 'From where have you come?' These angels, our own, being appointed to perform divine service for me, were performing this, standing before me, acting instead of a true standing—for their standing is not local—but you, from where? For you are not my minister. 'From where' then 'have you come?' You would grasp what was said to Adam by God as similar to this: 'Adam, where are you?' (Genesis 3:9). The 'from where have you come?' was a rebuke of the devil's futile movement.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God asks the devil where he has come from.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil goes around as one seeking someone to overthrow, using deceit rather than force against those able to resist him.
comments.comment: One should not be surprised if, being a subtle spirit, he passed through the aforementioned places. For even God did not rebuke him as a liar. And also the 'having gone around' is good; for he is not encompassing. But he goes around as 'one seeking someone to overthrow,' so that he might drag those who are persuaded by his evil deceptions, and he might seek out those who oppose him, which also happened regarding Job. Therefore, he does not use force, nor does he come upon us by power. For he is appointed to stand against those who are able to resist.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the devil means by going around the earth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God calls Job his servant, and his words to the devil show the devil to be rational, while no one on earth equals Job.
comments.comment:
The Lord has called Job "servant" according to both significations; for his servant was according to what was said by the Psalmist: "I am your servant and the son of your maidservant" (Psalm 116:16) …

It is also an explicit indication of the devil being rational to say: "Pay attention to your mind" (Job 1:8); for to think is proper to a rational being. Not only is this said about the devil here, but also in: "But you said in your mind: I will ascend to heaven" (Isaiah 14:13), which, as it is said, is a demonstration of him being rational himself. …

"Pay attention, therefore," he says, "to your mind concerning my servant Job, for there is none on earth like him" (Job 1:8). It is not a vain thing to say: "of those on earth." For there are rational things concerning him and on his behalf that happen regarding the earth. For it is not the same to say: "there is none like him" as to say: "there is none on earth like him." For how did he not exceed all those on earth, with the God of all things testifying to him in: "A blameless man, true, God-fearing, turning away from all evil deeds" (Job 1:8)?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Lovers of evil never grant that anyone's virtue is genuine, so the devil says Job is just only because of his wealth, though wealth itself adds nothing to virtue.
comments.comment:
For what does he say? 'Does Job fear God for nothing? Have you not encircled him and his house and all that he possesses on every side? Have you blessed the work of his hands and made his livestock many on the earth?' (Job 1:9-10). It is characteristic of lovers of evil, who loathe virtue, not to consider the beauties of those nearby as genuine, but to say instead: this one is just through an inability to do wrong, this one is prudent through the so-called foolishness, this one does not have wealth and resources because he is unsuited to them, even while considering the gentle hypocrite as such; and in no way does anyone base accept anyone's virtue as genuine.

The devil, being the leader of wickedness, conceiving such things concerning Job, made these things manifest to the one who knows the hidden, saying that Job is just because of external goods. And 'encircled' (Job 1:10) was said to him instead of security, providing emphasis, as if because of these things he is unassailable and has no vulnerability …

For having these things removed, he remained similarly unblemished. In truth, possessing wealth contributes something to virtue for one who uses it well, but wealth itself contributes nothing to it. … The blessed Job showed unshakeable virtue both in poverty and in wealth.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the devil's charge that Job fears God for nothing and why it fails.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil learned from being blocked that Job was fenced, for whatever is not handed over to the devil God has fenced.
comments.comment: "Did you not fence what is outside him?" How do you know the fence is there? Our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking someone to swallow. He came round Job wanting the same work; later, once authority was given, he did it. From being blocked he learned that everything was fenced, and said, "You fenced what is inside him and what is outside him." Whatever is not handed to the devil, you have fenced.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the hedge around Job is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God's hand may be a punishing or a protecting power, to 'touch' means to harm, and 'bless you to your face' stands for cursing.
comments.comment:
One may call his hand in two different ways: either the punishing and service-oriented power, which the divine Scripture is accustomed to calling 'vessels of wrath,' or the protective and guarding power, as it is said: 'No one is able to snatch from the hand of my Father. …

For 'do not touch my sheep' does not forbid simple contact, but the audacity against the saints to harm them. And 'he who touches you touches the apple of his eye' (Zechariah 2:8) similarly means one who touches for evil. …

For he says: 'Surely he will bless you to your face,' instead of cursing or blaspheming, using this expression so that the harshest words might not be brought against God …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the key words hand, touch and 'bless you to your face' in the devil's challenge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God gives the devil power over Job's goods but forbids him to touch Job, so trials come neither by fate nor by chance but by God's permission.
comments.comment: The words placed here seem to mean not to fall into trials apart from divine permission. For God says: 'Behold, I have given all into your hand.' But so that it may become clear that He also exercises permission with measure, it is added: 'but do not touch him.' Therefore, circumstances occur neither by fate nor of themselves, but by the permission of God, according to what has already been laid out for the demonstration of Job's virtue …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God gives the devil power yet sets a limit.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: That the devil 'went out from the Lord' means he stands outside the Lord, as Cain did, and is always found among those on the outside.
comments.comment: This is spoken more literally concerning the devil, because he becomes one who is outside the Lord, even more so than Cain. For concerning him it was said: 'And Cain went out from the presence of the Lord God' (Gen 4:16). And to go out signifies that he has become invisible to God. Therefore, this one will always be found among those on the outside, even if he came in a feigned manner among the attendants of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job was not disturbed by the calamities, for like the faithful in the Psalms and Paul he stayed inseparable from the love of the Lord.
comments.comment:
… However, despite the harshness of the occurring calamities, the holy man was not at all disturbed.

It has been said in one of the Psalms concerning a holy man: 'From an evil hearing he shall not be afraid. His heart is prepared to hope upon the Lord.' And even as it was said according to the blessed Paul: 'Who shall separate the faithful from the love of God? Neither tribulation nor distress, nor persecution, nor famine or sword' (Romans 8:35), following this, the most manly Job remained inseparable from the love of the Lord, having withstood so many attacks. …

But having heard even concerning the slaughter of the children, to have taken this up manfully demonstrates the manliness of the holy man and his patience. It should be observed, lest the one being saved alone, in order to announce, was being saved for greater temptation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil tried to bury Job under successive reports of evil, but he stood like a breakwater, thanked God, and tore his garment only at the news that the wind had struck his feasting children.
comments.comment: For the devil stripped away his prosperity in his household, but he planned to bury him under the successive reports of evils. For while the first messenger was still announcing one disaster, another messenger came, bringing the gloom of worse events. The terrors were joined one to another, and the disasters rivaled the onrush of waves; before the first tear had ceased, the occasion for another was brought forward. But the righteous man stood like a breakwater, receiving the assaults of the storm, turning the force of the waves into foam, and he sent forth the grateful voice to the Master: 'The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened' (Job 1:21). And he considered none of the things that happened worthy of tears. But when someone came announcing that a violent wind had struck the chamber of gladness while his sons and daughters were feasting, then alone he tore his garment, showing the sympathy of nature and testifying by what he did that he was a tenderly loving father.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on Not Clinging to Worldly Things

comments.capsule: Fire from heaven could tempt the weak to think virtue worthless and God a punisher of the good, yet the devil cannot bring down fire, so it came by God's judgment.
comments.comment:
For the simpler people might have reasoned that the ones coming to capture, having taken the livestock and being able to slaughter the children, were doing this not from God, but by the law of enemies coming in disorder and acting out of hatred. When fire was announced as having descended from heaven, there was fear, lest any of the weak should reason that virtue is nothing and that God punishes one possessing it.

But even when this happened, the holy man did not falter, being entirely mindful of God. For even the devil does not have the authority to bring down fire from heaven, but this has happened by divine judgment, so that God, who gave Job the authority, might present him to the devil, to show that the blessed one among men cares for nothing, even if he weaves many schemes.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the fire from heaven was a special trial and where it came from.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Each new report came while the last was still being spoken, to heap up his grief, but Job stood like an unbreakable wall on the rock of salvation.
comments.comment:
The successive announcement of the pains demonstrates the excessive and marvelous manliness of the blessed one. For see the observation, how while the one announcing the former things was 'still speaking,' the second one did not come for their healing, but was announcing for an escalation, announcing harder things, as it is customary for the announcement of pains to overturn the reasoning and to hollow out and thus disturb, as if to make one move outside of the proper state, being drawn toward the various sorrows.

But the holy man was not such a one. But as an unbreakable wall, remaining likewise unshaken against the majority of those attacking who were able to see him, so the holy Job, having 'the foundation' upon 'the rock' of salvation, was not moved when the temptations fell upon it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the messengers come one upon another and how Job withstood them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The three companies of horsemen may have been a military camp or a continuous attack of horsemen, moved by the devil's suggestion.
comments.comment: Perhaps there was a military camp in the land, which fell upon the camels divided into three divisions. For as he says it is well known: 'The horsemen made three heads for us.' It is also possible that a continuous attack of horsemen was occurring then, and was moved by the devilish suggestion, and thus the messenger said it because it was happening out of habit: 'The horsemen made three heads for us.' They did not only take the camels, but also killed the children.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the horsemen who made three heads might have been.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Many others were probably at the feast, but the messenger mentions only the children, as the Gospel gives only the numbers of the five thousand.
comments.comment: … For it is not doubtful that many were present at such a time, of whom the announcer did not remember, being satisfied with the exceeding loss of the children and following what happened to those present. For such a thing is customary in the Scripture; for when the Savior broke the five loaves, from which he satisfied five thousand men, the evangelist remembers, saying: 'apart from women and children' (Matthew 14:21), mentioning only the preceding numbers.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil waited for a drinking-party to destroy the sons, for had he found them reading or praying he could have done nothing.
comments.comment: … He also plotted against the sons and waited for a moment to destroy them. Had he found them reading, he would not have touched the house. Had he found them praying, he could do nothing. Opportunity came in drunkenness and a drinking-party. Note the spirit at the corners of the house: hypocrites pray in the broad places of the corners, and everyone off the straight road uses corners. A broad corner is much, loosened wickedness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the blow fell while the children were feasting.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The great wind that struck the house may have been a storm, a spirit serving the devil, or the devil himself.
comments.comment: Having touched the four corners of the house and having struck it down, one should investigate whether it was an excessive storm that thus battered the house and brought it down, or a spirit serving the devil, or the devil himself. For this is a great, evil spirit, having touched the four corners of the house and having brought it down. … For the devil is not able to move the wind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Tearing his clothes and shaving his head, as the ancients did at deaths, showed Job's family love, and falling to the ground in worship showed he did not despair.
comments.comment:
… For perhaps one of such people would say that Job was not fond of children, since he did nothing worthy of sympathy. But his feeling and his manliness are shown together, that he received the terrible horror and grief of the death of the children neither unfeelingly nor ungenerously; for through “tearing the clothes and shaving the head”—for the ancients were accustomed to do this at deaths—he shows sympathy and familial love. And the following things bring forth a sign of manliness and surpassing wisdom in advance.

For if he says, 'and having fallen to the ground' (Job 1:20), he did not despair, nor did he leave an unseemly word to a wise man, but he worships the Originator of all, being persuaded that these things happen not outside of divine judgment, and that they happen from the beginning followingly and according to some correct reason.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job's grief and worship in verse 20 show about him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's tearing of his garments may show the tester that he may have the rest too, and the shaving of his hair a symbol of counting all excess as nothing great.
comments.comment: The phrase 'So Job tore his garments' (Job 1:20) is to be taken typologically. It might be possible to say that for this reason he stripped himself, first showing to the one testing him that, if you desire even the remaining things, you have these also; then showing symbolically that just as a combatant departs from an opponent. And the removal of the hairs might be a symbol of considering all excess to be nothing great, but being well-disposed toward the just and wise man, neither being debased in 'reliefs' nor being distressed in 'tribulations,' which the blessed David also sang in presenting: 'I will bless the Lord at all times' (Psalm 34:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Naked I will depart there' cannot mean the mother's womb, so the verse teaches that the soul survives death.
comments.comment:
… 'Naked,' he says, 'I came out from my mother's womb, naked and I will depart there.' Concerning which those deliberating on nothing divine regarding the immortality of the soul ought to be questioned. For where will Job depart naked? Perhaps in the womb of the mother? For from there he went out naked according to what is said. But away with this false thought. It is evident that this was said for the instruction of not letting the soul be scattered, as it seemed to some.

For the blessed Paul also writes something similar, saying: 'For we have brought nothing into the world, and we are able to bring nothing out' (1 Timothy 6:7). For just as the bringing out implies the dead person existing, so the one not having brought in is existing and enters from some place bringing nothing of that kind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job means by departing naked 'there'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The Lord gives and takes away, and makes poor and rich, not by irrational whim as believers in fate suppose.
comments.comment: And that doctrine, being unknown to many, he introduces saying: 'The Lord gave, the Lord took away' (Job 1:21), presenting after this, that his possession did not happen to be unjust and having taken its beginning from some unbefitting assistance. 'The Lord makes poor and makes rich' (1 Samuel 2:7), not by any irrational whim, as those introducing fate deliberate …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's thanksgiving rebukes those who complain at such accidents, because he stays firm in his reasoning and becomes a herald of true teaching.
comments.comment: It is also wonderful that he says such a thing of thanksgiving: 'May the name of the Lord be blessed' (Job 1:21), which is a rebuke against those who complain about such accidents and bring such things forward, which is not even good to say. But the holy one is not such an unwise person, being unbending in his reasoning even when such things happen, becoming a herald of true dogmas and divine things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job's blessing of God in loss is a rebuke to complaint.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job speaks as a father only for as long as his Maker willed, and as a servant he does not quarrel with a verdict he cannot overturn.
comments.comment: He said, 'The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened' (Job 1:21). He was all but crying out: 'I was called a father for as long as the One who made me so willed. He has chosen to strip away the crown from my offspring again; I do not fight over what belongs to Him. Let the Master's will prevail. He is the fashioner of the race, and I am an instrument. Why should I, a servant, be pointlessly distressed and find fault with a verdict I cannot overturn?'
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain words the attitude behind Job's blessing of the Lord.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on Not Clinging to Worldly Things

comments.capsule: Job gave thanks to God not only in prosperity but when all was taken from him, and to say what God ought to have done imputes foolishness to God.
comments.comment: He who gives thanks to God does not do so only for pleasant things; he does this, but also for unpleasant things. Job, indeed, does not bless God only in prosperity and the salvation of children and the other surrounding wealth, but also when all was taken from him at once. When indeed all his ordered things, the existing things, were taken from him, he gives thanks to God, and 'he did not sin,' he says, 'Job did not act foolishly toward the Lord, nor did he give unfaithfulness to God' (Job 1:21-22). He who speaks concerning providence saying: 'he ought to have done thus or thus,' imputes foolishness to God and speaks of how much he did not consider God regarding what He ought to have done. When indeed someone says: 'it was necessary for the old to die before the young, the parents before the children, and the healthy not to die, but the sick,' he gives foolishness to the Divine...
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: That Job did not sin 'against the Lord' means no stumble occurred even in thought, since he was watched by God.
comments.comment:
A great testimony is given by the Holy Spirit to the blessed Job in saying: 'In all these things Job did not sin against the Lord' (Job 1:22). …

But the presence of 'before' indicates that no stumble occurred, for he was being watched by God. For 'no one sinned thus' is not the same as 'no one sinned against the Lord,' which shows a purity surpassing even in word, deed, or thought …

To this end, God used to call those repenting: 'Remove the wickedness from your souls before my eyes' (Isaiah 1:16), which implies that we must not only refrain from deed, but also from the thought of evil, as seeing God. The Savior also says in the Gospel: 'But when you give alms, do not blow a trumpet as the hypocrites do' (Matt 6:2). And also: 'He who sees in secret will repay you' (Matt 6:4). Just as he who gives alms in this way does not hear the praise of the many, so he who does not sin against the Lord is free from all evil.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the Holy Spirit's testimony that Job did not sin before the Lord means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Whoever is convinced that providence governs does not charge God with foolishness, as the unbelieving do when they say such things ought not to have happened.
comments.comment: It is also good to say: 'And he did not give foolishness to God.' For he who is convinced that what happens is managed by divine providence does not attribute foolishness to the God who governs, unlike the unbelieving who often blame God and say: 'This ought not to have happened, or that; this one ought not to have suffered poverty or to be rich or to be sick or to be healthy,' or: 'Why did the young man depart from the life of the elders while they were still in it?'. In short, those saying such things assume the governance is foolish. … But the holy man, even in such circumstances, blesses the Lord, being convinced that the judgment of God is just.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that Job gave no foolishness to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God questions the shamed devil to convict him, as he did Cain.
comments.comment: "The Lord said to the devil, From where do you come?" God saw Satan ashamed and distressed; when questioning shows him ungrateful, God convicts the wrongdoer, as he convicted Cain.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God asks the devil where he comes from.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil answers differently from his first visit, and the Lord's question shames him, since he has nothing to boast of and will not admit his defeat.
comments.comment:
It should be said regarding the question, 'Where do you come from?' that the most convicting thing was said by the Lord to the devil, as he had nothing to say of his own with boldness as an achievement, and something shaming: that he had been defeated, which he himself shamefully did not admit.

It should be noted how the devil does not answer in this way now. For then he said, 'Having gone around the earth and walking through under the heaven, I have returned' (Job 1:7), but now, 'Having gone through the heaven and walking through the whole world.' … For he knows that nothing is hidden from God. For he also did not say, 'Of those things which you gave me authority over, I have done; I have taken away the existing things of Job and the children they took away.' For it would have been consistent to say this, and, 'The same remained.' But he moves toward a second petition, from which he thinks he will overturn the purpose of the holy man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Innocence means freedom from wickedness, and Job still had it, so the devil's attack on his possessions was in vain.
comments.comment: Akakia [innocence, freedom from wickedness] signifies different things; for it denotes both the absence of wickedness and goodness of character. When the saint says, 'God judge me, for in my akakia I have walked,' he means akakia as virtue; for one possessing virtue is devoid of wickedness. … Job therefore 'still had akakia' with all words being made upright. 'But you have said that you will destroy his possessions for nothing.' The Lord exposes the vain work of the devil against the saints. For he who acts without cause labors in vain. So even if the devil, hoping to seize the saint, attempted through the destruction of possessions and children—and having recognized the attempt was futile against the saint's courage regarding his possessions—he fought him in vain; for nothing of what he hoped for happened.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'innocence' means and why the devil's first attack failed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil thinks only external goods are good and that Job thinks so too, so a man would give up anything to avoid suffering himself.
comments.comment: [The devil's thought:] Considering the three kinds of so-called goods—those external, which are divided into wealth, property, health, and other bodily things, and others which are virtues—he thinks only the undifferentiated goods are such, and he thinks Job has this same mindset, and he shamelessly says to the Lord—that is to say, speaking according to what we understand has been said before—that a man would lay out everything so that he might not suffer something himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil acts at once, wounding Job's whole body to undo the strength of his virtue.
comments.comment: Of the history, it is this: 'The devil went out from the Lord' (Job 2:7). Having gone out, he does not wait, but immediately performs the work of the temptation, surrounding him with a total-body wound, intending by the blow to dissolve the tone of his virtue. By mentioning the extremes, he shows that he also touched the middle parts.
comments.selected_reason: Says plainly what the devil does in the verse and why.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the devil could not shake Job, he struck his flesh and set him on a dung heap, yet Job kept his devotion untouched in his soul.
comments.comment: But when the enemy saw that he was victorious again and could not be shaken by any of these things, he brought the device of trial against his very flesh. He scourged his body with unspeakable blows and made springs of worms pour out from it. He brought the man down from the thrones of his kingdom and seated him on a dung heap. Yet even when struck by such sufferings, Job remained unmoved. While his body was being torn, he kept the treasure of his devotion inviolate in the hidden place of his soul.
comments.selected_reason: Tells in plain words what happened to Job's body and how he bore it.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on Not Clinging to Worldly Things

comments.capsule: Job kept patience in spirit and flesh, giving thanks at every bitter message and enduring his ulcers calmly, so that the devil's whole attack accomplished nothing.
comments.comment: Oh, how blessed was that man too, who worked out every form of patience against every force of the devil! His flocks were driven away, his wealth in livestock was taken, his children were snatched from him in a single crashing blow, and then his own body was tortured with wounds—yet none of this shut him out from the patience he had given to God in faith. The devil struck him with all his strength and accomplished nothing. He was not called away from looking to God by so many sorrows; instead, he stood as an example and witness for us, showing that patience must be carried through in spirit and flesh, in mind and body alike, so that we do not collapse under losses of worldly goods, or the loss of those we love most, or even the afflictions of the body itself. What a bier God built from the devil in that man! What a standard he raised from the enemy of his glory, when that man, at every bitter message, let nothing come from his mouth except thanks to God (Job 1:21), and when he cursed his wife, already worn out by evils and urging him toward wicked remedies (Job 2:9-10)! How God laughed, how the evil one was cut to pieces, when Job scraped off the foul overflow of his ulcer with great composure, and when he calmly called the little creatures bursting out of it back into the same hollows and feeding places of his reopened flesh!
comments.author: Tertullian

comments.capsule: Job scrapes his sores with a potsherd in helpless desolation and sits outside the city on the ashes, changed from his former prosperity.
comments.comment: 'And he took a potsherd, that he might scrape the sores' (Job 2:8). The verse signifies the wilderness and his helplessness, because no one was present with him while he was nursing, but also because the wife was absent due to her haste toward work, … To such an extent was his body dissolved, so as to be reduced to sores. … 'And he sat on the ashes outside the city' (Job 2:8). It is probable that in those cities they did not permit one having such a body to live. Therefore, outside the city on the ashes he sat, and he perceives the continuous change, from what prosperity and enjoyment he has changed into what kind of wickedness under the tempter, so as to be a stranger and to sit on the ashes …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the details of the potsherd and the ashes.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil attacks when long endurance has weakened a man and hope is fading, so a wife's advice is to be weighed by what it says, not by who gives it.
comments.comment: "After time had advanced, his wife said to him." See the craft: attack comes when long endurance has already weakened strength. Weakness is double — the bearer grows weaker by length of time, and hope is more nearly abandoned. Do not look first at the fact that she is a wife, but at what she advises. People now should weigh the manner of counsel, not the dignity of the person. A wife is to help, not to trip.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the wife speaks now and how to weigh her counsel.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil saves his strongest device for last and speaks through the woman as once through Eve, since words might win where events could not.
comments.comment: She asks, "Until when will you endure?" The devil saves the strongest device for last. "Would that you had taken her too! Would that you had buried her with the children!" Some say the words are not even hers, but the adversary speaking through her shape — unless calamity truly overturned her. Likely this was not the first counsel; she had heard harder things often. Diabolic deceit remembers Eve: what brought down the first human may prevail here too. Wretched fool — Eve found one weaker than the belly and sowed her venom; this man you see philosophizing and mastering nature itself. Loss of goods, untimely death of children, unconsolable bodily torment, and long time did not bend him. Will words master the one events could not catch? Why loosen the athlete’s hands?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: As a third trial the devil uses the wife, hoping to deceive Job through her as he deceived Adam through Eve.
comments.comment: [The devil's plan:] besides the immoderate affliction of the body, a third thing he devises for him: the conversation of the wife; perhaps through her he might have deceived Job, just as through Eve he might have deceived Adam. For having passed a long time, such that even he is not able to shake the athlete, the woman brings forward the matter of brevity, perhaps remembering the suffering, to rid him of it, if he should speak a word to the Lord irrationally.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Spoken in ignorance, the words about the memorial vanishing from the earth are true in another sense, since God removes the earthly remembrance of sinners so that, benefited, they may be written in heaven.
comments.comment: And it also appears through: 'Behold, I will make your remembrance depart from the earth', as if: you shall have no hope of ever coming to it for the enjoyment of good things, which he alone considered to be good, being irrational concerning the good according to truth. And being ignorant, he spoke a word otherwise true; for the remembrance of those who despised the heavenly human life is not earthly. For the Scripture confirms this, the Psalmist says: 'The face of the Lord upon those doing evil, to destroy from the earth the remembrance of them' (Psalm 34:16). For when some have sinned and are saying 'God is not in the heart' (Psalm 14:1), God brings hardship upon them, so that after they have been benefited, their remembrance may be destroyed from the earth and 'they may be written in heaven' (Luke 10:20), having been transformed into virtue.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wife does not openly say 'Blaspheme', since evil advisers dare not offer counsel uncovered.
comments.comment: [Job's wife:] she brings the shameless counsel. She does not even say openly, "Blaspheme." Evil advisers dare not introduce counsel uncovered. What are you saying, woman? One ought to propitiate and reconcile — and you advise provocation? If God did these things, entreat him; do not blaspheme.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil turns the wife's mind to blasphemy, and Job, grieved by her words more than by any earlier loss, rebukes her and bids her weigh the good against the bad, since no life is wholly blessed.
comments.comment:
So the enemy, having nothing left to do, returned to the memory of his ancient plot. He dragged down the woman's mind into an impious and blasphemous resolve, and through her he tried to shake the athlete. She, despairing at the long duration, stood before the righteous man, bent down, striking her hands together at what she saw, reproaching him for the fruits of his devotion. She recounted the old prosperity of their household and pointed to the present evils—what a life he had received from what circumstances, and what reward he had received from the Master for his many sacrifices. She kept saying words worthy of women's faintheartedness, but capable of troubling any man and overturning even a noble mind: 'I wander about as a vagabond and a menial servant. I who was a queen am a slave, and I am forced to look to the hands of my own household servants. I who once fed many am now glad just to be fed from what belongs to others.' And she said that it would be good and useful to use impious words and cut himself off from the earth, sharpening the sword of the Creator's wrath, or, by enduring the horrors, to prolong the labor of the contest for himself and the woman who lived with him.

But he was grieved by these words as by none of his earlier evils. His gaze filled with anger, and he turned to the woman as if to an enemy. What does he say? 'Why have you spoken like one of the foolish women? Put away your counsel, woman. How long will you insult the life we share by what you say? You have misrepresented my conduct in a way I never wished. You have slandered my life by what you have spoken. I now consider myself half guilty of impiety, since marriage made the two of us one body, and you have fallen into blasphemy. If we received good things from the Lord's hand, shall we not endure the bad?' (Job 2:10).

Remember the good things that came to you before. Weigh the better things against the worse. No human being's life is entirely blessed.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on Not Clinging to Worldly Things

comments.capsule: Job shows patience by calling her words foolish, understanding that they came from the devil's suggestion, as the first woman's did.
comments.comment: His patience of soul is shown in this, in not remaining under such pains and the word brought forward unsuitably by the woman, but also saying: 'You have spoken like one of the foolish women.' And looking intently, he has said this, understanding from her reproaches, the holy man that she had brought these things forward by a diabolical suggestion, and being wise, he knew that the first woman having been struck by the devil's suggestion had become the cause of Adam's transgression.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Job answers his wife and why.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Things called good or bad are so by how one uses them, not by nature, and wealth or affliction each showed some men foolish and others steadfast, as Job was.
comments.comment:
Because of this, He [Job] says: 'Just as one of the foolish women you spoke.' Then, having placed a reasoning before her that is appropriate, He brings it: 'If we received the good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure the bad?' For the same understanding is toward the pleasant things of the indifferent, not to be overcome, and toward the burdensome, not to be cast down.

For he who is expert regarding things knows that the things called good are not such by their own nature, but follow the opinion of the user; just as also the bad—the harmful, I say—are not bad in themselves, but the use occurring in them is what they are. For many, after wealth, both the foolish and the excellent appeared, like Abraham and those like him, and Pharaoh and those near him. When much affliction came again, some yielded, but some remained steadfast in their reasoning, of whom are the blessed Job and Lazarus, as having received these things from a physician, through incisions and cauterizations, for the sake of salvation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's saying that we must take bad things as we take good, in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The added words 'with his lips' show that the pain of Job's whole body strained his courage even to an unspoken thought, yet he did not give way in word or deed.
comments.comment:
This is said a second time; first, when the first affliction came, and second, now. And then it was said: "In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin against the Lord" (Job 2:10), but now: "In all these things that happened to him, Job did not sin with his lips against the Lord" (Job 2:10).

Some indeed think there is no difference between saying "not to have sinned with the lips" and "not to have sinned before the Lord," but others perceive them thus: that regarding the removal of what was present and the death of the children, it was said once, "Job did not sin against the Lord," neither in word nor in thought; but here, the "with the lips" lies as an addition, saying, as perhaps some slight variation occurred—for this is lesser—but rather the movement of human weakness, being compelled by the great pain of the whole body.

The written spirit therefore says, in order to show the endurance of the pain and his courage, that even though his courage was being compelled even to an inaudible thought, he was not shaken so as to do anything from faint-heartedness or smallness of mind, or to speak.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Struck from every side Job stood firmer, like a pilot who keeps his skill in storm and calm, neither puffed up by wealth nor crushed by poverty.
comments.comment: "If we received good things from the Lord’s hand, shall we not also bear the bad?" Struck from every side, the blessed man stood more securely. Countless arrows did not make him yield; he emptied the devil’s quiver and did not fall. Like an excellent pilot he was not sunk when the sea raged, and not careless when it was calm; in both seasons he kept the same skill. Wealth did not puff him up, poverty did not crush him; fair weather did not leave him slack, and nearly total ruin did not shake his courage. Let rich and poor hear: the story helps both prosperity and calamity. Handling both weapons, the contestant of piety — crown-bearer of the inhabited world — raised a trophy in each and met every kind of demonic war.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Every human calamity emptied itself on Job together and in excess, and he rose above all of it.
comments.comment: As a soldier trained for night fighting, walls, land, sea, bow, spear, sling, and javelin conquers everywhere, so this noble man bore every trial with courage: poverty, hunger, disease, pain, loss of children, friends, enemies, wife, and servants. No human calamity failed to empty itself into that body; still he rose above every net and higher than the devil’s reeds. More marvelous still: everything came at once, in excess, under one blow — not little by little. Other people rarely meet all together. Poverty may leave health; poverty and disease may still leave a consoling wife as a harbor; if not such a wife, still not one advising ruin; if children die, not all at once; if at once, not by such a death; if by such a death, still comforting friends; if not comforters, still not insulting; if insulting, still not servants reproaching and spitting in the face; if that, still not such disease on a dunghill without shelter or a hand stretched out. Job endured all of it.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's question means that we must not force the Master to give us the same things forever, but gladly receive whatever his wisdom arranges.
comments.comment: To do well at every moment belongs to God alone. But if you are pained by what is present, comfort yourself from what has gone before. Now you weep, but you laughed before; now you are poor, but you were rich before. You drank the clear stream of life, and now that you drink this muddy one, endure it. Even the currents of rivers do not appear pure throughout. And a river, as you know, is our life, flowing without pause and filled with wave upon wave. Part of it has already flowed past, part is still moving; part has just now sprung from its springs, and part is still to come; and we all hasten toward the common sea of death. “If we received good things from the Lord’s hand, shall we not endure the bad things?” (Job 2:10). Do we force the judge to supply us with the same kind of things forever? Do we teach the Master how our life ought to be conducted? He himself holds authority over his own verdicts. He orders our affairs as he wills. He is wise, and he measures out what is beneficial to his servants. Do not meddle with the Master’s judgment. Only love what is arranged by his wisdom. Whatever he gives you, receive it with pleasure.
comments.selected_reason: Gives the sense of Job's reply in plain words.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homily on Not Clinging to Worldly Things

comments.capsule: Bodily and external things that serve life according to nature are loosely called goods and those that work against it evils, as when Job asks his wife whether we shall not endure evil.
comments.comment: But we may also find bodily and external things called goods and evils in a looser sense: those that contribute to life according to nature are regarded as goods, and those that work against it as evils. It is in this sense that Job says to his wife: “If we have received good things from the hand of the Lord, shall we not endure evil things?” (Job 2:10). Now in the divine Scriptures we find, in one place, God saying in his own person, “I am he who makes peace and creates evils” (Isaiah 45:7), and in another place, again about him, “that evils came down from the Lord upon the gates of Jerusalem, the noise of chariots and horsemen” (Micah 1:12–13). These texts have troubled many who read Scripture, since they cannot discern what Scripture means by goods and evils.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's 'evil' means the plague and his children's death, and the 'good things' of men are not truly good.
comments.comment: And even if they are good things for men, they are not truly good. … For when Job says: 'If we have received good things from the Lord, shall we not also receive evil?' (Job 2:10), he says 'evil' regarding the plague, the most pitiable death of children, and other things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends, who were kings, came each from his own country out of sympathy, and the account teaches us not to give up love and brotherly affection when changes fall on us.
comments.comment:
When his three friends heard of all the evils that had come upon him, each one came to him from his own country: Eliphaz the Temanite king, Bildad the Shuhite tyrant, and Zophar the Naamathite king (Job 2:11-13). It is most surprising if these things happen to men of great reputation. Therefore, since Job was among the most glorious because of wealth and virtue, the friends, having heard of the severity of the things that had happened, came not from one place, but each from his own country, moved by sympathy, and since these were kings, they did not overstep the man undergoing such a change.

As for 'tyrant,' he says either as a parallel to king—since the name was not well known in that time—or to denote a difference in rank from a king. This is also in Proverbs: 'Through me kings reign, and tyrants decree justice' (Prov 8:15). And these who came to him were led by no other cause. The statement is useful for sympathy, so that we might not, because of the changes that fall upon us, abandon the things of love and brotherly affection.
comments.selected_reason: Says who the friends were and why they came.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends came late because they had to confirm the unbelievable report and set their kingdoms in order, and the delay prolonged Job's contest so that God could declare him just.
comments.comment: They waited to confirm the report through more witnesses, or to send and see if it was true; time was spent that way. Once they knew the truth, as kings about to travel they first had to set their houses in order and appoint deputies. That occupied them and delayed them. Had they not been deeply beloved and righteous, they would not have left countries and kingdoms to visit, but would have sent others. One may also see a divine arrangement in the delay: since the friends’ dialogue ends the whole contest when God speaks, recovers, and crowns the righteous man, the friends’ lateness stretches the illness so that, contending more, he may be declared more justly by God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the friends came late.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The friends' coming was a friendly presence, and each of their names carries a meaning.
comments.comment: "Each came from his own country: Eliphaz king of the Temanites, Baldad tyrant of the Saucheans, Sophar king of the Minaeans." Friendly presence; friendly exhortation. … Eliphaz — "God scattered me," or "contempt of my God"; Teman — their eclipse; Sophar — watcher or contempt; Baldad — aging and glorious; Saucheans — idle talk.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They came together to comfort and visit him, since he was wounded in body and robbed of property and children, and when they saw him from afar they did not recognize him and wept.
comments.comment: 'And they came to him unanimously to comfort and visit him' (Job 42:11). They had come to do both, since it happened that they suffered both; for he was deprived of property and children, and his whole body was held by the wound. They came to him 'unanimously,' either with much readiness or because, having their houses plundered, they had agreed together to come to him for the purpose of comforting; for the evils had not ceased but were already active. 'And seeing him from afar, they did not recognize him, and having cried out with a loud voice, they wept, …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The seven days and nights are said by common custom, not as unbroken sitting: the friends sat by him most of each day and came back early, as true friends do.
comments.comment: "They came to him with one mind to comfort and visit him." Symmachus: they arranged together to sympathize and comfort. Another stretch of time passed while they messaged one another and set a common arrival. "They sprinkled earth on their heads." "They sat beside him seven days and seven nights." Scripture does not mean continuous day-from-dawn and night-from-dusk without break. They sat the greater part of the day, withdrew for necessary needs, returned late into the night, left again, and rose early to him — the mark of genuine friends. Scripture speaks by common custom, as when Jacob served fourteen years burned by day heat and night frost without meaning he never entered a roof.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the seven days and seven nights mean.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The scene teaches two things, Job's courage when others were discouraged and the friends' sympathy in sitting with him, so we should not be stingy with patience toward the weak.
comments.comment: They sat with him seven days and seven nights (Job 2:13). In this, two things are taught by what has been set forth: the courage of the blessed one—while others were discouraged due to the immeasurable nature of what had happened to him—and the sympathy of the friends, who not only arrived, but having seen, did not recognize him because of his sickness, which had also altered his facial features; and having cried out with a great voice, they wept, each tearing his own clothing and scattering dust, which altogether, as it is said, demonstrates both the courage of the holy one and the sympathy of these. … And it is sympathetic that they should participate with him seven days and seven nights. Therefore, one should not be stingy with patience toward the weak and helpless ones
comments.selected_reason: Says what the scene teaches about Job and his friends.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends were silenced by the greatness of the evil, and perhaps by respect for a wise man.
comments.comment: Those who had come for consolation were silenced by the magnitude of what had happened. … And it is likely that, having a certain opinion of him as a wise man, they chose a respectful silence, not daring to bring forward a word before him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the friends said nothing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job opens his mouth only after the great trophy and his sufferings, with temperance and calm, so his words are worth hunting for their benefit.
comments.comment: Toward understanding he [Job] speaks mysteries; he philosophizes about what has already happened and assures what is coming — the way holy prophets always speak. … "After this Job opened his mouth." When a righteous man opens his mouth, do not attend casually; hunt the benefit in the words. Such sayings are always full of help, and a righteous mouth publishes hidden treasures. So the vessel of election writes, "My mouth has opened toward you, Corinthians," and of the Lord it is written that "opening his mouth he taught." The one witnessed to open a mouth is first taught the measures of silence. Job opens his mouth after the great trophy and those sufferings — not letting the tongue outrun devout prudence under bodily pain, but showing temperance in the voices. The witness that he opened his mouth also shows the soul’s calm and the seemliness of the words.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Scripture notes that Job 'opened his mouth' only after long silence.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job feels pain, for virtue is not numbness, yet he never blasphemes as the devil hoped but speaks well and gives thanks.
comments.comment: … the righteous man feels pain — no one denies it. Virtue is not numbness, but philosophy inside the passions. In appearance he is stung sharply in the flesh; in thought, as a God-loving man, he sees others scandalized at such sufferings, as if God’s glory were torn if the righteous endure this. … At the loss of goods and the sudden death of the children we heard his thanksgiving, how he schooled the wife who thought unseemly things of the Master, and how no human accident shook him. When righteous, sympathetic friends arrived, he judged it time — seeing their endurance and love — to publish the soul’s pains in a history without danger. The devil’s one aim was to make the righteous blaspheme God. Job nowhere does that; he rather speaks well and sends up thanks. He curses the day of birth, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains that Job's complaint is real pain without blasphemy.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job curses not the day as a stretch of time but the things that happen in it, since Scripture calls events 'the day'.
comments.comment: The wise man is not a babbler, nor does he bring forth by his tongue what is not possible to become. He curses not the day, which is a chronological interval, but the things happening in it. For by custom, in the Scripture, the things happening are called the day. This the Psalmist teaches, saying: "In a evil day the Lord will deliver him" (Psalm 41:1), not calling the evil day a chronological interval, but the evil things happening in them; and what is said by Paul: "for the days are evil" (Ephesians 5:16), refers to the mind. Thus, one might say the day is good for some because of what happens, and bad for others.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job means by cursing his day.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job calls the day of his birth worthy of a curse on behalf of the whole race, as an affectionate physician rightly curses the disorder.
comments.comment: Therefore, the evils happening for this cause, Job says they are a painful and worthy-of-curse day: 'Let the day perish in which I was born' (Job 3:3). And he says this on behalf of all the race. … Just as the affectionate physician will appropriately curse the disorder after having fallen from many's lawlessness, so the blessed one, healing, because these things do not happen arbitrarily, but according to a certain rhythm and a following intended so that the fallen might be benefited, curses the day of the fall of men, sharing the word.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's 'let the day perish' is a curse on the genesis, the coming into being, not on the day itself, which has already passed.
comments.comment: But how then does Job speak? (Job 3:3) If I say: 'Let the day perish in which I was born,' let the genesis perish; for I have come from better things to worse; for it is profitable for me that the evil should perish. As if Jeremiah speaks concerning the people of the Hebrews—and each of the captured Hebrews will say—'Let the day of captivity perish,' he does not say this: 'let there be no more captivity.' 'Let there be no more,' he says, 'that day, it has passed away'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The words about gloom and darkness are not curses but prayers that evils cease and that the cause of the fall be unknown.
comments.comment: 'Let a gloom fall upon it, let that day and night be cursed, and let darkness carry it away.' These things are not to be considered curses, but prayers for the cessation of the occurrence of evils. For according to what has been previously explained, it is right to pray that the cause of the fall and the way of this be unknown, 'so that there may not be prosperity in an evil man.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's words are a prayer, not a curse, that no one should fall into the state of human weakness and take pleasure in it.
comments.comment:
Being a fellow-laborer, the saint prays that no one should fall and be delighted or find pleasure in this. For often, seeing someone hastening toward evil deeds, we pray, saying: 'May he not happen to be the one striving.' With this same mind, the saint, while praying, sings, not cursing: 'Let the deceitful lips that speak lawlessness against the righteous with pride be made silent, and let them be brought to nothing' (Psalm 31:18). And for the deceitful lips to become silent, what would it be other than to cease speaking unjustly, once the speaker recognizes how improper such a thing is?

And he, therefore, prays that no one might be so perverted as to think that it is a matter of indifference or a source of joy to fall into the state that leads to human weakness. The Savior himself says: 'It would have been good for him if that man had not been born' (Matt 26:24), and in Ecclesiastes it is shown: 'Better is the one than these two, who has not yet become' (Eccl 4:3). But for the one not yet born, since the birth is clearly shown to be a good thing if it happens, it does not happen without foundation.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'He who is about to' points to the incarnation: the devil was to be destroyed not by naked divinity but through the temple of the Word born from the seed of the one he deceived.
comments.comment:
'But he will curse it, the one who curses that day, he who is about to grasp the great worm' (Job 3:8). … Since the devil has been called the cause of the fall of men, he brings a prayer for this, in order that it might be loosed, following the prophecy, as 'the devil, who has the power of death, shall be destroyed' (Hebrews 2:14); for this was foretold to the purity of the soul moved by the Holy Spirit, as also authority will be given to the saints 'to tread upon serpents and scorpions and over all the power of the enemy' (Luke 10:19), so that others, rising up from these, might be delivered from the clinging sin as they hear of progressing in virtue: 'he shall tread upon the shield and the basilisk and shall trample the lion and the dragon' (Psalm 91:13), who is the devil. For it is said concerning him: 'our adversary the devil, as a lion, walks seeking someone to devour' (1 Peter 5:8), and again: 'having crushed the heads of the dragon' (Psalm 74:13).

And well is 'he who is about to' said, signifying that according to the incarnation. For it was not fitting to destroy the devil by naked divinity, but through this temple of the Word having come to be, who was born from the seed of the one deceived and harmed by the devil. For it was a boast for him to have existed having seized him by naked divinity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The devil's many names mark the different ways he works evil, not his essence.
comments.comment: But the various names of the devil signify his various energies, not his essence. For devil, and adversary, and evil, and lion, and dragon, and serpent, and sea monster, are called because of the manner of his evil working in different ways, which is a subversion of the Manichaean dogma.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job knew the Savior was coming, as his words on the great whale show.
comments.comment: Do not marvel if the calf alludes to the Savior; for Job was not unaware of the coming of the Savior; for concerning Him he said: "he who is about to grasp the great whale" (Job 3:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'He who is about to grasp the great whale' is the Savior, who gives men another birth, 'from water and spirit', called regeneration and also the resurrection.
comments.comment: Then he says: 'May he who is about to grasp the great whale curse it' (Job 3:8). Why did he not say: 'He who made the sun, he who constructed the cosmos,' but 'he who is about to grasp the great whale'? For the Savior has come and, 'having grasped the great whale,' described the genesis of humans, so as to give them another genesis, the 'from water and spirit' (John 3:5), which is principally called regeneration. And regeneration is genesis upon genesis, just as 'repetition' is song upon song. And he called the resurrection of the dead regeneration; for he says to the disciples: 'You also will sit in the regeneration on twelve thrones' (Matthew 19:28), instead of 'in the resurrection, in the age to come'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: It is better not to have begun this life's path, since toil weighs on the righteous eye that sees many led astray by the works of the wicked.
comments.comment: For it is blessed to be outside of this life. To those who know, Jesus says: 'You are no longer of this world, but I have chosen you' (John 15:19). Therefore, it is better not to have even begun the path of such a way, even if it happens through divine economy. For it is good if no one in health needs a physician. … 'For he would have removed toil from my eyes' (Job 3:10). This indicates not only the one suffering and the toil surrounding him, but also that he saw many being led astray; for the eye of the righteous is weighed down by works being performed by the wicked. And the toil that encroaches upon life is not small.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's wish not to have been born in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's questions about God's judgments come not from ignorance but so that others may learn, as with Habakkuk and Jeremiah, who ask why the wicked prosper and the righteous suffer.
comments.comment:
But even Habakkuk allows such a voice, saying: 'Why have you shown me troubles and pains, to make me see violence and unrighteousness?' (Habakkuk 1:2-3). 'Why did I not end in the womb, come out from the stomach and not immediately perish? Why did my knees meet, why did I suck breasts?' He avoids the economy intended for the benefit of others, as it seems, according to Jonah, to demand the teaching of God's judgments, which is a private matter of the righteous, not being completely ignorant, but so that others may learn this kind of speech being personified. For Jeremiah approaches thus: 'You are righteous, Lord, but I will speak judgments to you' (Jeremiah 12:1), which is indicative of knowing, concerning which he asks: 'Why does the way of the ungodly prosper?' (Jeremiah 12:1).

The judgment of God in reality receives much variety: the unrighteous being prospered, and the righteous being distressed and partaking of filth, as Jeremiah himself, being holy and having been sanctified from the womb, suffered so many things as to be cast into a pit of mire. But also Lazarus and the rich man—the one suffering evil, the other living with much ease—bring forth the precision of God's secret judgments (Luke 16:19-31). And this 'prospering' is called so as toward the glory of the many. Therefore, the saint is not vain-speaking, but asks so that it brings about the others learning such things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's questions show that the saints come into life not as those responsible for faults but as carrying out God's plan, without which he would have rested.
comments.comment:
'Why then did I not finish in the womb?' (Job 3:11). For the saints, in reverence, entreat that they not grasp the benefit of the weaker ones. Because of this, he also says the following: 'And from the stomach I came out and was not immediately lost' (Job 3:11); likewise also: 'Why did my knees meet me? Why did I suck breasts?' (Job 3:12). For the holy one willed that disease should not happen to the rational ones, so that the pure might not come through them in a medicinal way.

And also good is: 'Why did my knees meet me?', which indicates a journey. For with others, because of their own faults, life followed here, but with the saints, they met not as those responsible, but as those executing an economy [God's plan of salvation]. 'Now, having slept, I have rested, but having awoken, I have not ceased with kings and counselors of the earth' (Job 3:13, 29:25).

For if, he says, such a sequence and order had not occurred as that which led me to this state through those needing treatment—that is, if I had happened to finish in the womb, not coming out from the stomach and being immediately cut off, and not having met knees nor sucked breasts—it would be, if not through the providential economy administered through us, 'now having slept, I have rested', which is: having ceased my course in that life of the divine and heavenly rational ones.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saint, no lover of war, did not want the company of kings proud upon swords, since his struggle is against spiritual forces and not against blood and flesh.
comments.comment: [On the kings and counselors:] taking for ourselves kings in high positions and counselors of a lower rank, over whom the kings rule. Such an analogy is contained in the parable in the Gospels: "become more than ten cities or five." "who were proud upon swords." The saint, not being a lover of war, did not want to have his social intercourse with such kings readily available, who, being ready to fight, consider such social intercourses to be good; but knowing "that our struggle is not against blood and flesh" (Ephesians 6:12) according to the apostle, "but against principalities, against powers, against the rulers of the darkness of this world, against the spiritual forces of wickedness," against whom those living well fight, having armed themselves with the salvation "panoply," he wanted to have his social intercourse without being provoked by human generation. … Being discerning, the saint knows and does not readily recognize that even the adversary often "is transformed into an angel of light" (2 Corinthians 11:14). These, however, are also men, not preferring arrogance, but rejoicing in the victory over the adversaries and "rejoicing in God" (2 Corinthians 6:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job, who lost all his wealth bravely, would not seek the company of rulers adorned with wealth; spiritually their 'much gold' signifies a pure mind approaching with the light of knowledge.
comments.comment: "Or with rulers, of whom there is much gold, who filled their houses with silver" (Job 3:15). Having the same mind and what has now been set forth, let us receive it familiarly with the person of the saint. For not being a lover of silver or a flatterer, it did not seem right for him to spend time with the rich, he who bravely brought about the loss of all possessions and wealth and did not accept riches, being without following friends and having a free intention and an unshakable word; how would he want to have his social intercourse with such rulers and kings, who happened to be adorned with wealth? To some, appearing as a good wealth, the wonderful Paul writes: "You have already become rich; you have reigned without us; and would that you had reigned, so that we might also reign with you" (1 Corinthians 4:8). For they have possessed much gold, which indicates a pure mind, pure ones, approaching clearly with the light of knowledge.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Why some do not reach life or die at birth is a question for the philosopher, who treats it as the just ordering of God, and Job praises the better state not without anxiety.
comments.comment: For in truth, such a thing would not be outside of perplexity and seeking, regarding those not reaching unto life, and those dying immediately after birth, which the philosopher will investigate not as if these things happen by chance, but as being the just and good of God, the God of all things, governing all things by word and order and measure and weight. The saint himself knows the judgment and does not say this without anxiety, but praises the better state and being persuaded that this is to be preferred.
