comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'There' refers to the other world, as in Job's 'naked I will depart there'.
comments.comment: 'There the ungodly burned up a fury of wrath' (Job 3:17). By saying 'there,' he refers to the other world from this one, as in: 'Naked I came from my mother's womb, naked I will depart there' (Job 1:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'there' in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints, having struggled in the body, rest eternally with the angels, which shows that souls are eternal, though 'eternal' is said in several senses.
comments.comment:
… God forewarns through His economy and has given laws to each to prevent sinning, so that while passing through this life, one might think heavenly things and desire a similar life there, so that having worn out the body, one might have a rest as one who has become a combatant against the habit of wickedness. For this is what is meant by: 'There the combatants rested from the body' (Job 3:17).

For the saints, having been pleased, through many tribulations on earth—of which they become combatants in body and not in mind—have a rest with the angels, having attained it eternally. And if those are eternal, and their rest is communal, it is evident that the souls too are eternal; for they are immortal and, having despised the temporal, possess the eternal.

It should be noted that 'eternal' is spoken of in several ways; it also signifies the without-beginning and the without-end, as in: 'God is eternal.' For God is called eternal because His existence has neither beginning nor end. And something else is eternal, as it is said: 'The things not seen are eternal' (2 Corinthians 4:18). For these are not eternal as God is, but because they remain always without falling away. And differently is the eternal, when it is measured against the present, as it is said: 'The sons of this age are wiser in their own generation' (Luke 16:8). And the time extending the life of a man is also called an age.

Regarding the Hebrew who was unwilling to be set free in the seventh year, it is said: 'He shall be a servant for an age' (Ex 21:6). For no human being remains a servant at all through death. According to this, Paul also writes: 'If meat makes my brother stumble, I will never eat meat for an age' (1 Corinthians 8:13), instead of 'through life.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: There no tax-collector is heard, but this age is full of tribute that sinners pay to the adversary.
comments.comment: 'They did not hear the voice of a tax-collector.' For this age is filled with tribute, in which one has come here for the sake of the economy. For there are many who, having come under the yoke of sin, pay taxes and dues to the adversary …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In this life small and great, slave and free differ, but in the coming age works decide, and the servant of God finds shade and rest, having escaped the heat of sin.
comments.comment: It is to be expected also differently; in this present life, a difference has been established between the small and the great and the slave, bringing greed into variety. But in the coming age, Paul says, 'there is neither male' 'nor female, there is neither slave nor free' (Galatians 3:28). Similarly he would say, as neither rich nor poor, but the demonstration of works, by which the one in this living will be considered great and free there, though small or a slave. … And the servant who serves God intellectually is there, obtaining shade and rest, having escaped the heat of life: 'a wise son was saved from the heat' (Proverbs 10:5), not being consumed by the heat, according to those in the parable who did not receive the seed into depth and fell by the flame of sin. This promise is said to David in the Psalms: 'the sun shall not strike you by day, nor the moon by night' (Ps 121:6), which according to the literal sense we do not find. For he himself, being righteous, was labored upon by the heat of the sensible, but was unlabored upon by the heat of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse about small and great, slave and master.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The holy teacher examines the hidden judgment of providence for his hearers, so that they are not displeased at what happens or think it accidental or fated.
comments.comment:
… 'Why then is light given to those in bitterness, and life to souls in pain? Who are partakers of death and do not find treasures by digging, but become content if they happen upon them' (Job 3:20).

The hidden and not manifest to all, the judgment of providence, the holy teacher examines for the sake of those hearing, so that first they may not be displeased with the things happening, and later, knowing that it comes from God, they may not consider the things happening to be either accidental or caused by fate.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job asks why light is given to those in bitterness.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: In asking why light is given to those in bitterness, Job instructs us to endure and to receive from God the teaching about sufferings.
comments.comment: Regarding various sufferings, such as being in poverty, or passing from wealth into poverty in different ways, or being in various crises and others in some evil, and not only experiencing such bad things but also important ones, examining the judgment, he asks saying: 'For why is light given to those in bitterness?' (Job 36:30). For if he knows, but indeed wishes us to be enduring, he instructs, as it is fitting to receive the teaching of these things from God. And regarding those being embittered because of the injustices of men, he says: 'For why is light given to those in bitterness?' (Job 36:30). Such a thing even Jeremiah, alluding to it, said: 'I sat alone, because I was filled with bitterness' (Jeremiah 15:17). And he fell into bitterness because he saw the irregularities and injustices concerning men. And these same ones also grieve.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Longing to depart and be with Christ is like digging for treasure: the saints labor in hope of the crown and are no lovers of life, since they know divine rewards await.
comments.comment:
[Paul:] And he also shares in death, saying: 'It is better to depart and be with Christ' (Philippians 1:23), just as 'digging up a treasure' … is the desire for this, as one of the saints says: 'Woe, that my sojourning has been made long' (Psalm 120:5), … Therefore, not even being lovers of life are they ready to die, as the blessed Paul says: 'Daily I die' (1 Corinthians 15:31). For because of this readiness he wrote thus. For a lover of life would not say this. For the saints know that if they come out of this life, they will receive the divine rewards.

Therefore, just as they are 'digging up a treasure' … it happens even if the digging is done with toil. Just as also the saints themselves through much toil look forward to entering the kingdom—but hope deafens the toil—so also those contending in the struggle suffer much, looking toward the crown.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Death is a rest' is said of a man of valor, who is ready for death and is released on departing from the pain and sorrow that the decree on Adam shut him in.
comments.comment:
If this is so, how are the saints not without joy, encountering the end of this life, after which the kingdom of heaven shall receive it? 'Death is a rest to a man; for God has shut up the door against him' (Wis 1:15; Ps 108:7). If anyone wished to take this according to what is at hand, he might say, that for those in circumstance and in pains death is a rest, since 'God has shut up the door against him' (Ps 108:7), dismissing the circumstances. But he who follows with the first thought will have nothing to complain about, saying, as if not all those who end in rest become so by receiving the bad blows.

And this should also be noted, that he did not say: 'death to a man,' but 'to a man of valor'; for he who has courage and is in virtue is unshakeable toward death, having himself most ready for it and singing: 'My heart is ready, O God, my heart is ready' (Ps 57:7). And this same shall have rest, receiving the promises directed toward him. And moreover, he shall have rest while suffering, because that which 'God has shut up against him' (Job 3:23) through the common decree of that which is said concerning Adam, 'Dust you are and to dust you shall return' (Gen 3:19), is released by 'departing' from him 'pain and sorrow and sighing' (Isaiah 35:10) …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Where others in luxury say 'Let us eat and drink', the holy man sighs before his food from human weakness and longing for the Savior's table.
comments.comment: Let us see from the beginning the things set forth: 'For before my food a sigh comes to me' (Job 3:24), which is instructive, that others, having lived a life of luxury, and finding only pleasure and enjoyment and caring for nothing else through their works, cry out to themselves: 'Let us eat and drink; for tomorrow we die' (Isaiah 22:13); but the holy man, also according to the blessed Paul saying: 'Who is weak and does not faint? Who is scandalized and am I not burned?' (2 Corinthians 11:29), approaches sensory food not without a sigh because of human weakness and not for the sake of pleasure, but understanding the pure and incorporeal life and that table which the Savior promised to his own disciples, saying: 'That you may eat and drink at my table in the kingdom' (Luke 22:30) of the heavens, sighs; even while receiving this, he sings in his mind: 'My soul longs and even faints for the courts of the Lord' (Psalm 84:2).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job sighs before eating.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's fear is neither the passionate nor the perfect kind but a middle one, like Paul's fear for others' salvation, for even a perfect man knows he may lapse while he lives.
comments.comment:
"For before my food a sigh comes to me, and I weep, being seized by fear. For the fear which I cared for has come to me, and which I was afraid would meet me." Fear does not always signify the passionate, nor the refined and perfect, but also a middle kind, concerning which neither the passionate nor the refined occurs, but as one might say, one of these things occurs either for the benefit of others or due to a fall

For if the blessed Paul says: 'I fear, lest as the serpent deceived Eve' (2 Cor 11:3), he does not have the fear passionately, nor is the perfect and pure signified in this, even if the wise Paul had it, but rather a care for the salvation of others. … And since the holy man, even if he be perfect, knows that it is possible for a man to fall into a lapse as long as he is in life, he leads into: 'And I weep, being seized by fear.' And because the mind is strengthened, the weeping in the pains is according to the saying: 'I shall wash my bed every night, with my tears my couch' (Ps 6:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints prepare for coming temptations without cowardice, fearing for themselves as they have preached to others, as a steady pilot does not wish to be tried by a storm.
comments.comment:
Nor are the saints any less anxious because of approaching temptations, not giving themselves over to negligence, but preparing themselves for these, fearing lest they, having preached to others, themselves become unproven. And they do not avoid the stumbles. They are not without reason ready for preparation. For this reason, the blessed one himself always remains, holding back the uprisings from the devil. He wished not to be in circumstances, since human weakness, as far as it reaches its measure, cannot bear the immeasurability of labors, unless a brave calculation overcomes the weakness. For this reason he says: 'For the fear I thought was not there came upon me, and which I thought would meet me' (Job 3:25).

And he did not say these things by being overwhelmed, but according to the understanding assigned to him. For he had fear, lest he be delayed in his life and be tested by tribulations and circumstances, from which it happens to trip many. Even if they were invincible, they do not want to be drawn into temptations, so that neither the adversary may have more torment through them, nor may he cause them to trip the human weakness as we said; just as a pilot steering the ship straight does not want to be tested by a storm, lest he also fall by a stumble.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job feared what then came upon him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The first friend opens by reminding Job that he had often spoken words to those in trouble, and asks who can weigh the strength of words.
comments.comment: From this very confusion, the first friend brings forward the words, beginning by asserting: 'Not many times has it been spoken to you in toil' (Job 4:2), which indicates that: you yourself also many times used words toward those fallen into tribulations, so that we might hear actively what has happened to you. … 'But who will estimate the strength of words?' (Job 4:2). He himself brought consolation to many, but no one is able to bear your words, which are filled with brevity. And he was saying these things, not knowing the magnitude of the things spoken by him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friend reminds Job that he had encouraged and strengthened many afflicted people, which the words present as sympathy and compassion.
comments.comment:
And he accepts a comparison from him, saying: 'For if you have encouraged many' (Job 4:3), and the following, indicating that: … and doing many things for help and consolation to those being afflicted, as if stretching out a right hand to them, according to that said in Isaiah to the leaders: 'Call upon the hand' (Isaiah 35:3), the words signify sympathy and compassion.

'And to those whose knees are failing, you have provided courage,' providing strength to men persuaded by weakness through the diligence toward them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the words about strengthening the weak hands and failing knees mean.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The trouble that struck Job was made worse because his friends' heavy words brought him discouragement instead of comfort.
comments.comment:
'Now trouble has come upon you and has struck you' (Job 4:5), signifying a severe onset of the situation.

Following what was said there, one should understand that a more severe tribulation than the situation existed: an onslaught brought on by friends through their words. For since the comforter was not present, the matter was even more terrible, and the words being heavy, they provided no small amount of discouragement.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the friends' words added to Job's trouble.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Eliphaz, thinking Job suffers because of sin, treats his fear and hope as folly and his way as wicked, though the Spirit testified that Job gave no folly to God.
comments.comment: 'Is not your fear in folly, and your hope and the wickedness of your way?' (Job 4:6). The inspired Spirit testified to Job that he did not give folly to God, but this accuser having a different impression concerning what had happened to him and calculating that he suffers because of sins, … says: 'Is not your fear in folly'—thinking himself righteous—'and your hope and the wickedness of your way' (Job 4:6). For folly, he says, is also the hoping that one will appear righteous. For such things are not brought upon the righteous. And this very way is called a way of wickedness, because Eliphaz thought throughout that the blessed one suffers because of sin. Thus he also attributed folly to him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Eliphaz calls Job's fear and hope folly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Eliphaz, still thinking Job suffers for sin, argues that no pure man perishes and that those who sow injustice reap thorns by the Lord's command.
comments.comment:
'Remember then, who being pure perished, or where have the true whole-rooted ones perished? In the manner in which I saw those plowing the uneven ground, but those sowing them shall reap thorns for themselves. They shall perish by the command of the Lord, and shall be destroyed by the spirit of His wrath' (Job 4:7-9; 27:18).

Still holding the same mindset, that Job has received experience of the circumstances through sin, he says these things to him, thinking that no human being, being pure in life, fell into tribulations and 'perished whole-rooted' (Job 4:7), alluding to the loss of children and goods and possessions. For this 'perished' means this to him.

He compares the wicked ones, these, and assuming that they fall into injuries—saying something true like 'those sowing injustice reap thorns' (Job 4:8)—he is seen to propose retribution, which he says is sent from God, and regarding this, being rightly disposed, he says: 'They shall perish by the command of the Lord, and shall be destroyed by the spirit of His wrath' (Job 4:9).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the friend's argument that the pure do not perish.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lion, lioness and dragons of the verse stand for arrogant and bold men who are brought down, such as Nebuchadnezzar.
comments.comment:
'the strength of a lion, the voice of a lioness, and the roaring of dragons was extinguished. The ant-lion perished because it had no food, and the cubs of lions left one another' (Job 4:10).

… For he [Eliphaz] … says he sees these as a figure of speech, having suffered a change of many who are arrogant and think greatly of human things, such as Nebuchadnezzar, who came from kingship to the lowest private person.

… 'Lion,' indeed, is how he has been seized by boldness, and 'pride' as if 'having trusted in himself.'

… And the 'lioness' is accepted instead of a profligate manner, which has such a nature. For when she needs food, she does not cry out, lest the beasts who owe food to her should flee.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dragons stand for deceitful, serpent-like men, and the lions' young that leave one another stand for lawless men who turn on each other.
comments.comment:
And he [Eliphaz] has made a memory of the 'dragons', alluding to serpent-like men, as they themselves are subject to change and concerning them change is happening. But these are deceitful and working deception, according to that which is said: 'But I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve through his craftiness, he corrupt your minds' (2 Cor 11:3). And he seems like a 'myrmecoleon' to a boasting and forward man, who because of the unstable and unweighed thing falls down. It is said that this is born from a lion with an ant having come together, not by the life-giving nature, but by another, which indeed has the size of a lion, and so it is called. And the historians say that because the father is flesh-eating and because the mother is poison-producing, he perishes, being unable because of the birth from both to use a single food. As to how it is, let the one encountering it judge.

… 'And the packs of lions left one another', which he said alluding to the lawless and wild men. For indeed the packs, until they are under the mother, are together, but when they become men, they tear one another apart.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Before the judgment and wonders of God, human reasoning is filled with fear and fails, so that the bones tremble and hair and flesh shudder.
comments.comment:
But with fear and a nocturnal sound, a fear fell upon men; and a shudder met me, and trembling, and it greatly shook my bones, and a spirit came upon my face, and my hairs and flesh shuddered. I stood up and did not recognize it; I saw, and there was no form before my eyes, but rather a wind, and I heard a voice (Job 4:13-16).

… For indeed, if human understanding is imposed upon that which is from God, it is filled with fear according to the saying: 'I understood your works and was terrified' (Habakkuk 3:2). And to the same thing, 'sound' is followed by 'nocturnal,' which is much ambiguity, from which it happens to shudder and be afraid for one who has begun to perceive something of God's judgments. Not only that, but also 'the bones' of such a thing are disturbed, which is the power of the soul. For every human reasoning fails before the precise understanding of divine things. This is the same thing Habakkuk, having perceived, says: 'From the voice of prayer, trembling entered into my bones' (Habakkuk 3:16). Therefore, when one, desiring to ascend according to the intellectual faculty, encounters the fearsome divine works as previously stated, there comes a certain type of non-precise understanding, which is indicated by: 'and a spirit came upon my face.' Next also is: 'and my hairs and flesh shuddered.' For a man does not endure a great disturbance if he should dare to impose himself upon the judgment and wonders of God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When a man tries to rise to full understanding of God, the precision of the spoken word escapes him, as Paul's cry about God's unsearchable judgments shows.
comments.comment:
For if a man wishes to rouse himself toward comprehension, the precision of the spoken word flees from him. This is similar to the saying: 'A deep depth, who will find it?' 'But I heard a wind and a voice.' For one using understanding receives certain wonderful things and echoes of the administration from God.

And he cannot grasp it entirely, and most certainly not; for if Paul, speaking in Christ, says: 'O the depth of the riches and the wisdom and the knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments and untraceable his ways' (Rom 11:33), how much more will the one imposing human reasonings be at a loss toward comprehension?
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Eliphaz's question whether a mortal is clean before the Lord would be plausible if affliction always came from sin, and no one is justified before God, not even Abraham, who calls himself dust and ashes.
comments.comment:
Therefore also Eliphaz says regarding the things before him: 'For what? Will a mortal be clean before the Lord or blameless because of his works?' (Job 4:7). This, indeed, would be plausible if he were examining according to his own concept, and it holds the rebuke. For if the one falling into bitter afflictions is so because of sin, no one has been clean, no one has existed apart from bitter things.

… by the Psalms: 'No living thing shall be justified before You' (Psalm 143:2). For he did not say, 'no one is justified,' but rather, 'before You.' For you will find that all are lacking when they are toward God, and they do not possess righteousness in excess.

… But even Abraham, the 'friend of God,' having been humbled, says: 'Since I have begun to speak to my Lord, I am dust and ashes' (Gen 18:27). He does not utterly dishonor himself, but speaks thus from when he began to speak to God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the question 'Shall mortal man be more just than God?' in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The argument runs from the greater to the lesser: if God thought even his angels crooked, he will not spare sinners who live in houses of clay.
comments.comment:
'If he does not believe according to his children, but regarding his angels he thought somewhat crookedly, he struck those dwelling in clay houses, from which we ourselves are from the same clay, in the manner of chaff. And from morning until evening they are no longer.'

He wants to lead the proof from the greater thing and make it certain that every man is under sin, saying that even the children of God are not believed by Him, which is to say: they are not as if they were unshakeable. 'But regarding his angels he thought somewhat crookedly' of those having sinned. And if this is so, much more according to those dwelling in clay houses. Since they have happened to be from the same clay, He will not spare those sinning, sending the punishments to them in the manner of chaff, who also will not endure His judgment many times from morning until evening.

But indeed this is the most complete understanding of the things said; for if anyone were to seek whence this man has this impression concerning the departed angels, through whom he says God thought somewhat crookedly, it would be said to this: that while being a sensible man, he knew that the angels are not naturally good, but are liable to change.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Men dwell in houses of clay because the body is clay, though the soul is not.
comments.comment: And he [Eliphaz] says that men dwell in houses of clay instead of the material things, saying more simply that men were composed of the same clay. For not even the soul is of clay; for the body has been said to be clay.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'houses of clay' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The punishments are shown as slight, for God needed only to breathe on them to destroy those who lacked wisdom.
comments.comment:
'He struck them in the manner of a threshing floor.' This indicates the punishments sent against them as being insignificant. This is shown in Wisdom 11.

… 'Because they were not able to help themselves, they perished. For he breathed into them and they were dried up; they perished because they did not have wisdom.'

… This indeed and what follows seems to signify: 'For he breathed into them and they were dried up.' For it indicates that an overwhelming onslaught was not necessary against them, but only the breathing, which sufficed for their destruction, which he called loss. And from the same failing intellect follows: 'They perished because they did not have wisdom,' unaware that many wise men are afflicted …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The call to cry out and to look for a holy angel is an exhortation toward repentance, though some read it as irony.
comments.comment: 'And call out, if anyone will obey you, or if you see any of the holy angels.' It seems as if he is providing an exhortation leading the holy one [Job] toward repentance, so that having come for the purpose of entreaty, he might happen to find one who assists and listens. And he also presents the phrase, 'or if you see any of the holy angels,' as being aware that they are not holy angels. For if he did not know this, the addition would be superfluous; it is as if he is distinguishing a holy one from a non-such. But those who say he is mocking claim that he says this ironically.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the call to cry out to a holy angel means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He prays that discipline may come on the boastful so that human good things turn away from them, and holds humiliation to be profitable to the proud.
comments.comment:
'Would their children be far from salvation. But they were punished at the doors of Hyssop and there shall be no one being taken out' (Job 5:4). He prays that some discipline may come to the boastful, so that pleasant and human good things may turn away from them, which he called 'salvation'; for such a labor will happen to them. He says, 'they were punished,' meaning they were treated with contempt, being humbled by lesser ones, with no one being a helper.

For humiliation is profitable to the proud, first, so that through such a thing an immoderate evil may be generated, and second, so that they may be disciplined again.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Taken as a proverb, the saying that the righteous receive what the wicked gather points to the wealth of the Jews passing to the nations, though it will not always happen to the wicked.
comments.comment:
'For what those gathered, the righteous shall be given' (Job 5:5). Even if saying this humanly, he would provide a good account, claiming that just as the impious gather, the righteous eat, … And in the Divine Proverbs it is said: 'Wealth of the impious is stored up for the righteous' (Prov 13:22),

… Yet we do not necessarily accept this for the sake of history. Since it has been said proverbially, it follows that the Jews are said to be rich, having both law and prophet, though they did not use them properly. This wealth was transferred to the nations. For the vine 'shall be removed' and 'shall be given to a nation that produces its fruits' (Matt 21:43). 'And they themselves shall not be set apart from evils; their strength shall be siphoned off.' He says that not only do the ungodly grasp at wealth, but they shall never be set apart from evils. And their power itself shall be completely emptied, from the transfer of that which is being siphoned until nothing even liquid remains; consider these things, if he speaks them in a proverbial way.

Know, however, that these things will not necessarily happen to the wicked; for many have received the end of this life in clarity of mind.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Suffering is the common lot of men, who are born to toil, and the saying also serves as an exhortation that no one has suffered anything outside human nature.
comments.comment: 'For toil shall not come forth from the earth, nor shall labor spring up from the mountains, but man is born of toil, and young vultures fly the heights' (Job 5:7; 38:7). The curses which he brought upon the ungodly, or which he wished to show must fall upon them, he says he did reasonably; for it is the lot of men to fall into tribulations and not to be without suffering (Job 5:7). And the word may also be exhortatory, as it is the custom to say to the many: 'You have not suffered anything outside of human nature; for indeed we have life in toil.' And the very being born of us happens in toil and ill-suffering, among the myriads of those existing and those being born in hardship.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why trouble is the ordinary lot of man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Calling upon the Master of all, he confesses God as provider and creator of all things, visible and invisible, whose works are beyond human counting.
comments.comment:
'Not indeed, but I will pray to the Lord, and I will call upon the Lord, the Master of all' (Job 5:8). Having accused the foolish and having said the following about them, he says, 'I do not rejoice as they do, but as one perceiving providence and knowing the Master of all, the God, I call upon Him, considering this to be proper.'

… 'The one doing great and unsearchable things, glorious and wonderful, of which there is no number. The one giving rain upon the earth, sending water upon the heaven below' (Job 5:9-10). He confesses God to be a provider of all things and a creator. … And these concepts are clearly present in many of the Scriptures, and not least even in Paul writing: 'In Christ were created the visible and the invisible, the earthly and the heavenly' (Colossians 1:16).

And this also must be considered, that from what happened to the holy Job, as a man having been led into fear, he marvels at the works of providence. And the 'there is no number' must be understood as referring to a man; for God knows all things.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the praise of God as provider of rain and water and of all things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God from on high raises the poor and the lowly and humbles the proud, and the way to exaltation from God is our own lowliness.
comments.comment:
He ascends also to the providence according to men, and this, while remaining in discussion concerning God of all things, is that He Himself from on high makes the poor rich from the needy, … and also the reverse. It is evident that these things, both being actually so and being seen and understood, exist for benefit, according to that which was said by the Holy Spirit: 'The Lord establishes kings and removes them' (Daniel 2:21), and 'Through me kings reign' (Proverbs 8:15), and 'He raises the poor from the dust and lifts the needy from the ash heap' (Psalm 113:7).

And the precursor of the exaltation from God is our lowliness: 'For whoever humbles himself will be exalted, and whoever exalts himself will be humbled' (Luke 14:11), and again: 'God opposes the proud, but gives grace to the humble' (James 4:6).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse about setting up on high those who are low.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Glory comes to the one who humbles himself, as Peter exhorts, and Job says God makes the humble into height.
comments.comment: Again, glory is brought to the one humbling himself, so that he may be un-blinded. Before this glory, it is necessary to be humbled; it is necessary to work, so that he may receive a reward. … In this way also Peter exhorts, saying: "Humble yourselves under the mighty hand of God, so that you may be lifted up in due time" (1 Peter 5:6). And Job indeed says: God is the one "making the humble into height" (Job 5:11).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even when men use great wisdom and counsel, it is God who provides the end, so their schemes bring nothing true.
comments.comment:
'They devise many schemes, and their hands shall not do what is true' (Job 5:12).

… Having explained concerning the providence of God and that through it dishonors and honors come about, and that certain humble things do not happen without Him, he [the speaker] moves to show that even if men use a great variety of wisdom, it is God's to provide the end. For indeed, 'the devising of many schemes' signifies to him that even if they should counsel and think themselves clever men, God erases these things, doing toward the benefit of each one. Often many men, having hoped, did not a little fail, and they received what was not expected, God governing, not man managing. Nor do such people have anything true in their own actions, those who, casting themselves upon themselves, thought to be self-sufficient in all things through their own counsels.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the schemes of the crafty come to nothing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The word 'cunning' is praiseworthy in Scripture when it means prudence and reproachful when it means deceit, and God seizes the devices of the wise as he did those of Gehazi and Ahithophel.
comments.comment:
To know that in the divine scripture the name of cunning is placed not only in a reproachful sense but also in a praiseworthy one.

For when it is said regarding wisdom, 'that I might give cunning to the guileless' (Proverbs 1:4), it is clear, as it speaks of prudence and a praiseworthy deed; for such a thing is given by wisdom. … That cunning is also placed reproachfully is shown in: 'I fear lest, as the serpent deceived Eve in his cunning, your thoughts might be made frivolous' (2 Cor 11:3). … 'He who seizes the wise in their prudence, and turns aside the counsel of the many-scheming' (Job 5:13). That is, he seizes the devices of the wise by his own prudence, or by the prudence of those who shared from him, as Elisha seized the sophistry of Gehazi, whom he caught scheming, saying: 'Your servant has not gone right or left' (2 Kings 5:25). To whom, having understood his movement, he said: 'Was not my heart with you?' (2 Kings 5:26). He also turns aside the counsel of the many-scheming ones, like that of Ahithophel, having prayed the blessed David and saying: 'Turn away the counsel of Ahithophel' (2 Sam 15:31).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the word 'craftiness' in the verse and gives two examples.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: What men grasp without God's inspiration leaves them groping in darkness, like a film over the eyes, and even a believer may be blinded by not using the light he has.
comments.comment:
'Darkness shall meet them by day, and the noonday, having felt it, shall be like night; and they shall perish in war' (Job 5:14).

… What they grasp without the inspiration of God, they find nothing, being overtaken by darkness and groping as if they were handling things in the night, being unable at all to perceive anything with precision. For just as a film lying over the eyes prevents the power of sight, so a passion of this kind acts upon the mind, causing it to fail to see even in bright and manifest things. Furthermore, their being stretched out signifies that ignorance is occurring, for they fail to see even at midday.

You might say that even one who believes in the evangelical message might still be called out in sins, being unable to see despite the presence of a great light; for in what he believes, light appears to him, but in what he does not use toward what is necessary with that light, he is blinded. This happened symbolically to the Egyptians; for they spent three whole days and three nights in darkness.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of darkness at noon.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God rescues the powerless from the hand of the powerful, as he did for David, who spared Saul in the cave.
comments.comment:
'But the powerless one comes out from the hand of the powerful.' These things might be clearly indicated according to the form of the words, so that what is said might be: may the weak chance to find help, as if escaping the hands of the powerful. It is also possible to carry it forth from the narrative, so that it is thus: 'He who does great and unsearchable things, both glorious and wondrous, of which there is no number, he who gives rain upon the earth, who sends water upon those under heaven, who lifts up the lowly, who raises up those stumbling,' (Job 5:9) as it has been said, and the following. This one rescues all, even the powerless, from the hand of the powerful.

We have this in the Kings (1 Samuel 24), for Saul pursued David so fiercely that he had to hide in a cave, in which Saul was delighted. And what is the paradox? For being surrounded by enemies, he was saved by divine power, as if the enemy were given into his hand, even though by the virtue of non-retaliation (1 Samuel 24:10) he surpassed the slaughter against the opponent, not only by not striking down but also by teaching him to turn away from hardship. For having cut off 'the lobe of the ear' (1 Samuel 24:10) of him, he showed him that he was able even to cut off the head. Therefore, he instructs both: the care of God regarding his own servants, and his own non-retaliation, for which he calls upon the enemy to imitate him, teaching him that God rescues the powerless from the powerful and the oppressors.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hope is for the powerless, who should not give up every expectation, and the mouth of the unrighteous is stopped when they swell with arrogance.
comments.comment: 'May there be hope for the powerless, and may the mouth of the unrighteous be stopped.' And the wording accords with the argument of Providence. If one is powerless, lacking in strength, let him not reject himself, let not every expectation be turned away; for hope is for the powerless. And the mouth of the unrighteous is also stopped when they swell with arrogance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says about the hope of the weak.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The unrighteous man whose mouth is stopped is the devil, who no longer has anything to say.
comments.comment: Therefore, 'let the mouth of the unrighteous be stopped by unrighteousness,' that is, the unrighteous man, who is the devil, no longer having anything to say, just as Paul writes, saying, 'so that the one against you may be put to shame, having nothing to say concerning you' (Titus 2:8) instead of 'against us.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man the Lord reproves is blessed, for the Lord who causes pain also restores, as a wise physician is trusted even when he cuts, and as Moses says, 'I strike and I myself will heal.'
comments.comment:
'Blessed is the man whom the Lord reproves, and the instruction of the Almighty shall not offend' (Job 5:17). For He causes pain and again restores; He chastened, and His hands healed (Job 5:18).

… But also that which is said in Proverbs, 'Whom the Lord loves He disciplines, and scourges every son whom He receives' (Proverbs 3:12), subjects the mind to the same. And one of the saints, having this readiness and speaking boldly, offering words of repentance to God, said, 'I am ready for the lashes'; for I know that it happens profitably from You, just as one says to a wise physician, 'I am even ready for the incision, being confident in your skill.'

… For 'he causes pain and again restores' (Job 5:18). And regarding the words, they are authoritative concerning God. Moses himself says from the beginning: 'I kill and I will make live, I strike and I myself will heal' (Deut 32:39).
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the one the Lord reproves is blessed, with the picture of the physician.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who quote only 'he causes pain' overlook the rest, for the whole saying shows that God puts the wicked to death and brings in a better life for them.
comments.comment: In this he [Celsus] acts much like the impious, who listen to the divine Scriptures with malice and “speak injustice on high” (Psalm 73:8). For they too seem to have heard “I will kill,” and they often throw it in our faces, but “I will make alive” (Deuteronomy 32:39) they do not even remember. Yet the whole saying shows that those who live to the common harm and act out of wickedness are put to death by God, and that a better life is brought in for them in its place, the life God would give to those who have died to sin (Romans 6:2). In the same way they have heard “I will strike,” but they do not go on to see “and I will heal” (Deuteronomy 32:39). That is like what a physician might say who has cut into bodies and made severe wounds in order to remove what harms them and stands in the way of health, and who does not stop at the pain and the cutting but by his treatment restores the body to the health he intended for it. Nor have they heard the whole of “For he causes pain, and restores again” (Job 5:18), but only “he causes pain.”
comments.selected_reason: Explains the whole saying 'he causes pain, and restores again' with the picture of the physician.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eliphaz's words about six troubles and a seventh may echo sayings of the wise before the law, and point to rest from the afflictions of the world.
comments.comment:
'six times out of necessity you shall be delivered, but in the seventh no evil shall touch you' (Job 5:19). If one were to stand upon what is said and consider, as Eliphaz is not of the holy ones, how such words are spoken by him, which might even be spoken to holy ones.

It must be said toward this, that the wise according to God, and before the law and the inscribed teaching, said many things unwritten with wisdom, which someone later handed down in written form by divine supply. It is therefore probable that even the friends of Job, having a well-ordered understanding, remembered the words arranged by the holy ones. This is that which leads them to bring forward sensible words, even if in some respects they erred.

What the laid out verses then suggest is this: to whatever extent someone possesses a world having come about in six days, the injustices and tribulations enduring in it. For even if someone is holy, he has the necessity of the need from the body, from which he is delivered, having surpassed the world and having come to a seventh rest. This is made clear from: 'pain and sorrow and sighing fled away' (Isaiah 35:10).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Righteous men, such as the sons of the prophets and Lazarus, endured famine and war, yet they had spiritual food and were kept from the death of the soul.
comments.comment:
'In famine he will save you from death, and in war he will release you from the hand of iron' (Job 5:20).

… for many diligent men died in famine, and not all those destroyed in war are wicked, the word remains unquestionable as it unfolds. For that which is said in the Psalms: 'I became younger; for I grew old and had not seen the righteous forsaken, nor his seed seeking bread. All day long he shows mercy and lends' (Ps 37:25-26), is true and necessary to be taken according to understanding; for even a righteous man does not need those who feed, being a soul filled with the 'life-giving spirit'.'

… For the righteous were famished and in war endured many tribulations, it is evident to the reader in the royal histories, of the sons of the prophets famishing and of Lazarus, and David having been in many circumstances, showing that they had spiritual food according to what is said: 'Open your eyes and be filled with bread,' and being found outside of temptation according to thought, they did not consent to undergo death of the soul or the bond of sin, becoming outside the threat, by which it is said, 'not a famine of bread nor thirst of water, but of hearing the word of the Lord' (Amos 8:11), drinking from the water which Jesus provides of the righteous, which also 'becomes in them a spring of water leaping into eternal life' (John 4:14).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The promise is repeated to the one the Lord admonished and who repented, though righteous men like Joseph were often reproached.
comments.comment: 'He will hide you from the scourge of the tongue, and you will not fear the evils coming' (Job 5:21). Concerning the one being admonished by the Lord and as if having repented, he [Eliphaz] says these things again, following his own principle, … For the righteous were often reproached, of whom Joseph is the prudent one in Egypt …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The lash of the tongue is a false word, a slander.
comments.comment: Furthermore, it is not said improperly: 'I will hide you from the lashes of the tongue' (Job 5:21). What is this 'lash of the tongue'? Do not take it in a sensory way. It is a false word, a slander.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the 'scourge of the tongue' is.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A house of virtue needs many virtues and one wickedness is enough to wreck it, and the one progressing must not stumble in the conduct of his tent.
comments.comment:
Thus also Job had a house, which the wise man, "having built," established firmly "upon the rock" (Matt 7:24). Having this, even the disciples of Christ held an immovable stance, observing the life-saving words.

And "the house" of the intellect brings peace, being unmixed and unyielding, working the peace of virtue because it follows them; for nothing is discordant in the important matter. Concerning the virtues, the proverb is aptly spoken: 'Wise women built a house, but the foolish one dug it down with her hands' (Prov 14:1).

… One virtue toward the building of a house is not sufficient. For this reason it is said in the plural: "Women built a house." But one wickedness is sufficient for distortion. For it is said: if anyone performs all the righteous acts, but performs one lawlessness, all his righteous deeds are set aside. For they no longer stand, nor do they remain, upon one wrong entering.

And his own virtue happens to be "not even to complain about the conduct of his tent" (Job 5:24). For it is necessary for one progressing, which is shown through the tent, not to stumble nor to sin …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The seed of Abraham are those who do Abraham's works, and the offspring of the holy mind multiplies like the increase of a field, bearing fruit a hundred, sixty and thirty fold.
comments.comment:
And the seed is often called a child: 'the seed of Abraham'—his children—not necessarily being both seed and child already. Regarding the Jews who cry out that they are the seed of Abraham, the Savior did not say: 'You lie,' but led forward: 'If you are children of Abraham, do the works of Abraham (John 8:39); for not all these are from Israel, the descendants of Israel. Nor is it that they are the seed of Abraham always a child.' He therefore says to them as not being children of Abraham: 'Do the desires of your father.' But those doing the desires of the devil, accepting him as father, are not children of Abraham. Blessed is the one becoming the seed of Abraham according to having the virtues of godliness and becoming a child, through being formed and not becoming dull, but bringing forth.

And there is when both the seed and the child are said in parallel, as is also set forth in the present. The intellect of the holy, which must be understood, brings forth offspring corresponding to the 'increase of the field' and a multitude exceeding in vital power, so that this 'man of the kingdom of heaven' (Matthew 13:24) might thus 'become like' according to the Gospel, sowing in the field of his own heart, so that he might bear fruit 'a hundred, sixty, thirty' (Matt 13:8) at first, middle, and last, 'sowing in tears' (Ps 126:5), so that 'he may reap in joy' (Ps 126:6) and 'seeking the Lord, so that he may bring to him fruits of righteousness.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The man is laid in the tomb like ripe grain harvested in season, for nothing that exists is without its proper end.
comments.comment: 'He will be released in a tomb like grain ripe being harvested in season, or like wheat of a threshing floor being gathered according to the hour.' Nothing of the existing things is without a proper end, even if it is taken by art. Nature and art both have an end and a purpose; for a vine is grown for the reasonable enjoyment of man, and a house is built by a craftsman having a purpose to complete a house for habitation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of ripe grain gathered in season.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He claims to have searched out and heard these things from old saints, and tells Job to know himself and repent.
comments.comment: 'Behold, these things we have searched out, these are the things we have heard. But you, know yourself if you have done anything' (Job 5:27). The aforementioned is confirmed, that being wise and perhaps having heard from old saints who taught divinely without writing, … For through 'we have searched out' his wisdom is demonstrated, and through 'we have heard' … 'But know yourself,' which is to say: having known, repent, …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the friend claims for his words and what 'know yourself' means.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job asks whether even beasts cry out without cause, to show that a saint may cry out in pain, since virtue lies in rising above pain through God, not in feeling none.
comments.comment:
'For does a wild donkey cry out for nothing, but seeking grain? Or does an ox cry out on the threshing floor having the foods? Will bread be eaten without salt? Or is there taste in empty words? For my soul cannot cease. For I see my food as the scent of a lion' (Job 6:5-6).' …

He asks: 'What then? Does a wild donkey cry out for nothing, but seeking grain?' (Job 6:5), which is: does a wild donkey not leave a cry in vain, lacking food? But neither does the ox cry out on the threshing floor where the foods are lying. So, do not blame me, if I cry out according to your assumption because of the painful things of a nature being weak, so that he might lead him toward sympathy so that he is not blamed for the one grieving if he cries out; for it is not necessary for the saint to be unfeeling, even if he bears the afflictions patiently. For this is virtue, when someone, receiving the perception of external things, surpasses the painful things through God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's question about the donkey and the ox in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Salt, like toil, is needed for virtue to be perfected, and a word without action is empty.
comments.comment: The nourishment of this thing [the benefit of the soul] exists not without toil and tribulation. Similar to this is the saying: 'through many tribulations it is necessary for us to enter into the kingdom of the heavens' (Acts 14:22), so that the bread might signify benefit, and the salt the toil, without which it is impossible for virtue to be perfected. From the same reasoning is also: 'and if there is indeed tasting in empty words?'. Every word lacking practical action is vain and empty.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the bread and salt and the empty words of the verse plainly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job prays to be wounded by God yet not carried off to the end, like a brave athlete who knows his fall does not come without God's help.
comments.comment:
'For if he might grant, and my request might come, and the Lord might grant my hope, let the Lord begin to wound me, but let him not lift me up to the end' (Job 6:3, 7:17-18). He who asks to be wounded by himself, not returning his request to come, but aiming to be fully satisfied in his own right, prays; and this was the end of the perfection: to lift up or even to appear to friends, for their benefit, the cause of the toils, that they were struck for the sake of the struggle.

For in this way they would not only not sin against the just, but also receive divine zeal, hastening to imitate the patience and courage being perfected in the holy one, through which also he was saying: 'if he might grant'—instead of: 'would that the Lord might grant'—'and my request might come, and the Lord might grant my hope'. For he prays for both, so that he himself might receive the crown of the contest and those who follow might not think their patience to be in vain. And it is possible to see and to marvel at him, even in the most extreme toils.

He is manly, because first he does not lack the initial response to a friend, treating the troubles as a leisure; and again, just as a brave athlete says, he stands militantly against the one set against him, knowing that his being brought low has happened not without the cooperation of God, saying: 'Let the Lord begin to wound me, but let him not raise me to the end,' instead of saying: 'May he grant the escape from tribulations.' Similar to this is: 'And let us not be brought into temptation' (Matt 6:13), which is often interpreted instead of: 'May it happen that one does not fall to the deceivers.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saint accepts a wound from God as from a teacher who tests him, not as from a tormentor.
comments.comment: Being a perceiver, therefore, the saint accepts the wound from God, receiving Him as the best teacher, not as a tormentor, but as one seeking a testing, just as the Psalmist says: 'Test me, O Lord, and try me' (Ps 26:2), and the proverbial saying: 'He disciplines every son whom he receives.' This happens so that he may not become a tormentor by not being sympathetic to the discipline. For the saint, having surrendered himself entirely to God, does not waive reproof, 'knowing that tribulation works patience, and patience, testing, and testing, hope; and hope does not disappoint' (Rom 5:3-5).
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's prayer to be wounded by God in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job asks what strength he has, so that his friends will see that he endures by God's help and not by being unfeeling, and that his suffering is not for sin.
comments.comment:
But the holy man, casting nothing upon himself, entrusts all to God. 'For what is my strength, that I endure? Or what is my time, that my soul is sustained? Is the strength of stones my strength?'

“Or are my fleshly parts made of bronze? Or did he not rely upon them? But help from me has ceased. Mercy failed me, but the Lord's oversight looked down upon me.” (Job 6:12). Being loving, he wants to instruct his friends, so that they do not wonder why he endures such a heavy burden of painful things, and to show them that, if not by a divine calculation, he would not have borne these things given human weakness—for by what strength, he asks, do I endure these things, or for what length of time will I be able to live enduring these? My strength is either of stone or my flesh is bronze, so that I do not feel the pain through them? —so that they do not despise patience by remaining unfeeling. For some even reason about the martyrs that they do not feel the pains, which would deny them virtue.

But he also wants them to grasp this with their mind, that he does not suffer because of sin, saying: “Did he not rely upon it?” (Job 6:13). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's questions about his strength and flesh in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The absence of friends in affliction is no small pain, and David knew it too.
comments.comment:
… “My closest ones did not attend to me, like a mountain stream leaving or like a wave passing me by.” (Job 6:15). And this happened to him for testing; for the absence of friends in afflictions is no small pain. …

… Enduring this tribulation, the holy David also sang: “They looked to the right and looked, and there was none recognizing me.” (Psalm 142:4). …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job reproaches those who now speak against him without knowing the cause of his trial, and many others despised him in his suffering.
comments.comment: 'Those who deceived me have now fallen upon me' (Job 6:15). Perhaps he reproaches them, saying: 'Unaware of the cause of these inductions, you dare to say such things which you did not say before.' It is also likely that many others despised him because of his suffering, and this was also the doing of the one who made the request. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: As snow or crystal melted by heat leaves its place unrecognizable, so trial reveals who is a friend and who is not, while true friends keep friendship in ease and adversity.
comments.comment:
'Like snow or congealed crystal, as it was arranged that heat should come and it was not recognized what it was, so I too was left by all. I was lost and became a stranger' (Job 6:17). The phrase 'Like snow or congealed crystal, as it was arranged' is spoken hyperbolically, being rendered as: 'As snow or crystal was arranged.' The example is appropriate to the hyperbole of his change, making him utterly unknown, like snow or crystal being dissolved by heat and thus making the place where it was, unknown. And it is good to use such an example; just as snow and crystal make the place indistinguishable when dissolved by heat, so also a friend, appearing to be one, is revealed when trials arise, and what he hid before, he makes manifest.

When a distressing time is present and the forming of friends is tested, the saints have certainty, while those who love possess this condition of friendship, keeping it incorruptible both in ease and in adversity. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of snow and crystal in the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Trusting in wealth and cities brings shame, because prosperity does not last and those who fall away may return.
comments.comment:
He makes the Word say: 'Behold the paths of the Bold, the ways of the Sabeans who see' (Job 6:19), which is: seeing with intellect, so that his whole mind might be such; but I became a stranger and was stripped of all.

Understand the paths of the Bold, judge the ways of the Sabeans, even if they are well-off; we think with minds that, trusting in wealth and glory, they do not have right paths or ways. …

If you would also take the interpretations of the names, this thought would occur, that the 'Bold' are those falling away, while the 'Sabeans' are those returning. Therefore, he exhorts those falling away from virtue, who have trusted even in wealth, to observe them, but he also exhorts to understand those returning to the nature of things, because it does not always remain in prosperity, but also frequently turns back.

Therefore, there is shame in trusting in money or in cities, saying 'cities' meaning the human glories and as if they were in safety. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job speaks as a pastor, taking the start of his exhortation from his friends' own fear at seeing his wound.
comments.comment:
'Even you also have come to me compassionately.' And he who admonishes those who have fallen into false accusations with a gloomy countenance is not correcting them according to reason by being moved. For this is not the purpose, but rather to urge them toward manliness and to engage bravely. For to say: 'Why then did we sin?' is more heavy than to be light in toil.

For in truth, they approached him compassionately to rescue him from being tossed about concerning the cause of the indictment, and because they were trying to correct him by accusing one who was not submissive. …

… 'So having seen my wound, you were afraid.' The saint is most pastoral and toward those who are not rightly disposed toward him, he approaches by correcting them from their own error and receiving from their own state the beginning of the exhortation …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job will not accept his friends' rebukes as righteous, since they fall upon the helpless and strike at a friend without regard for friendship.
comments.comment:
… 'For I will not endure even a single word from you.' This is courage; for many men, hearing words while in the midst of heavy burdens, often falter, so that they even weaken through them. But the holy man accepted neither the rebuke from friends nor the words regarding brevity, not at all receiving them as things capable of shaking him.

'Instead, you fall upon an orphan, but you strike at a friend.' Because of this, I do not accept the rebukes from you as being righteous, because just as you fall upon an orphan and a helpless person, not seeing that everyone is a helper, you also strike at a friend, not recognizing the duties of friendship. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's 'I will not lie' teaches speaking to a person's face what is necessary and not gossiping about the absent.
comments.comment: 'But now, looking into your faces, I will not lie.' The saying is instructive for not bringing forward words of gossip concerning those who are absent, but for speaking what is necessary to one's face. For it has been said: 'Do not speak, nor listen easily to one gossiping.' And it is a matter of outspokenness to say: 'I will not lie,' just as Paul says: 'That I do not lie'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job asks his friends to sit and examine what is said, for it is great not to act unjustly in speech.
comments.comment: 'Sit down then, and let it not be unjust. And again, come together to the righteous.' These things are permissive and not harsh, teaching with leisure and attention, which is shown by the 'sit down,' and examining what is to be spoken. This is also said elsewhere: 'Before you examine, do not condemn.' And great is the command: 'Let it not be unjust.' For it is great not to act unjustly in speech, as it has been said: 'If anyone does not stumble in speech, he is able to bridle his whole body' (Jas 3:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's question to God does not strike at God but laments that God's name is blasphemed through him and fears being abandoned by God.
comments.comment: … When he [Job] says, "Why have you set me as your opponent in prayer?," he is not striking at God — far from it. To whom else would he petition? He means: Why, through me, Master, is your name blasphemed? He also grows dizzy lest abandonment from God be greater still. A God-loving soul suffers nothing like the suspicion of being left by God, and chooses death ten thousand times over life under that suspicion.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job's question about being set as a target is not an attack on God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job says that his friends, by charging him with sin, lay a burden on him, but that God is training him and not punishing him.
comments.comment:
Since the friends thought that those in distress were as those who must encounter God concerning sin, as if this were the cause of their sufferings, he prays that he may make known to them why he set himself as a rod for himself, that it is through struggle and not through sin; for not everyone who encounters God suffers this because of sin. 'Am I a burden to you?' I think I am a burden.

It is upon me; for they weigh me down saying, 'You suffer because of sin.' And because of this, they impose a kind of burden upon me through me, as if punishing the innocent. … But I say that you do not punish me, but you train me, even if they thoughtlessly consider that anyone receiving the trial unhappily suffers because of sin.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's friends think that if he departs to the earth he will be no more, but the holy voice hopes to rise at dawn from this age into the coming age.
comments.comment:
Now I shall depart to the earth, but I am no longer rising at dawn. He explains the disposition of those who do not correctly take this to mean: if these have taken me to be a sinner and suffering because of sin, they think that having me thus established with nothing after this, 'I have hoped most in this life alone,' and according to them, if I depart to the earth, I shall no longer be; and after days pass, I shall no longer be; for another age will not receive me at all according to them.

But it is a holy voice, upon which also the blessed one hoped, saying: 'I shall rise at dawn' (Psalm 57:8), and again: 'Out of the night my spirit rises toward you, O God' (Ps 42:5), and: 'O God, my God, toward you I rise' (Ps 42:5); which also indicates the daily staying awake and the awakening from this age into the coming age. If anyone should say plausibly that: until I am in the shadows, I happen to be in night, but having risen and having become in the day, I am no longer in transitory things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Bildad rebukes Job for much talk and holds that God would be unjust if a righteous man suffered, but he does not know that the suffering has been permitted to show Job's courage.
comments.comment: Thus, this one also rebukes the blessed one, saying: 'Until when?'—saying only: 'Until when?'—'Do you not perceive the cause of the pains?' And he charges him with much talk, he who ought to have marveled more at him, because, as if forgetting the pains, he was making these words regarding doctrines, which the friends did not know, even while they were not imposing themselves upon investigation, although they were being driven by distress. Then, further confirming his opinion and presenting a reasoning to him as well, he says: 'Will not the Lord judge unjustly, or he who made all things trouble the righteous?' For there was a disturbance of justice according to their assumption, if being righteous he suffered. But they are ignorant of these things; for the concession made against him has happened for the sake of highlighting and for the purpose of courage.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Bildad says that even if Job did not sin, his children did, and he hints that their fall is why lawlessness was sent upon them.
comments.comment: 'If your children have sinned against him, he sent it at the hand of their lawlessness' (Job 8:4). This one also holds the word together and carries himself along with the doctrines, saying: 'Even if you did not sin, but your children did, you would not have considered that one would punish another for another.' But this also he was merely striking at, because through his own sin lawlessness was sent at the hand of them, hinting at the fall through which his children were lost. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'The pure' means the upright, those without the impurity that comes from evil, and Bildad contends against Job by saying God will hear him if he is pure.
comments.comment:
… 'But you rose up early to the Lord Almighty, praying: If you are pure and true, he will listen to your prayer and restore to you a way of righteousness' (Job 8:5-6). He says this while contending. For having said that 'he sent it at the hand of the lawlessness of your sons,' he says to him: 'You rose up early to the Lord; if you are pure, he will listen to your prayer. …

… But we have 'the pure' signifying instead 'the upright', just as it has been said: 'blessed are the pure in heart' (Matt 5:8); for this reason it is said, because they do not have the impurity which is from evil; 'as it has been said' concerning the wicked: 'it is crushed through the impurity of the soul'; and again concerning something: 'its impurity toward its feet.' Such also are those whose 'feet run toward wickedness' (Prov 1:16).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: If righteousness has to be restored to Job, Bildad is saying that he does not have it now, yet Bildad's own words show that a good man may fall into such trials.
comments.comment: But if righteousness is being restored to him, he does not have it now; and if he does not have it now, how is he pure? Or how does he waver, that he is pure, remaining in doubt, because he is a sinner by falling in circumstances? And this opposition of theirs followed from having placed a beginning that errs, which follows every heresy. For saying to the one in wrongdoing: 'if you are pure and true, he will listen to your prayer and restore to you a manner of righteousness' (Job 8:6), he shows that it is possible for the good and true to fall into these things; which follows by necessity, that not everyone who is in circumstances is wicked and in sins; therefore your first things shall be few, and your last things unutterable (Job 8:7).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Bildad rests his word on former men and their writings.
comments.comment: For 'inquire of the first generation, search out according to the lineage of the fathers' (Job 8:8). He wishes to establish his own word from the former men or writings, which contained their lives. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Just as a papyrus withers without water, so human affairs and the mind bear no useful fruit without the benefit of providence from above.
comments.comment:
The teaching of the ancients and the fathers is passed down to those who come later; he prepares it by way of a parable, saying: just as a papyrus without water does not flourish nor rise up as a reed unless it is watered, while it is still upon the earth—so it will not be harvested—so it is impossible, without receiving benefit in the mind from superior things, to bring forth useful fruit.

And he can also speak concerning human affairs, saying that just as these things are watered by water through providence, without which they would be thin and dried up, so also, if anyone falls into calamities and then experiences a change, it is due to providence. And if the things happening through men have even the appearance of a human root, they will not have substance without providence directing them.

Similar to this is what is well said by the Psalmist: 'Unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it' (Psalm 127:1). Before drinking, every herb will be dried up (Job 8:12). This is said regarding the former parable concerning every herb. He says, therefore, that whether it be small or great, that which is in life is under providence, being dried up unless this providence watches over it. Thus, in all things, the end of those who forget the Lord will be so.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the plant image of the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hope of the ungodly perishes because it is not set on lasting things, for hope is an expectation of good things and they expect nothing that endures.
comments.comment:
In reality, the hope of the ungodly is not concerning a subsisting thing. For hope is nothing other than, by nature, an expectation of good things. And he who fears expects, but not good things; for fear is an expectation of evils, while hope is of good things. Since, therefore, the ungodly do not expect subsisting things, their hope is destroyed; for as they remain, they use things for pleasures, and in this they have a vain hope. …

… But those 'hoping only in this life' and 'saying: Let us eat and drink,' have a vain and empty hope, stretching themselves toward this visible thing; but Paul says naturally: 'But the hope that is seen is not hope; for what one sees, what does he hope for?' (Romans 8:24). …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why the hope of the ungodly perishes in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He who turns the words of Jesus into works builds a dwelling that is never desolate, while the works of the wicked are like a spider's web, easily dissolved and not firm.
comments.comment:
… It is clear, however, that he who transforms the words of Jesus into works builds a dwelling; and this is the virtue, of which the one holding fast will never have this house desolate; for the righteous must remain in his own virtue; for 'his righteousness remains unto the age of ages.' Since evil is without substance, for this reason the wicked man is desolate, being always unstable and possessing nothing firm, because evil itself is a following-after; … 'Therefore the house of the ungodly shall be desolate'; for clearly the truth dissolves the deception. And his tent shall fall away like a spider's web. The spider's web shows variety, constructed from a natural fabric, which is easily dissolved when someone touches it. Thus the works of the wicked and the construction of their way of life resemble a spider's web, not standing firm.

And in Isaiah it is said concerning the wicked who have conceived iniquity and spoken injustice: 'They weave a spider's web, for they conceive pain and bring forth iniquity' (Isaiah 59:5); …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the spider's web of the verse in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mountains are the prophets, Moses and those after him, and whoever gives his mind to their words will find his help from the Lord who made heaven and earth.
comments.comment: “He who makes the mountains old, and they do not know it, who overturns them in wrath” (Job 9:5). The mountains are the prophets—Moses and those after him. And the Scripture makes this clear: “I lifted up my eyes to the mountains, from where my help will come” (Psalm 121:1). The one who gives his reasoning mind to the words of the prophets lifts up his eyes to the mountains, seeing that his help will come from the words understood in the prophets, from the Lord who made heaven and earth and filled the pure heart of the prophets with mysteries.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms who the mountains of the verse are.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ is the one who makes the mountains, Moses and the prophets, old and also renews them, and those who did not know this clung to the oldness of the letter.
comments.comment: So as long as the new covenant had not come, the prophets were not old, for nothing had been said outside of a covenant before this. But Christ is the one making old the mountains—Moses and the prophets. “And they do not know it” (Job 9:5). Who does not know it? Those to whom he said, “If you believed Moses, you would believe me, for he wrote about me” (John 5:46). If the Jews had known that the mountains were being made old, they would have abandoned them—that is, the oldness of the letter—and would have passed over and come to the new covenant, and they would have worshiped God in newness of Spirit and not in oldness of letter (Romans 7:6). So he adds: the Jews do not know either the one who made them old or the things that have been made old. Therefore, he says, he is the one overturning them in wrath—that is, the Jerusalem according to the letter [or: of the letter]. … When he came, his own prophets he has both made old and renewed. He made them old—how? “The ministry of death was engraved in letters,” it says (2 Corinthians 3:7). He renewed them—how? “The law is holy, and its commandment is holy and just and good” (Romans 7:12). But those who did not learn the spiritual name did not know these things.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ shook what is under heaven, as the apostles were shaken at the passion, and the sun and stars were sealed at the cross.
comments.comment:
“He who shakes what is under heaven from its foundations” (Job 9:6). Christ is the one who shook what is under heaven. Many earthquakes happen in part: an earthquake happens here, but those in the neighboring city do not know it. But with Christ it did not happen partially. Therefore he is the one shaking what is under heaven from its foundations. And its pillars are shaken—clearly the apostles were shaken at the time of the passion. “All of you,” he says, “will be scandalized because of me this night” (Matthew 26:31).

“He who speaks to the sun, and it does not rise, and seals up the stars” (Job 9:7). This also happened at the cross. “And seals up the stars”: it is reported that during the three hours when the sun failed, stars appeared in the sky as at night.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the verse's shaking and sealing are read as the passion of Christ.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job foresaw the Mediator with divine sight, being fully informed of God's plan when God was revealed to him.
comments.comment: For the blessed Job also foresaw this Mediator with divine sight, which is clear from 'he who is about to grasp a great beast' (Job 3:8) and from 'he who walks as if on land upon the sea' (Job 9:8). For when God was being revealed to him, there was no room for doubt that he was fully informed concerning the economy [God's plan of salvation]. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: He wonders why Job, speaking in the Spirit, named only the Pleiad, Hesperus and Arcturus out of so many stars.
comments.comment: “He who makes the Pleiad, and Hesperus, and Arcturus, and the chambers of the south” (Job 9:9). These matters are beyond me. For since there are many stars—Pleiads, planets and fixed stars—listed by those who do not know, as they suppose (there is Hesperus, and Phaethon, and Phainon, and Stilbon, and Phosphorus), why then did Job, speaking in the Spirit, name only the Pleiad out of so many stars in the fixed sphere?
