And out of so many planets spoken of, why did he mention only Hesperus? And one other, Arcturus, the one in the bear, called by some the bear-keeper?
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: All things under heaven have been subjected to God, and the opposing powers have no authority to approach with evil unless God permits it.
comments.comment:
And according to the account of history this is true; for if he himself had not subjected them, these things would have been beyond doubt to men. And even in the other predatory beasts you will find this by passing through the reasoning. But also the evil spirits, the cattle named allegorically, he himself bent. For neither was human nature such that it would not be scorched by God without being so. And it is fitting that he also spoke of those under heaven, in order to make all things manifest, those in the air and in the earth and in the lower regions. For all things have been subjected: 'for the cattle was spread by knowledge' (Job 39:25).

And if God had not said so continually, not even to Job: 'the beginning of evil is the devil' (Job 1:6). For the opposing powers do not come by their own wicked intention. For they do not have authority to approach with evil and hardship, unless God permits it. But they hasten to cast evil by their own impulse. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job speaks hypothetically, since God does not always give what we ask but what is profitable, so that his judgment triumphs.
comments.comment: There are some who have read the verse without a substantiation, that it is: "He will not listen to my righteousness" (Job 9:15). Understand then, that the repayment has a reason, because the one who spoke before, the friend, was saying: "But you rise up early to the Lord praying; if you are good and true, he will listen to the prayer of supplication" (Job 8:6), teaching him that God does not always give to us the words we ask, but those that are profitable; he says this hypothetically, that "for if you are righteous, he will not listen to me;" for thus the judgment triumphs.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even if God hears a prayer he does not simply approve our words but gives by his own wise judgment, so we should ask for the truly good, which are the virtues, not the customary pleasant things.
comments.comment:
If he obeys me, does he discern my words? … 'For what we ought to pray for according to what is necessary, we do not know.' What therefore he says is such: that even if he obeys, he does not discern human words to approve them in this way, but his own judgment, being wise, will impose it upon us, being a lover of mankind and doing nothing unjustly. …

He spoke hypothetically because even the holy one knows that the judgment must persuade him and not demand a solution from him unseasonably. Even if I call and he obeys, I do not believe that he has listened to me, lest he should turn me away through my ignorance. …

For since the kind of good things is twofold—the first being the truly good, which are the virtues, and the second being the pleasant and customary good things—one must not ask God unseasonably for the customary things, but for the truly good; for God will judge whether we are being removed from hardships or being kept in them. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why God does not always grant what we ask in prayer.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job fears that even if God hears him he will be crushed by what he cannot understand, and he turns his friends' charge of sin against them.
comments.comment:
… So one must fittingly make the entreaty to God. For if God grants the request, he does not grant altogether according to the manner of the request, but according to a reason which he knows to be beneficial. …

What the blessed Job says in a hypothesis is this: that even if I boldly call and he hears, there is fear, lest by the obscurity of the circumstances I undergo crushing. “Many are the bruises he has made upon me without cause; for he does not let me breathe, but has filled me with bitterness” (Job 9:17–18). Again he says all these things against their apprehension. For if you say that I have received punishment for sins, but the punishment remains not permitting me to breathe, how can I escape the charge of having lived badly?

For in vain according to you have the things of the affliction come to be, if indeed, conscious of nothing in myself as having sinned, I am punished, and the things of correction are unaccomplished through having no time of yielding. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is strong and reigns, not because of our sins, and no one can oppose his judgment or ask him what he has done.
comments.comment:
… “For that he prevails with might, who then shall oppose his judgment?” (Job 9:19). If “with might” is a noun, “prevails” is a verb: that he is strong in might. But if “strength” is a noun, it would be thus: “he prevails with strength”; for this is a verb. However it may be, the same thing is signified: for God being strong prevails, and prevailing is strong; reigning is strong, and being strong reigns.

For this reason it must not be said that he is strong so as to rule because of our sins; …

… But it is not of a king to rule lawlessly, nor does he, proposing one thing, do another through weakness; for the Lord is “just, strong, and long-suffering” (Psalm 7:11), wherefore no one “shall oppose his judgment,” no one being able to say: “What have you done?” — as we set forth the apostolic saying in what went before: “Shall the thing formed say to him who formed it: Why did you make me thus?” (Rom 9:20).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job says he is righteous only because his friends compelled him, and 'blameless' can mean either one who does nothing or one who does righteousness.
comments.comment:
“For even if I am righteous, my mouth will be ungodly” (Job 9:20). Being righteous, I ought not to say this very thing, that I am righteous; for the righteous man does not speak concerning himself as concerning another. Like this is the “I have become foolish; you compelled me” (2 Cor 12:11). For when the friends set forth that he suffers because of sin, in a way he was compelled to say that it is not because of sin, but “I am righteous.” For this form can be found in scripture, as Paul also writes to the Corinthians: “If the dead are not raised, neither is Christ raised” (1 Cor 15:16). For he does not say this from his own person, but with regard to their suspicion.

“Even if I am blameless, I shall turn out crooked” (Job 9:20). This also is of the same thought, signifying that if, conscious of nothing in myself, I am subjected to circumstances, you say this happens because of sin: being “blameless,” I “shall turn out crooked” according to you. But “blameless” and “righteous” differ in conception. The blameless is twofold: one by doing nothing, the other by doing righteousness; which is praiseworthy, as was also said to Abraham: “Be well-pleasing before me and become blameless” (Gen 17:1); but the blameless of the Hebrews is not from virtue. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job speaks of his own righteousness in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job says he is conscious of no sin and yet his life is taken away, showing that one who has not sinned may fall into toils.
comments.comment: “For even if I was ungodly, I do not know it in my soul; yet my life is taken away” (Job 9:21). That is, having been ungodly in soul I do not know, or I do not know myself as having been ungodly, nor is my soul conscious of this; and Paul also says something like this: “I am conscious of nothing in myself” (1 Cor 4:4). “Yet even if I do not know,” he says, “having been ungodly, my life is taken away”; which is: he meets with sufferings unto death. And he said this fixing their attention, that it is possible even for one who has not sinned to fall into toils. And it is a great testimony to be conscious of nothing against oneself. …
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job means in plain terms.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Toilsome things, which Job calls wrath or death, are common.
comments.comment: … Wherefore I said: wrath destroys the great and the mighty … He wishes to teach that the toilsome things, which he calls wrath, or even death, are common …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job says that the One who judges him is not a man, so that his friends may see that his conscience is ready for judgment and that he suffers for a struggle, not for sin.
comments.comment:
… Thus also the blessed Job says with gratitude, making manifest to God the sincerity of his intellect: 'For he is not a man according to me, against whom I am judged' (Job 9:32).

The word is thus being smoothed out without following: 'I myself know the things concerning myself. And since the friends, not being moved by right reasoning, and from the distressing ones standing around, think that I have suffered through sin, I am satisfied with Your testing.' Then, through them, in a certain way teaching them again, that the things concerning him are not human, he says: 'He is not a man according to me, against whom I am judged,' as knowing all things concerning him and therefore bearing it, so that the friends might imitate him, considering that the word according to him is a secret, and thus they turn away from the single delusion, so that we may come together in judgment.

As has been said, he teaches the friends to perceive that the conscience is well-situated and ready for judgment; for the conscience does not wish to come to judgment with itself. He says these things not losing boldness toward God, testifying with Him concerning righteousness, but in order to teach, as has been said, the friends that he is not afraid of reproof. For he did not have anything worthy of reproof. David, participating in this boldness, sang: 'My heart is prepared, O God, my heart is prepared' (Psalm 57:7). I wish He were our Mediator, who reproves and discerns in the midst of both. Again, these things are said in a general way, in the manner in which the first things were said, being the clearest evidence of the freedom of his soul. He prays, therefore, that there might exist some examination which demonstrates to the friends that he suffers these things not because of sin, but for the sake of a struggle. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Because man is far removed from God, the Son joined both sides in himself and as high priest carries God's things to men and men's things to God.
comments.comment:
… Since the title of the Mediator is now at issue, it is worthy to understand how the Savior is called 'a mediator of God and men'. Man, therefore—and what am I saying, man—is far removed from the creature of the Creator.

… Since God has separated man greatly, the Son, being consubstantial [of one being] with God, possessed the human in himself, so that by the familiarity toward men and the consubstantiality toward God he might join both sides and 'break the middle wall of the partition, the enmity, in his flesh' (Ephesians 2:14), assuming the rank of a high priest.

And the high priest is a middle between God and the consecrated ones, bringing the things of God to men and the things of men to God; he offers prayers and supplications to God as sacrifices, and provides the knowledge of Him to men. He sends up a prayer, saying: 'just as I and you are one, so that these also may be one in us.' Then this will be, when God becomes 'all in all' (1 Corinthians 15:28), so that the rest may be joined to God without a mediator, becoming one spirit with Him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms why a mediator between God and man is needed and what he does.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The name of the rod signifies severe discipline, especially in rebuke.
comments.comment: … 'Remove the rod from me, and let his terror not turn me aside' (Job 9:34). The severe discipline is signified by the name of the rod, and especially in rebuke when it is spoken. …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job answers the friends who count his suffering as sin by saying that God does not punish him as a sinner or search out his iniquity.
comments.comment: He says this while reproaching them again, that the calamity concerning me is the result of many having sinned. Since the friends reckoned him as suffering through sin, he shows them abruptly that it is not so, by saying, 'O God, your years are not like a man's, for you have searched out my iniquity' (Job 10:5). For according to these words, he suggests that you do not punish me as a sinner, and you do not seek out our iniquity or sin through inductions against those disposed in this way.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: An innocent man can fall into afflictions, which come to the righteous as a struggle and proof of endurance, and being rescued means not being defeated by them.
comments.comment:
'For you know that I have not been impious' (Job 10:7). He reveals the knowledge of the matter to them by saying to God, 'You know that I have not been impious.' But these friends think that the things coming upon me have been brought about because of an impious man. But who is the one being taken out from your hands? He again suggests the idea that it is possible for one who has not sinned to fall into afflictions; for God knows that Job did not act impiously.

And the question, 'But who is the one being taken out from your hands?' brings on the instruction of the friends, showing that the one who has not sinned and has not acted impiously comes under the hand of God into afflictions through struggle and the demonstration of endurance. …

But to be rescued from tribulations is not to not be afflicted at all, but to not have been previously defeated by them, to not have been trapped by the nets of the tribulations being brought forward.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a man God knows to be innocent can still suffer.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's hands made and formed Job, and even when He sends troubles He spares His own handiwork, 'made' being applied to the soul and 'formed' to the body.
comments.comment:
'Your hands made me and fashioned me' (Job 10:8). …

To say, through the phrase 'but who is the one being removed from your hands' Job 5:9, the expression 'your hands made me and formed me' Job 10:8 is brought forward, saying that even if he brings tribulations, he spares his own handiwork; for it is written: 'but he spares all, because he is merciful, O Lord, lover of souls' Ps 145:9. And good is the 'your hands made me and formed me', so that the 'made' is applied to the soul, while the 'formed' is applied to the body; for 'formed me' signifies the opposite, which is appropriate for the body.

And in Genesis it is said: 'God made man, according to the image of God he made him' Gen 1:27; for not the body is according to the image, but the soul, for God is not anthropomorphic. And elsewhere it is said: 'God formed man, dust from the earth' Gen 2:7, taking the body, so that, as we say, we may receive the making regarding the soul, and the forming regarding the flesh. And if even the making lies regarding the flesh, it is not to be treated as strange; for to form is to make according to a kind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording of the verse, made and formed.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's 'your hands have made me' shows God as Creator, and the blows after it show His providence, which makes a brave man a pattern.
comments.comment: He demonstrates, through 'your hands have made me' the creative aspect, and through 'after these things, having changed me, you have struck me' the providential aspect. For this is the work of God's providence: to surround the brave man with distress through struggle, so that he may set up a character and a goal for men, whom they become imitators of when looking toward him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job asks God to remember that he is weak and made of clay, and being turned back to dust is said of the body, since the soul is not turned back to dust.
comments.comment:
'Remember that you formed me of clay, and to dust you turn me back again' (Job 10:9).

Consequently, knowing Him as the Author and Lord of both creation and providence, the word turns to Him in prayer, saying: even if you have brought things upon me as if exercising authority over painful things, yet remember that I am weak and have a constitution from clay—this, however, should be understood concerning the body—and having formed me, you turn me back to dust again. And it is clear from this that he speaks concerning the body; for the soul is not turned back to dust. … Similar to 'and to dust you turn me back again' is that which was said to Adam: 'Dust you are and to dust you shall return' (Gen 3:19).
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job compares the forming of a human being to milk curdling into cheese, the seed congealing into a nature until the limbs differentiate and the living being appears.
comments.comment: 'Did you not curdle me like milk, and harden me like cheese?' (Job 10:10). … Regarding the living being, he says, 'as milk unmilked'; and just as milk, being curdled, becomes cheese, so also the seed, being congealed, becomes a nature. And this is the constitution before the embryo. For the seed cast into the channels of the womb, when it is curdled like cheese, becomes a nature; which moreover is spread out or, as the Scripture says, 'is imprinted' (Job 10:9) and receives it like a character. But when the limbs differentiate and each becomes its own and moves, for instance, like an animal's hand or foot, then the birth of the embryo clearly demonstrates the living being.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Skin and flesh' in Job's words mean the body, as with the garments of skin God made for Adam and his wife, and bones and nerves complete the account of how the body is built.
comments.comment: 'Having clothed me in skin and flesh, and having placed me in bones and nerves.' This is used by those desiring to show that those whom God clothed in skin tunics, these thick things, are their bodies. For it is also said in Genesis: 'And God made skin tunics for Adam and his wife and clothed them' (Gen 3:21). … It is clear that 'skin and flesh' here signifies the body; for he connects what follows by saying: 'and placed me in bones and nerves.' Thus he announces the whole way and the harmony of the body's constitution through those things before these and through those contained within.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Life' means that the creature is placed in existence, 'mercy' means providential grace, and 'spirit' in this verse means the soul.
comments.comment:
Having made me consisting of flesh and skin and bone and nerves, you clothed me, but also, 'you have practiced life and mercy toward me.' Through 'life' it signifies that the creation is placed in existence, but through 'mercy' the providential grace. For since it happens that one must also endure attacks against such a life, there is a need for mercy, as it is said: 'you have practiced life and mercy toward me.' For the Creator God does not act according to debt, but according to mercy and goodness; for it has come to be that he grants life to favorable matter rather by mercy than by any other way.

Furthermore, what follows declares more clearly the things concerning providence and its care: 'your oversight has preserved my spirit,' saying 'spirit' for the soul. For although 'spirit' signifies many things, here it signifies the soul; for if James says, 'just as the body without the spirit is dead' (James 2:26), and Stephen, encountering God and saying, 'Lord, receive my spirit' (Acts 7:59), he signifies the soul.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'You are able to do all things' must be heard with faith and prudence: what is possible for God is what is fitting for God, so Scripture says that He cannot deny Himself or lie.
comments.comment: Having these thoughts within yourself, I know that you are able to do all things; nothing is unable for you. … And 'you are able to do all things' should be heard faithfully and prudently, so that we do not fall into the folly of the opinionated. … Therefore, I say, those things are possible for God which are fitting for God. … For the Scripture also knows this, it says concerning God: 'If we deny, he remains faithful. For he cannot deny himself' (2 Tim 2:13). And again: 'In whom it is impossible to lie to God' (Heb 6:18).
comments.selected_reason: Explains how to take the claim that God can do all things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God is patient and does not bring wrath every day, but guards the sinner so that the law forbidding sin may make him hate evil, and Job's words show sin to be common to men.
comments.comment: For if I sin, 'keep me; from lawlessness you have not made me innocent' (Job 10:14). He says this reasonably; for since I know him to be creator and provider of himself and of all things, he follows by teaching also concerning his patience. For he himself knows, according to the blessed David, that 'he does not bring wrath every day' (Psalm 7:11). But God guards the one sinning, not desiring him to sin—'for he does not desire the death of the sinner as the desire for repentance' (Ezek 33:11)—but so that, giving the law which forbids sinning, he might cause the one practicing it to hate evil. … And he teaches the turnability of human nature through 'from lawlessness you have not made me innocent,' while also presenting a pattern of moderation and indicating the succession of Adam, showing sin to be common to men.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job says that one who stumbles through ignorance is not to be punished, yet he cannot bow his head as one completely cleansed, and even the righteous must not think greatly of themselves.
comments.comment: Just as one learning to write, since he cannot write well immediately, stumbles during the learning process—not such that it is considered corrupt as if someone were writing evil by malicious intent—so also the one striving toward virtue, if he first stumbles through ignorance, is not to be punished. For if he were impious, woe to me! If he were righteous, I would not be able to bow my head. He might say, 'If I sin by choice, woe to me; but if, as we have previously stated, I have it only by succession from Adam, again I will not be able to bow my head as one completely cleansed of filth.' For of sins, those from our own choice stand as bad, but those are different as previously stated; for punishment follows those from choice, but purification is owed to those from ignorance. He might say, 'Even if I am righteous, I do not think greatly, knowing the obvious.' For many, having spoken highly of themselves, fell in practice. … But I am full of dishonor. The sign of human weakness is thin, for man is full of dishonor by being a body surrounded by such a thing, about which Paul says: 'It is sown in dishonor, it is raised in glory' (1 Cor 15:43).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The enemy, the devil, hunts and surrounds Job like a lion among wild beasts, yet he would have no power if God had not permitted it.
comments.comment: And I am hunted like a lion for slaughter. Thinking myself to be full of dishonor according to the previously stated sense, the enemy seeks to cast me down through those standing around, as if surrounding with dogs, and tries to envelop me with nets. But the lion is a great animal. It has been said: 'A lion is stronger than cattle.' 'For the righteous has become like a lion.' However, the one set out for a combatant knows that some beast is trying to hunt him; and this is the adversary, the devil. … Through the saying, 'I am prowling like a lion' (Job 10:16), it is meant that the enemy is like a lion driving the wild beasts and not leaving him to avoid temptation. This is not arrogance, but it reveals the plot. For again, 'you turn me terribly' (Job 10:16). It shows that even if I prowl like a lion, so many things have surrounded me, but they do not attack by themselves; for the permission is small. If God had not permitted, the prowler would not have had the power.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's change from wealth to poverty and health to sickness came as successive attacks, and the great wrath is an onslaught and not punishment, since those who undergo trials do not suffer by their own fault.
comments.comment:
The 'turning' must be understood actively as the change that happened to Job from wealth to poverty and from health to sickness; … 'Renewing against me my distress' signifies the successive onslaughts of the attackers. For just as an enemy, being repelled from the opposing sides, prepares himself again to fight, the one who has taken authority devises new pains like against a man, increasing the affliction in magnitude.

This is shown by: 'while he was still speaking, another messenger came' (Job 1:16). For the calamities were frequent and successive. 'And with great wrath I used you; you brought trials upon me' (Job 10:17). And here again the magnitude of the afflictions is shown, not ceasing, but making it known to friends that this exceeding wrath is not, as one might think, because of sin, if one were to judge his life.

Anger here should not be understood as a passion, but as the attacking onslaught, just as Moses says to God: 'You sent out your wrath and consumed them like a reed' (Exodus 15:7). Some suffer because of sin; but here it is shown through 'you brought trials upon me' that it is not because of sins; for those being punished in this manner are not said to undergo trials. Thus, the bringing of trials must be understood not as if they had fallen upon them by their own fault.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job, who had been rich and healthy and then lost it, taught that the pleasures of this life are vain and not to be desired, since riches do not follow a man in dying.
comments.comment:
Having tested this life and the pleasant things in it—for he had been happy in many ways and was indeed rich and healthy—having fallen from these things into their opposites, and having become experienced in these things through works, having known their vanity, he instructs us not to have desire for them by saying: 'Why then did you bring me out from the womb and I did not die, my eye not having seen, so that I might not become as one who is not?' (Job 10:18).

The vanity of the combatants in this life, such as wealth, is shown from: 'Do not fear when a man becomes rich or when the glory of his house increases, for he will not receive all things in his dying' (Psalm 49:16-17)—for all these things do not follow the one being released from them—'for the glory of his house will not descend together with him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job is not denying the resurrection of the dead when he speaks of the place from which one does not return, for he knew that he would be raised incorruptible.
comments.comment: It is not necessary to consider that Job denies a resurrection of the dead, but rather in this way: 'from whence one does not return' (Job 10:21)... in bitter life; for he knew that he would be raised incorruptible. Into a land of darkness and gloom, into a land of eternal darkness, where there is no light and one cannot see the life of mortals. And while experiencing pains, the most manly man was preaching concerning the coming age; in this way, he was not denying a resurrection when he said, 'before I had gone from whence I do not return' (Job 10:21).
comments.selected_reason: Explains a verse that could be misread as denying resurrection.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Zophar says that the eloquent man thinks himself righteous, and many who sin use impressive words to hide their sins, which the righteous Job does not do.
comments.comment: Having understood, Sophar the Minean says: he who speaks much and is heard, or even the eloquent man, thinks himself to be righteous. … For many of those committing sin, by making the words impressive through the words themselves, think they are hiding sins by the probability of the words, wanting to deceive regarding the difficulty of the things done to them; but such is not the righteous Job testifying toward God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even the eloquent man who seems righteous, and even one thought long-lived, is short-lived as regards the coming age.
comments.comment: Blessed, a child of a woman, short-lived. He uses a probable word now, but the appropriate knowledge of the man is left behind. He says, therefore, that even if someone is eloquent and through the probability of the words brought forth by himself is thought to be righteous, he must recognize that he is short-lived. Even if someone is blessed by God and thought to be long-lived—for they thought a man blessed to be long-lasting and for many years—yet even this one is short-lived as regards the coming age; in order to show him, desiring, that he does not have precise knowledge of the things, for being short-lived according to men. And this is evident from the following things being brought forward: and 'a child of a woman' signifies the man circumspectly.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Much speaking is not a matter of how many words, for Paul extended his word until midnight.
comments.comment: And the divine word, training him not to have excess in words, says: 'From much speaking, one will not escape sin.' Here, 'much speaking' refers to the announcement that was not approaching. But the apostle makes it clear that it is not the multitude of announced words that makes it 'much speaking,' saying 'extending the word until midnight' (Acts 20:7) to those listening.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job never claimed to be blameless before God, for even those made righteous have a dim righteousness before the Judge, as Paul shows in saying he is not justified by a clear conscience.
comments.comment: For he does not say, 'I am pure in works and blameless before him.' Thinking he is advising him regarding his own assumption of purity, he approaches him as if the confession of this purity and blamelessness were a rejection of Providence; for friends think that if he had not sinned (1 Cor 11:30), he would not have fallen into dark places. But they do not show that Job said to God: 'I am blameless before you.' For he knew that 'stars are not pure before him' (Job 25:5), and what was said by those having been made righteous: 'All our righteousness is as a filthy rag before you' (Isa 64:6). For as toward you, the one being Judge, even if we have righteousness, we have it dim compared to you. And Paul, saying, 'I am not aware of anything against myself' (1 Corinthians 4:4) and adding, 'but I am not justified by this' (1 Cor 4:4), shows the weakness of natural kind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job must make himself fit for purity, not say he is pure, so that God may speak to him.
comments.comment: Therefore he says, 'Do not say, I am pure;' (Job 11:4) but rather, make yourself fit for purity, so that in this way God might speak to you and open His lips with you through goodness. His speech and His lips are to be understood as the conversation occurring invisibly in the intellect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When God sends pain for sin, He brings it as a physician for the soul's health, and His judgments, though too deep for us, work toward our good.
comments.comment: It is indeed true, when God brings on pains through sin, that one capable of understanding must see the induction through His wisdom and in the bitter things, that He is not defending the sinner, but is bringing the tribulations medically and toward the health of the soul; which one of the saints, knowing this, said: 'I will bless You, Lord, because You were angry with me for the sake of salvation.' To receive the knowledge of the judgments of God is a gift of God, concerning which it has been said: 'Abyss is the multitude of Your judgments.' (Psalm 36:6) We know this much: that they are being accomplished toward what is beneficial, even if we do not grasp it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Zophar speaks with presumption, not knowing why such things happen under God, since Job endured them out of manliness.
comments.comment: You have departed from the Lord because of the sins you committed (Job 11:6). He says he is still engaging in the same kind of reasoning as if speaking to one who has sinned, that if the Lord were to speak to you and make you understand according to his own wisdom, from which having known his superiority you would learn, 'that you have departed from the Lord because of the sins you committed.' … And he speaks these things with presumption, not knowing the causes of those things which happen under God, toward the one being addressed, that because of manliness he endured these things, awaiting the praise from God, …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job will not find a trace of the Lord, for the administrations of providence are too great to grasp.
comments.comment: He reasons with the holy man with a certain plausible boldness; for since he knew that the administrations of providence are great to grasp, he makes a discourse to him, saying: 'You will not find a trace of the Lord, nor will you reach the ends,' saying 'ends' in reference to the outcomes of things happening.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Heaven, Hades, earth and sea show that human knowledge is measured and does not reach God's judgments.
comments.comment: He wishes to show through all these things that the knowledge of men is measured, not reaching the judgments of God. And now indeed: heaven, he says, is deeper and more distant than Hades, and the earth and the breadth of the sea; say something about them, if you are able.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: These words refute those trained in Greek philosophy, who speak much of such things yet cannot demonstrate them.
comments.comment: This can be used to refute those experienced in Greek philosophy who are said to speak of the nature of heaven, earth, or sea, when they are actually empty regarding these things and say much about Hades, claiming it is a place for souls and other things, seizing words whose demonstration they cannot make manifest; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one can say to God 'What have you done?', since no one resists His will.
comments.comment: But if he searches out all things, who will say to him: 'What have you done?' and this he truly says, even if he does not look toward the proper goal. 'For who resists the will of God?' (Romans 9:19) It is like this: 'Does the creature say to the Creator: Why have you made me thus?' … For he himself knows the works of the lawless; having seen the absurd, he will not pass them by. It is clear, then, that he spoke through the 'if he searches out all things'; for he says he knows the works of men, not being indifferent to their faults—demonstrating the unrequited justice of God—and he sees them among the foolish.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Calling a mortal born of woman equal to a wild donkey presents the extreme slowness of men to grasp God's judgments.
comments.comment: But a man is differently sounded by words, and a mortal born of woman is equal to a donkey in the wilderness. He says that those who compare the secure knowledge of God to the impositions of men are sounded in vain, comparing him to a donkey, thereby presenting the extreme slowness of men toward the apprehension of judgments, using the word excessively.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The luminous life promised is either the life to come or life without toil, enlightened by the sun of righteousness, and gives hope of the good things prepared.
comments.comment: He says it is either the life to come or the life without toil, by transitioning from the burdensome things. And the luminous life is found being enlightened by the 'sun of righteousness' (Mal 4:2). It has been said: 'In the morning I will stand by you and watch' (Psalm 5:3). And it shall be certain to you that there is hope for you. And again he says that he believes from the preparation concerning the hoped-for good things.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Peace is the soul's tranquility, the fruit of the Spirit, which comes to the one who casts his care on the Lord, while the life of the ungodly is disturbed by anxiety.
comments.comment:
And from the absence of anxiety and care, peace is revealed to you. He says this, that having been freed from the burdensome and painful things through the hope having come from the preparation, 'peace is revealed to you,' saying peace as the rest from circumstances.

And we have in the divine writings things said concerning peace of the kind according to the soul, concerning which it is said: 'great peace is in those who love you, and there is no stumbling block in them' (Psalm 119:165). And this, being the tranquility of the soul, is the fruit of the Spirit: 'for the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace' (Gal 5:22). From this they are blessed, concerning whom it is said: 'blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God' (Matt 5:9).

For when anyone 'casts his own care upon the Lord' (1 Pet 5:7), he shall have this peace; but the sinner shall not be in this peace, 'for all the life of the ungodly is in anxiety' (Job 15:20) being disturbed. And you shall be at rest, and he who wars against you shall not be, but many, changing their minds, shall entreat you. Understand, if again this one says that he no longer is insulted as a worthless man through any kind of maltreatment; the fact that this is coming implies 'but many, changing, shall entreat you,' signifying that those who formerly rushed against you shall entreat you because of the change in you.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The peace of the holy one is that of a man resting under his vine and fig tree, fearless of any deceiver or demon.
comments.comment: And the peace which is principally the tranquility of the soul is given to the holy one, the Word saying: 'every man shall rest under his vine and under his fig tree, and none shall terrify him' (Mic 4:4). And this is not sensually; but he who has the practical life, signified by the fig tree, and the contemplative, which is signified by the vine—being a poetic thing of gladness—is therefore fearless, not having a deceiver to terrify him or demons.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Quietude belongs to human nature and disorder is an intruder, and earthly men take up quietude when fear of judgment brings them to repentance.
comments.comment:
Furthermore, regarding Cain, it has been said that one ought not to be moved: 'You have sinned, be still' (Gen 4:7). For quietude of tranquility is a dwelling in human nature, whereas disorder is an intruder.

And now a symbol is interpreted as the soul dwelling in the earth: 'The earth was afraid and was still when God arose for judgment' (Psalm 76:8). For when those doing earthly things become through the fear of judgment in repentance, they take up quietude instead of disturbance, hearing: 'And you will be still, without fear of every evil' (Proverbs 1:33), and salvation will remain for them.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The expectation of the wicked is destruction in the sense that destruction follows from what they expect.
comments.comment: For their hope is destruction. Regarding the evil-doers, he says that expectation is destruction; he might say that their expectation is not exactly that which they themselves are expecting, but as that which follows having that expectation; just as we say to one falling into punishment: 'You brought these things upon yourself,' not that he himself set this forth, but that he followed it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dimmed eyes of the ungodly are not their bodily eyes but the eyes of the soul, which God's commandments enlighten.
comments.comment:
'But the eyes of the ungodly will be dimmed' (Job 11:20). Perhaps he hints at the envious and their sorrow which comes upon the change of having fallen into misfortune, as he wrote. But he does not speak of these eyes—for many of the ungodly remained sharp-sighted until their later breath—but of the eyes of the soul.

You have in the divine writings concerning the eyes of man: 'The commandment of the Lord is a bright light, enlightening eyes' (Psalm 19:8), meaning that God's commandments save the eyes of the inner man, even if they are blind.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's question 'Are you then men?' says that his friends think greatly of themselves and suppose wisdom ends with them, though God's judgments surpass human things.
comments.comment: Job says: 'Are you then men? Or will wisdom end with you?' (Job 12:2). He says: 'You are indeed men, but thinking great things about yourselves and regarding yourselves as the only men, you think that wisdom remains until you; but you suppose that you can grasp the judgments of God and decide something about them; and in reality, it surpasses human things.' For he says, 'Your judgments are a great abyss' (Psalm 36:6). But Paul also writes that these things are 'unsearchable' (Rom 11:33). And it is shown through 'will wisdom end with you?' that the wisdom of God is not limited to the human.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who mock and overpower the righteous provoke God and will be examined, for they are instruments of wrath who rejoice in the service and act without mercy.
comments.comment:
They provoke the Lord, so will there not be an examination of them? He teaches that even if someone mocks the righteous and overpowers him, he will not be innocent, even if he conquers him by appearing to do so. For such a person provokes God. For there will be an examination of the things done, through which judgment is hinted at, just as Paul says: 'For it is necessary for us all to appear before the judgment seat of Christ, so that each one may receive for what he did through the body' (2 Corinthians 5:10). It also suggests to understand that 'even if those who made claims are acting wickedly by taking authority over me, these are not innocent, having become instruments and vessels of wrath, even if they do this while acting against a sinner' (Romans 9:22). For they rejoice in such service. …

To whom indeed is it said: 'I gave them into your hands, but you did not give them mercy' (Isaiah 47:6) and 'I was angry with them a little, but they persisted in evils' (Isaiah 47:6)? For God does not hand them over so that they may use mercy without restraint; but they, doing this with much eagerness, act without mercy; and Pharaoh toward the sons of Israel is such.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's call to ask the animals, birds and earth shows the depth of God's judgments, of which man knows only in part, and means that one should inquire of creation whether the deepest things can be grasped.
comments.comment: But 'ask the four-footed, if they tell you; and the birds of heaven, if they announce to you; command the earth, and it will explain to you; and the fish of the sea will explain to you' (Job 12:7-9). He wishes to show the depth of judgments and the value of man here, saying that the judgments are incomprehensible, of which man receives knowledge only 'in part' (1 Corinthians 13:12). But it is not appropriate to take it quite this way, that one must ask the four-footed as if to receive an answer from them, but 'inquire of the four-footed, and in the birds, and of the creation in the earth, and judgments, and examine, if it is possible to grasp the deepest things in these words.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The hand of the Lord made these things, so the general reason is plain even where the reason for each event is hidden, and those who ascribe things to chance must be rebuked.
comments.comment: Who then has not known in all these things that the hand of the Lord made these? Having said that the reason for each of the things that happened is hidden, through which he taught his friends to understand, and claiming that for the sake of sin it happens to him as something hidden and not readily available, he presents something else as instruction: that the general reason is manifest, even if the other part happens to be hidden. … From these things, those who introduce the automatic must be rebuked, for everything is governed by order and providence.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul of every living thing and the life and death of men are in God's hand, so the friends should not say unrighteously that Job suffered through sin.
comments.comment: Is not the soul of all living things and the spirit of every man in his hand? He who teaches them the things of instruction confirms this, that everything is under the hand of God, both the life of men and death—this is similar to that in the Gospel: 'Are not two sparrows sold for an ass's coin? And will not one of them fall into a snare without the Father of him who is in heaven?' (Matt 10:29)—constructing nothing else through this except to make them understand their own intellect regarding the judgments of God, and not to say unrighteously that he has suffered through sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The mind distinguishes words as the larynx tastes food, so knowing the judgments of providence belongs to the mind and not to irrational creatures.
comments.comment: For the mind distinguishes words, but the larynx tastes grain. Understand, if these things are given toward those: 'But ask the four-footed, if they tell you' (Job 12:7). It is clear from the sequence that knowing the judgments of providence is not irrational or soulless, but of the mind. And he takes a paradigm: just as the larynx is a critic of foods, so the mind is of the things spoken and of the things contained in the nature of the whole. 'Discern therefore also you,' he would say to his friends, 'these things, and you will find my way.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains what the verse says in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom comes only with much time, which rebukes those unwilling to toil for it.
comments.comment: Wisdom comes in much time, and science in much life. … From this, those unwilling to toil, but thinking that the occasional imposition of some science is enough for them, are to be rebuked. For the knowledge of perfect things does not occur at the same time as one begins.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom and power are not from outside God but in Him, and the power with Him is Christ, the power and wisdom of God.
comments.comment: With Him are wisdom and power, with Him counsel and understanding. Having said "wisdom in much time," in order that you do not think him to be speaking about human wisdom, he teaches not to seek it among created things, but how it is found, saying: "With Him are wisdom and power." For it is not from without Him, but in Him it is, being of the same essence as Him; for the source of it exists, and the source does not receive from elsewhere. And the power is with Him, which is Christ; "for Christ is the power and wisdom of God" (1 Cor 1:24). And with Him also are counsel and understanding, so that these things are not sought by human impositions, but from Him.
comments.selected_reason: Explains whose wisdom and power the verse speaks of.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's counsel cannot be withstood, since the sufferer and the afflicted are as they are by his will, and no one may say 'Why did you make me thus?'
comments.comment:
If he casts down, who will build up? If he shuts according to men, who will open? …

The word concerning providence, as also previously was said, he teaches by silence to those contradicting him. For even if they were setting forth providence, they were falling into oppositions. He says therefore: "Who has withstood his counsel?" (Job 42:3); for indeed one finds the one suffering, the one in distress, the one weighed down by disease, and others being seized in various accidents and not being able to stand, being cast away. For they happen according to the will of God. Not only concerning building, but also concerning the aforementioned, there is no one who will be able to say according to the apostle: "Why did you make me thus?" (Rom 9:20); but also those who dare something apart from the will of God, since they did not call upon Him, are turned away.
comments.selected_reason: Explains that no one can withstand God's counsel in what befalls us.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's speaking to the Lord shows his confidence, meaning he will state his own case, knowing God knows the cause of his harm.
comments.comment:
'But not, but I will speak to the Lord, and I will contend against him, if he pleases' (Job 13:3). Having accused them as being mistaken, he says 'I will speak to the Lord', showing his own self-confidence. And 'I will contend against him' is instead of 'I will demonstrate my own position, if he wishes according to the hypothesis; for I know that he himself knows the cause of the harm'.

… Similar to this is 'Do I now persuade men or God?' (Galatians 1:10) and 'The one who judges me is the Lord' (1 Corinthians 4:4). It is not small, but perfect, and as God testified in the beginning 'righteous and blameless' (Job 1:8), so to say 'I will speak to the Lord' and 'I will contend against him, if he pleases' is perfect.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's boldness in speaking to the Lord.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends were unjust physicians because, thinking to console Job, they blamed his suffering on sin without knowing its cause.
comments.comment:
And you are all unjust physicians and healers of evils. …

… These ones who were rebuking Job said to him, more out of ignorance than out of malice, 'You suffer because of sins,' thinking they were bringing words of consolation; they were therefore unjust because they were ignorant of the cause. As for 'all are physicians of evils,' this might be said regarding those who think highly of themselves, as if they were able to heal what is happening to others by chance.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'physicians' in terms a reader can follow.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job prays that his friends may learn when to speak and when to be silent, since recognizing their own stumbling is the beginning of wisdom.
comments.comment:
May you be struck deaf, and may it result for you in wisdom. He prays that they might have knowledge of the seasons, when it is necessary to speak and when it is necessary to be silent, having recognized that they stumble; for this shall be to them a beginning and a precursor of wisdom. For if they would learn that it is also possible to be afflicted in a different way in order that the present virtue might be revealed, wisdom shall be to them.

… For when anyone recognizes that there is need of students and of a teacher who enlightens, it shall result to him in wisdom. Just as he who is able to speak about wisdom and to teach is wise and a teacher, so also he who is able to ask what ought to be asked is in part wise.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how silence or being struck deaf could become wisdom.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Mouth and lips stand for the word, and the holy man rebukes and judges skillfully, lawfully, and never untimely or falsely.
comments.comment: 'Hear the rebuke of my mouth, and pay attention to the judgment of my lips.' He says mouth and lips instead of the word. But the holy one rebukes as holy and judges as becomes Him; he uses rebuke and judgment skillfully and legally; for the righteous does not have an untimely rebuke, nor does he do this falsely, but having judged.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job begins to teach his friends by appealing to their conscience, warning that they speak deceit as if God were not present.
comments.comment: Whether you speak not in the presence of the Lord, and speak deceit toward him, or whether you shrink back? From their own conscience he begins to teach them by reproof, that whatever they bring forth, seeing God, they speak; but he also announces to them the deceit as being brought forth in his presence for the sake of correction, so that they might cease from such a disposition, since they have the Lord watching over them. And therefore he prevents their audacity, because just as they shrank back from a man, hiding deceit and speaking against him, so they do to God.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sinners, enticed by pleasure, forget God's eye, but a righteous man's call brings the conscience to see that God watches the inward thoughts.
comments.comment: But you yourselves become judges. It is well, if it searches you out. If anyone says: "How is it that he just said 'you are unjust doctors' (Job 13:4) and 'whether you speak not in the presence of the Lord, and speak deceit toward him'" and now says: "but you yourselves become judges"? To this it must be said: that each of those sinning, being enticed by pleasure, does not perceive the eye of the God who watches. But if a righteous and wise man, or even another such, is called, the conscience of the sinner leads him to the realization that God sees the inward thoughts of each, striking him into perception. This is therefore what the saint does, saying: "but you yourselves become judges. It is well, if it searches you out." For those being conscious of a slip do not wish to be searched out even by a righteous man, how much less by God; for of the saints it is such, according to David saying: "refine my reins and my heart" (Psalm 26:2).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even one who has done all that is required may still be reproved for unintended faults, because only God's judgment justifies.
comments.comment:
“Having done all things that must be done, you shall be added to him”—instead of “you shall make yourselves his own”—“you shall again be subject to reproof through ignorances.” This indeed the blessed apostle was saying: “I do not consider myself my own conscience, but not in this have I been justified” (cf. 1 Cor 4:4). For it enters into me to overlook something of the ignorances, and I have not been justified because of that. And as far as I think I have no conscience against myself, I think I am without responsibility. But it is not my judgment that shows me having been justified, but the judgment of God.

The blessed David also confirms this, saying: “Who will understand trespasses? From my secret parts cleanse me” (Psalm 19:12).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A good judge looks to the actions and not to the faces of rich or powerful men, as God's law commands.
comments.comment: And if even in secret you should admire faces, whether not his agitation will trouble you, and fear will fall upon you from him? The best judge of matters is the examiner; he does not look toward the faces of those being judged. For if those being judged were rich or rulers or others possessing superior value, he does not look toward their face, but toward the actions, which he judges. … But God, standing as protector, does not will thus, but lays down law: "according to the great and the small you will judge, you will not receive a face," clearly of the rich, and "you will not have mercy on the poor in judgment" (Deuteronomy 1:17).
comments.selected_reason: Explains in plain terms what showing partiality means and why God forbids it.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, angry at sinners, will shake those who secretly show partiality, and fear will fall on them.
comments.comment: … 'if you also marvel at faces in secret' (Job 13:10); for every bribetaker does not accept the things of those providing from the visible, but in secret, often also in a disguised manner, according to that, he wishes to come together. And he brings fear, saying that if someone dares to hide the thing of partiality by craft, but God, being angry through the onslaught against the sinners, will shake them, instead of 'he will let the passion be provided to them.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The fear that follows sinners is a threat meant for their benefit, and differs from the reverent fear of the Lord, which lacks nothing.
comments.comment: Let us return to the beginning, to those 'marveling at faces in secret,' whom also the anger of God according to a whirlwind will shake, as it was given; and upon them also fear falls from God, and this is for benefit, so that they may know that a threat is brought against them as sinners. And of this fear, which I say according to the threat, is another by which it is said: 'the fear of the Lord surpassed all' (Sirach 25:11), which is primarily reverence. For there is no other fear of God or heightened respect, through which those having it become lacking; 'for there is no deficiency to those fearing him' (Psalm 34:9). But the passive fear follows the sinners.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Ashes mean worthlessness, so the boasting of those who judge in secret will be consumed and come to nothing.
comments.comment:
But your boasting shall pass away like ashes. The word shows the state after the wrath of those sinning, being brought to nothing in the revelation occurring through the wrath, the conceit of those judging secretly being consumed.

Since ashes signify worthlessness, it is to be learned from one of the twelve prophets saying, 'And you shall trample down the lawless and they shall be as ashes under your feet' … For ashes are something burning that has lost its own power.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what ashes stand for in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Sins burned up like thorns no longer defile the soul but call it to repentance, and one who receives the saving fire turns to a rigorous life.
comments.comment:
And it is for some benefit that sins are burned up; just as thorns and thistles, being burned, do not bring a little harm, so also the sins—even if they are burned according to what is said, 'the lawlessness shall be burned like fire and shall be consumed by fire like dry stubble' (Isaiah 9:18)—they no longer defile the soul, but are called out toward repentance according to what is said in the Gospel: 'If the powers that happened in you had occurred in Tyre and Sidon, long ago, sitting in sackcloth and ashes, they would have repented' (Matt 11:21).

For if anyone receives in his mind the salvation-fire, about which the Savior said, 'I came to cast fire upon the earth, and what do I want, if it is already kindled' (Luke 12:49), he burns up the former sins; and sitting, instead of 'having ceased from sinning,' he is turned toward repentance, choosing a somewhat severe and rigorous life.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The body shows itself to be clay when a man cares nothing for his salvation, though under the soul's rule it serves the soul.
comments.comment:
But the body is clay. Man is composed of soul and body. And there is a time when the body is led away as a slave by the soul and, in a certain way, is no longer being treated as clay, but being a servant to the soul along with reason and with the mind acting.

But when someone cares for nothing of his salvation, his soul, turning toward wickedness and serving the flesh, doing such things as do not differ from an irrational animal, he shows that his body is clay, as nothing helping from the soul's movements.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'the body is clay' means in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No deceit can come before God, either because deceit does not dare approach the truth or because there is no deceit in God's nature.
comments.comment: For no deceit will enter against Him. Desiring to present its truthfulness and its reverence, he says: 'What I say, I speak as one seeing God. For it is not possible for any deception to occur to God, as to let deceit enter before Him.' This, however, could be understood in two ways according to the similar parallel, which is thus essentially evangelical: 'And the light shines in the darkness, and the darkness did not overcome it' (John 1:5). For that which is overshadowing is released by the presence of the light, or whatever approaches as a deception near the light is turned away; when the deception is released, it does not grasp at all. For all those who deceive and scheme are ignorant in their zeal; for the beauty of the truth they shall not grasp. Thus, deceit does not approach the spring of truth because those using it do not dare to bring it to itself. And in another way, there is no deceit in God; for it is not His nature to be in Him. 'For God is faithful, and there is no injustice in Him' (Deuteronomy 32:4). And again: 'If we are faithless, He remains faithful' (2 Tim 2:13). For He is unshakeable and unchangeable.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job repeats 'Hear' to call his friends firmly to listen, since a voice can strike the ear without being heard.
comments.comment: Hear, hear my words; for I announce them to you as you are listening. The word repeats, so that He might call them firmly to listen. For it is possible for the hearing to be struck by the voice without having heard, because of not paying attention with the mind. Therefore, the Savior, awakening those listening so that they might listen truly, said: 'He who has ears to hear, let him hear' (Matt 13:9). … Thus also the blessed Job, desiring to prepare their hearing, said the 'Hear'; for as He says, 'since you have been prepared, I am pleased to speak,' desiring them to become wise listeners
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job repeats 'Hear' in the verse.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's 'I shall appear righteous' looks to a future time and is not a claim that he is already righteous.
comments.comment: And if Job once said, … 'I know that I shall appear righteous' (Job 13:18), … he said this … saying: 'I know that if I should use courage until the end, "I shall appear righteous."' For he did not say: 'I am righteous,' but he inclined his expectation toward a future time, announcing the proper characteristic of virtues.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the wording 'I shall appear righteous'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's confidence that he will appear righteous is not arrogance but a discipline of his friends, so that they hold no impression of him other than the truth.
comments.comment:
But the desire of a wise man is to listen. 'Behold, I am near to my judgment' (Job 13:18). This is the beginning of instruction for them, and now it is being cast down as a discipline, because he has been judged to suffer not because of sin, but because of a struggle, so as to know the time according to which the judgment will end. I know that I shall be revealed as righteous.

For who is the one to be judged by me, saying, 'That I will now deafen and exclude him'? He does not say this out of arrogance, but to discipline them so that they may not have any impression concerning him other than the truth. … In this way, do not blame Job for self-love, but because of the stated reason he says these things and says them with pure boldness: 'Who is he that will be judged by me so that I may deafen,' instead of 'I will be silent' (Job 13:19), 'and exclude,' instead of 'I will cease speaking.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hiding from God's face is the sinner's lot, as Adam hid, but being hidden in the secrecy of God's face is protection for the earnest.
comments.comment:
It will be necessary for me to die: 'Then from your face I will hide; withhold your hand from me, and let your fear not terrify me' (Job 13:21).

The ambiguity of the things foretold would be smoothed out by him saying, 'If as the friends say, it will be necessary for me to do this, showing it as trivial, "from your face I will hide"; but if as I say, "withhold your hand from me and let your fear not terrify me".' 'For every one who sins, working unworthily, is hidden from the face of God,' just as Adam was hidden from the face of God. Contrary to this is being hidden by God according to what is said: 'You will hide them in the secrecy of your face from the disturbance of men' (Psalm 31:20). This too covers the earnest one with God's protection, so that he may not fall by human disturbances.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's bold challenge to God proves his righteousness, and his asking God to teach him his sins is reverent, for good men learn from mistakes.
comments.comment:
Then you will call, and I will answer you; or you will speak, and I will give you a reply' (Job 13:22). Through many things he shows his boldness toward God, so that in this he might lead them to a true understanding of what is happening to him. And this is proof of his righteousness.

… 'How many are my sins and my lawlessness? Teach me what they are' (Job 13:23). Again through them he says such things, so that they may learn that one who has sin and lawlessness does not know God. And he himself, having said 'I know that I shall appear righteous' to the friends, speaks reverently to God, saying, 'Teach me how many my sins are' (Job 13:23). Similar to this is 'I know nothing about myself, but I am not justified by this; the one judging me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:3). It is also good to learn from mistakes, so that we may turn away from them.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's boldness and his request to be shown his sins.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job's complaint of a hidden God was spoken because of his friends' misunderstanding, since God was not hidden from him.
comments.comment:
'Why do you hide from me, and consider me your adversary?' (Job 13:22). This is due to their misunderstanding; for God dwelling in him was not hidden from him, but because of their thinking this, these things were said. 'For these think that you are against me, supposing that I suffer because of sin (Job 13:24).' Or, like a leaf moved by the wind, or like grass carried by the spirit, you have opposed me.

Regarding me, the whole of the understanding would be thus: 'Why do you hide me, supposing me to be against you, like a leaf moved by the wind and grass carried by the spirit?' This turns out to be characteristic of a changeable manner and fickleness, according to that which is said by the Savior concerning John: 'Why did you go into the wilderness to see? A reed shaken by the wind?' (Matthew 11:7)—instead of 'something easily dismissed and falling by chance.' These things, as previously said, Job says toward the dispute of the friends.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job speaks of recorded evils, sins of youth, and a foot in the mire to suit his friends' assumption that the afflicted suffer for sin.
comments.comment:
'That you have recorded evils against me, and you have left for me the sins of youth.' It is clear that he speaks toward their assumption; for now he says 'evils' regarding the afflictions.

… 'You put my foot in mire.' He does not say these things according to his own will, but toward the one supposing that every one being afflicted undergoes this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The saints often speak of their own sins of youth out of moderation, and Job says this to match his friends' assumption.
comments.comment: … And if he speaks of his own 'sins of youth' and presents 'you have guarded all my works' as having sinned, it is not to be wondered at; for all the saints, for the sake of moderation and good-mindedness, offer such voices, just as the men in the furnace and the blessed David said: 'Do not remember the sins of my youth and my ignorances' (Psalm 25:7). 'You have reached to the roots of my feet.' This means 'you have made all that concerns me as exact as the roots, that is, both the reasons and the beginnings of my practical progressions, to observe so that you might lead me to punishment.' And this again he says based on their assumption.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why a righteous man like Job can speak of his own sins.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job answers that a man born of woman is short-lived, so the weight of his trials cannot be put down to sin and are for a struggle.
comments.comment: He presents the cause of his suffering by joining together the weight of the temptation and human life; … he brings forward as a supporting argument for the matter not being so, 'but man born of woman is short-lived and full of wrath' (Job 14:1). Because of the hardship of life, he would not have brought such punishment upon the short-lived and full of wrath, unless he had encountered it for the sake of a struggle. For if the goodness of God and the brevity of men's lives had coincided, these things would not still have been reckoned as having happened because of sin.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how Job uses the brevity of man's life in his argument.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A passing man, like a flower and a shadow, was not struck with such evils because of sins, for if God marked iniquities none could stand.
comments.comment: That for the passing man, like a flower and a shadow, such evils were brought upon him, it is not according to the present context because of sins. 'For if he observes iniquities, Lord, Lord, who shall stand? But with you is the atonement' (Psalm 130:3-4). So it was to be understood by the friends, that not because of mistakes, but as is foretold, because he was set before the goal of manliness, these things happened to him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God, who cares for men, would not demand justice from man so unyieldingly and absolutely as his friends suspected.
comments.comment: But indeed I have composed a discourse of this, not bypassing it so as to let it enter into judgment before you. A proof of this would be what is said toward God: 'My people, what have I done to you?' (Micah 6:3) and again, 'Behold, I am being judged against you.' For God, bringing in such a care concerning men, would not have demanded justice from man so unyieldingly and absolutely, as his friends suspected him of punishing.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: No one is clean from filth, so Job shows he does not suffer for sin, since otherwise no one would be without trouble.
comments.comment: For who is clean from filth? Not even one, even if his life on the earth be but one day, and his months be numbered before you. And he joined these things together so that they might understand that he does not suffer because of sin. For if it were so, no one would be without trouble, even if he lived for a short time.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's argument from the universal filth of man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Filth and sin differ, since the filth is the unintentional acts which the Savior cleansed, as Isaiah says.
comments.comment:
And filth and sin, someone else might say, signify the same thing, with the one saying the filth of sin as something lesser of the other.

You have concerning filth and sin in Isaiah thus: 'The Lord will wash away the filth of the sons and the daughters of Zion, and will cleanse the blood from their midst' (Isaiah 4:4), the blood signifying sin there, the unclean thing, and the filth the unintentional acts, which the Savior, having come, cleansed by himself.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man's span is shown to be set by God's judgment and will, not by fate or chance.
comments.comment: The providence concerning man is made clear here, not as if it remains in life as it happens and as it pleases, but from the judgment of God, not exceeding the time appointed by Him. And these things are not to be said as being held by fate, but as the will of God, 'having appointed each thing by limits and measures.'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse about man's appointed bounds.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: A newborn, even if he lives only a day or a numbered few months, is not purified, because ignorance remains in one who begins to tell the false from the good.
comments.comment: And 'neither is the life of the one on earth even a single day' can be interpreted in two ways. There is the one being born now who has the sin of Adam by succession, … Nor will such a person be purified in a day, because ignorance remains for the one who has also begun now to distinguish the false from the good, even if he lives for a day, even if he lives for a numbered number of months.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Depart from Him' means 'cease your anger,' since under so many afflictions man would have no opportunity to repent.
comments.comment: Depart from Him, so that he may be at rest and find the life well-pleasing like the laborer. Since God is present to him through providences, the 'depart' has been said instead of 'cease your anger.' … For if he imposes such a multitude of afflictions upon him, man has no opportunity for repentance. He instructs them, therefore, that they do not understand this sensibly, through 'depart from Him, so that he may be at rest.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job would rather await his resurrection hidden in Hades than undergo so many pains, and the righteous before Christ's coming live better there.
comments.comment:
… being hidden there, 'until the wrath passes' (Job 14:13), as it is being said of God to remember him, in order to say more clearly that he would rather receive the time of his resurrection in Hades than undergo so many pains.

… the righteous man lives better during the time before the coming of Christ, since he is about to be liberated from the clamorous and sickly body to enjoy the incorruptible. … Not unsuitably, being persuaded and knowing concerning the resurrection of the dead, he places the more excellent deliverance from the painful life here, that it is more beautiful 'to be dissolved and to be with Christ' (Phil 1:23)
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Man's nature is not scattered like an animal's but immortal, so 'until I become again' signifies the resurrection.
comments.comment:
"If a man dies, he shall live having completed the days of his life" (Job 14:14), from which a doctrine concerning resurrection is presented and a judgment of each life in this life, not occurring randomly or by chance when death happens. …

… For the nature of man did not have it as they thought, that having possessed subsistence until the present life, having cast off this life, he is no longer, just like the irrational animals.

For the souls of irrational animals are scattered with their bodies, and therefore they are destroyed. But since the nature of man is not scattered, nor is he destroyed; for he is immortal. … "I will wait," for he says, "until I become again," signifying the resurrection
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the verse points to the resurrection and the immortal soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: 'Until I become again' means resurrection is a kind of birth, in which the rising body is raised incorruptible.
comments.comment: The phrase 'until I become again' must be explained in this way: resurrection is a kind of birth. For this reason, 're-birth' is spoken in relation to the Savior. … Thus also of the resurrection, whether it is a transfer into the dust of the body, or into something else according to these changes, the rising body is raised incorruptible. It is, therefore, a birth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God's call and Job's answer show that not only the body but also the soul is raised, so God does not cast away the works of his hands.
comments.comment:
But 'I will respond to you when you call again' stands in opposition to the opinion of those who mock: 'Let us eat and drink, for tomorrow we die' (Isa 22:13). …

Then 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' Wishing to show that not only the body is raised, but also the soul possessing the thoughts concerning God, he says, 'you will call, and I will respond to you.' For to listen to God calling is proper to a rational being. 'Do not cast away the works of your hands' (Job 14:15). Having taught concerning the resurrection of the whole human and the immortality of the soul, he instructs his friends so as not to consider him judged as insignificant by God.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's call and answer as pointing to the resurrection of the whole man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job speaks as a sinner out of moderation and for his friends' instruction, so that they may imitate his words of repentance.
comments.comment: 'You have enumerated my faults to me, and you will not pass over any of my sins' (Job 14:16). … 'I will note if I have passed by unintentionally' (Job 14:17).
