As if speaking to them again, he says these things while they are at odds, as if he were undergoing these things as a sinner, and by moderation and for their instruction, so that they might imitate him being so pure and bringing forth words of repentance. 'You have sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Job 14:17). That is to say: 'You have included in them both the quality and the number.'
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The rock seems unshakeable, but the falling mountain and aging rock show that whatever rises through pride or hardness will be condemned.
comments.comment:
And the rock is mentioned because it sends out the impression as unshakeable, and because Christ is being formed and is an imitator of the true rock, concerning which it was said: 'And the rock was Christ' (1 Cor 10:4). …

… And even after saying that 'you sealed my iniquities in a bag' (Job 14:17) and how regarding his own sin he had brought forward the previously set forth things, he applied the words 'but the mountain falling shall fall, and the rock shall be made old from its place' (Job 14:18) to show that 'even if a mountain arises through pride or through hardness, its condemnation shall be,' having perceived this.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Water smooths stones as repentance frees a man of sin's roughness, so hope in man must not be lost, though without God his endurance is vain.
comments.comment:
Waters smoothed the stones, and waters overwhelmed the depths of the earth's soil; and did you destroy the endurance of man? He confirms through these things the previously spoken, that repentance is powerful.

For through 'waters smoothed the stones' (Job 14:19), he demonstrates that the one beginning to repent, persisting in this, according to the water which removes the excess from the stone, frees himself from the superfluities of sin, as if no longer having the roughness from it, and just as lying in the depths of soils, he works the flood of sin. 'If these things have this manner, do not recognize the endurance of man, nor say that this is destroyed when it has worn him down and gone to an end.' He moves the word toward God. For after saying that repentance is possible and that one must not lose hope in man, he brings the 'having worn him down and gone to an end' as an instruction, that unless God is a co-worker, the things of endurance are in vain. …

For unless the Lord builds the house, they labor in vain who build it (Ps 127:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: God turns his face away not from the worthy but from the sinner who thinks himself hidden, though God fills heaven and earth.
comments.comment:
God does not push away the worthy person, but the one positioned in such a way, saying: 'Depart from me, workers of iniquity, I never knew you' (Matt 7:23). He turns His face away and drives them out.

It is said: 'The face of the Lord is against those doing evil' (Psalm 34:16); and again the saints pray: 'Let your face shine and we shall be saved' (Psalm 80:3); and in others: 'May His face shine upon you and give you peace' (Num 6:25). Therefore, if the sinner, through God's great patience, remains unfeeling toward his failings, not thinking himself to be God, but desiring to remain hidden, saying: 'Darkness covers me from every side and the walls, who sees me?', God says: 'I am a God drawing near and not a God far off. Shall anyone hide in secret and I shall not see him? Do I not fill heaven and earth? says the Lord' (Jer 23:24).

Having turned His face from the sinner, He sends him away, instead of 'showing him to be a stranger to Himself,' according to: 'God will drive them away because they did not listen to Him, and they shall be wanderers among the nations' (Hosea 9:17) and: 'Like wounded women cast down sleeping in a grave, of whom you no longer remembered, and they themselves were driven from your hand' (Psalm 88:5). And though many of His sons became so, he did not know; even if a few became so, he does not know.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God changes his countenance and sends the sinner away.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one who falls under wrath suffers and mourns without knowing why, while the brave man bears hardships looking to the crown.
comments.comment:
Rather, his flesh grieved and his soul mourned. This shows that as the wrath against the sinner moves according to the secret words of providence, the one falling into it suffers and mourns, but is ignorant of the words of the handing over. These things are instructional, so as not to say to friends that they know that one suffers through sin.

For the one who does not endure suffers and is consumed when he falls into calamities, but the brave man, even if he is stung by hardships, bears them courageously toward the goal, looking away (Heb 12:2). For only the one who seeks nothing good or useful suffers if he is afflicted. But the virtuous man, like a crowned athlete, does not regard the hardships because of the expectation of the crown.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse's pain of flesh and mourning of soul.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The speaker begins foolishly, charging Job with empty, profitless words that come from the pains he cannot restrain.
comments.comment: Existing in a state of delusion and thinking that he suffers through sin, he begins his words by asserting that it is wise to answer with understanding, implying that Job does not answer with understanding. This one, then, is a fool, and he is striking at the holy man regarding his lack of understanding. And he filled his belly with toil by reproving with words that are not to be used, and in words that have no profit. As it has been said, he begins foolishly; for he says that it is wise of the wise to answer sensibly, but 'he filled his belly with toil by reproving with words that are not to be used,' instead of saying 'from the pains, which he had in his heart and is unable to restrain, he brings forth words that are not to be used, and words in which there is no profit,' scattering his words as if they were useless and futile things sent forth.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The accuser, thinking Job suffers for sin, counts his bold words before the Lord as blasphemy and as proof against himself.
comments.comment: 'Will you not also cease from fear?' The preceding things are confirmed; for he reproves him as one who has not had fear, and it is clear that he also, by subjecting God, claims that because he has not had fear, but has suffered these things through sins, and that one not having fear uses such words. For they thought him bold, not knowing his virtue, supposing that having renounced fear, he says these things. 'Have you completed such words before the Lord?' Perhaps because of the easy availability of the words, which he brought forth purely from the one having conscience, he says these things, which this accuser considers as blasphemy, assuming the false beginning that he suffers through sin. 'You are guilty of the words of your mouth.' He dialogues with him with boldness as if he were bringing forth words against one who is not righteous. And he also thinks that he reproves him from his own words, asserting that 'you shall be reproved by words from yourself' (Job 15:6).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They tell Job he does not differ from other men and has no more grasp of the truth than they do.
comments.comment: For what? Did you not first come from men, or did you come upon the earth before the dusts? They want to present to him that 'you do not differ from other men, nor do you exist outside of their nature so as to have grasped more than the others,' in order that they might present themselves as having reached the truth, for which he suffers a cause.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Eliphaz denies Job any special wisdom, though he himself, not knowing God's judgment, should not have pre-judged Job a sinner.
comments.comment:
Or have you heard a divine arrangement, yet wisdom has come to you? Proposing the unsearchable nature of judgments from this, he thinks he is wandering into not knowing, that he suffers through something other than sin, being held by this. For he himself was not one having heard a divine arrangement or having wisdom come to him, so as to have a dispute concerning the Holy One as one suffering through sin. For what do you know that we do not know, or what do you understand that we do not? (Job 15:9).

He makes it common to all men, as if he were ignorant of the greatness of his virtue, and from this, as it is foretold, he is apparently overturning the idea of himself being righteous; which it was necessary that he, even while ignorant, should not pre-judge the judgment and be persuaded that he is bowed down as a sinner.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The charge that Job knows more than they do is spoken from arrogant authority, and falsehood may come from honest error or from arrogance.
comments.comment:
"an elder," he says, "you are, and an old one among us, becoming more weighty than even your father"—instead of "more venerable"—"knowing more than we do." And he says these things from an arrogant authority.

… "A few of your sins have been scourged." He says this meaning: "You have sinned and because of this you undergo lashes. But since, enduring this, you add injustice to God, your sin has become more weighty." And he says these things not with understanding; for he did not know the matter as it was, so that he was speaking falsely. And there are various ways of being false. For there is a way of lying that is not malicious; for often we hold an opinion about something as being such and we say it, having the intention of speaking the truth, yet that which is reported is false by its own nature, but it is not said by one who is lying. And there is also the case of one who, not knowing anything at all, brings forth a false word out of arrogance, which is what happened to him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: They took Job's bold words, which came from a pure conscience, for arrogance, in vain and without understanding.
comments.comment: "What did your heart dare, or what did your eyes lift up?" (Job 15:12). And they held these opinions about him, both hearing of his sins and because of his words of boldness. Since the blessed one brought forth words from purity, they thought this was an excess of arrogance, in vain and without understanding. "That you have broken a heart before the Lord, and have brought forth from your mouth such words."
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those without virtue think it too hard for anyone to be blameless, yet Scripture speaks of man both as weak and as crowned with glory.
comments.comment:
For what mortal is there that will be blameless, or that, as he is to come, will be a righteous offspring of a woman? It is a characteristic of those who do not possess virtue to consider this undertaking difficult and to place it as if no one possessed it, just as the one before says, stumbling because of the body's nature as it is likely to be weak.

If he had observed according to the soul and according to the intellect, he contemplated the greatness of human nature, which the hymnographer teaches on both sides, saying: 'What is man, that you take thought of him? Man is made like vanity' (Psalm 144:3-4), which he has said regarding the weakness of the body as comparing it to divine things. But instructing on greatness, he says again: 'You made him a little less than the angels, you crowned him with glory and honor' (Psalm 8:5).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: To 'believe' often means to be certain, and the 'heaven' not pure before God is the fallen angels, whose sword of punishment is drunken.
comments.comment:
He does not believe according to the saints. Similar to this is the 'if he does not believe according to his children, he thought something crooked concerning his angels.' Thus, there he says the angels are the saints, presenting that 'if even angels are corruptible, how can a man be blameless?' It should be noted that to believe often signifies the certain, as it is said: 'All his commandments are faithful' (Psalm 111:7). And he interprets their faithfulness saying: 'established unto the age of ages.' And again: 'the word is faithful and worthy of all acceptance.' And again: 'God is faithful and there is no injustice.' For God is not faithful from participating in faith, but from having certainty. And heaven is not pure before him.

Just as even the stars will not be compared to God's light, being without any darkness, and the heaven itself is not pure, not at all, but rather in addition to God. And it is possible to call these ones who 'left the heavenly dwelling' heaven here, whom he said 'his children, concerning whom he does not believe.' For God himself says in Isaiah from his own person: 'My sword is drunken in heaven' (Isaiah 34:5). And the sword signifies punishment, as it is said: 'My sword shall eat blood of wounds, and my arrows shall be drunken with blood' (Deuteronomy 32:42). Thus, among the angels who have fallen, he says the sword becomes drunken, bringing punishment called heavens. Therefore, this heaven is not pure before him.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even a ruler who acts arrogantly has only a numbered span of years and carries fear of death in his ears, while the diligent man, knowing it is better to be with Christ, is hopeful.
comments.comment:
The Lord, commanding his own disciples, says: 'Do not worry about tomorrow' (Matt 6:34). And it is a command, so that 'we should throw all anxiety upon the Lord' (1 Pet 5:7). And if he also says that life is 'in care,' and that years are a numbered amount given to a ruler, then his fear is in his ears. This he says, that even if someone is a ruler and acts insolently, let him know that he has a numbered number of years.

Power does not make him long-lived; for time is measured for men by God toward His own judgment. Therefore, even if the ruler acts arrogantly, his life and his years turn out to be few, and he always has fear in his ears because of the uncertainty of the manner of death. Such a person has a fearful nature. For when he is in care regarding life, he reveres even death. But the diligent one, knowing that it is better 'to depart and be with Christ' (Phil 1:23), is hopeful, not being such as the wicked, but one who fears; for it has been said that 'the impious flees when no one pursues' (Prov 28:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: When the wicked man seems at peace in his wealth, his destruction comes, as it did to the rich man in the Gospel.
comments.comment: When it seems to him that he is already at peace, his destruction will come. Even if someone exists in great prosperity, like the one saying in the Gospel: 'I will pull down my barns and build greater, and I will say to my soul: Soul, you have many good things, eat, drink, rejoice' (Luke 12:18-19); but the Lord says to him: 'Fool, this very night they will demand your soul from you; and what you have prepared, to whom will it belong?' (Luke 12:20). For when it seemed to him to be at peace in wealth, his destruction came.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the verse with the Gospel parable of the rich man.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner's sudden destruction is like the pangs of a woman in labor, since he has stored up for himself punishments of iron and gypsum.
comments.comment: The phrase 'when it seems to him to be at peace, his destruction will come' is similar to 'when they say: It is peace and security' (1 Thess 5:3). He says, 'Then, sudden destruction stands upon them just like the pangs of a woman in labor.' For he has already been committed into hands of iron, and has been arranged into pits of gypsum (Job 15:22b–23a). For the one sinning has hoarded for himself punishments, which will come through iron and gypsum.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The conscience of sinners knows it remains in a state of falling, and necessity and tribulation will cast down the evil one as a leading general.
comments.comment:
He knows in himself, as in Job 15:23b, that he remains in a state of falling. He says that the conscience of those committing sin knows the expectation of the habits of the wicked, that this is a state of falling.

A day of darkness shall surround him (Job 15:23c), instead of 'he is being tossed about by afflictions.' You have in Amos concerning this day: 'Woe to those who desire the day, and why is this day of the Lord upon you? And this is darkness and not light' (Amos 5:18–20), 'and a gloom where there is no light' (Amos 5:20). This is also in Job 10:22a. Necessity and tribulation shall cast him down (Job 15:24a). He says, therefore, that the wicked will fall into these things, preparing for all evil, because through sin he suffers these things (Job 15:24b), like a leading general falling. Even if it is not Job who is saying these things, but he possessed some knowledge of the devil, which it is likely he obtained from the words of Job or from other ancients. He calls him a leading general because of his primordial wickedness. He says, therefore, that necessity and tribulation, as mentioned in the preceding things, shall cast him down in such a way as a leading general; thus he too shall fall, being primordially wicked.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked man is bold in evil as if his thick shield made him invincible, and like false prophets in sheep's skin he deceives by disguise.
comments.comment:
Insolence ran against him (Job 15:26a). It is manifest through the fact that he does not act in secret, but against the Lord. And insolence can be both arrogance and every injustice; for those being reproached makes them worthy of insolence. The one insulting someone says these words and calls them wicked. But he does not entirely make him worthy of insolence; for neither praise makes one good, nor reproach makes one bad. He is in the thickness of his shield. Because he is bold in evil, he shows this in this: for as he uses the shield as if invincible, through its thickness and through fleshly habits. So also the false prophets, having put on the skin of a sheep, were 'wolves snatching' from within.

… Being transformed into an angel of light, he deceives and snatches away, and not as the devil; for if he were openly so, we would have fled him. So also the prostitute, personified in the poems, injects the venom with goodly words.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Evil enters 'uninhabited houses', the souls from which every virtue, God and the Holy Spirit have departed, and finds no place where a great dwelling stands.
comments.comment:
But he enters into uninhabited houses.

These things seem to be said about the devil, or about every evil and opposing power and soul partaking of the same wickedness; for their receptive qualities are of the same kind. And if anything is said about the devil as evil, as a worker of evil, it is possible for this same wickedness to be said about another evil power. Therefore, in general, we say about every evil that it enters into uninhabited houses; for where there is a significant dwelling, the evil one has no place.

And we have from the Gospel to demonstrate this: 'When the unclean spirit,' he says, 'goes out from the man, it passes through dry places seeking rest and does not find it' (Matthew 12:43). But dry places in these matters are the souls that are destitute of wickedness.

… Therefore, the souls there are 'uninhabited houses,' from which every virtue has been separated, and in the absence of which God has departed, and His word and the Holy Spirit; into which the devil, the opposing power, enters.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked prepare evil through malice and pleasures.
comments.comment: And pay attention, that he did not say 'what they have done', but 'what they have prepared', and they prepared through malice, through pleasures, through other evils.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked man will not be enriched, and since he is not from the beginning and malice will not last, he casts no shadow on the earth.
comments.comment:
Neither shall he be enriched, nor shall his existing things remain with him.

… Similar to this is 'the partridge has hatched what she did not lay; at the end of it they will leave it, at the end of it it will be a fool' (Jeremiah 17:11). It will not cast a shadow upon the earth. Bodies are the makers of shadows, and it is impossible for a shadow to exist without a body. And this one, since having undergone a certain way, does not remain—I do not say that his essence does not remain, but that he does not remain as he wished to be—therefore he does not cast a shadow; 'for he was not from the beginning' (Wisdom 14:13), he says, and malice 'will not be unto the age' (Job 15:35).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Malice is not essential but enters from outside, so when temptation strikes like a wind it withers, as a physician cuts away a tumor to bring health.
comments.comment: Nor shall he escape the darkness. And rightly so; for the one who is an instigator for others toward malice receives an irrecoverable punishment. A wind withers his sprout. Even if it seemed to flourish in those whom he deceived and in those in whom he would fulfill his malice, but this sprout is withered by the wind; for he does not have a root. For malice is not essential, but entering from without, which, when struck by temptation, which is called wind, is rebuked and falls and withers. And his flower will fall. The flower is the beginning and the precursor of fruit, and this therefore falls. Even if the one participating in malice boasts, a little later he is humbled. And this is often even beneficial, just as a physician often cuts away the tumor attached to the body with iron and does not cease to apply painful things, until he fulfills the goal, the healthy state.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Those who pervert God's judgments fall under punishment.
comments.comment: Judgment will come against the gifted. Because 'the judgment of God is present' (Rom 2:5), those who pervert the judgments of God fall under punishments. And in the belly, pains shall be taken. He means this: the man becomes a father of ill-born ones, being the cause of punishments.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: His labors are filled with futility and his belly with deceit, which Scripture uses as a name for all wickedness.
comments.comment:
It will depart from him empty, and his belly will be filled with deceit. All his efforts, as it is foretold, are filled with futility, … And deceit here he says is all manner of wickedness.

For deceit is indeed a kind of wickedness, and nothing less, and all wickedness is called by the name according to what has been said: 'O full of all deceit and all trickery' (Acts 13:10) and 'therefore laying aside all deceit and hypocrisy' (1 Peter 2:1).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends accuse those in distress without distinction, so 'all' may mean all who misjudge suffering, or the three, whose number makes a multitude.
comments.comment: … since they bring their accusations to those in distress without distinction, as if to separate them as bad ones, it is appropriate—just as the three friends have done—that he brought the phrase 'all are accusers of evils,' meaning that all, through ignorance of what is happening differently than it ought, either raise up or contract the painful things; or he said 'all' regarding the three, for from this number comes the multitude.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Had Job stayed silent he would have been judged more unjustly, as if conscious of the charges.
comments.comment: 'And if I keep silent, how much less shall I be wounded?' 'And if indeed in silence,' he says, 'I were to contain the insults, I would not only fail to attain the glory of philosophy, but on the contrary, I would be judged much more unlawfully for the silence of one thought to be conscious of the things being said.' He had not previously done this, but it happened because the adversary requested it.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job could not keep silent and why he was misjudged.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Hard words are a heavy load that reaches the soul more than bodily torment, and only a great man bears insult.
comments.comment: "Until when will you make my soul weary?" Heavy loads make beasts weary; heavy words do the same to a hearer. Pressed by the harsh, insulting speech of the other two who came with Baldad, Job feels a heavy load and asks how long they will weary his soul. The Sauchean is labeled tyrant beforehand; his words are tyrannical. Nothing reaches a human soul like a hard word. Many endure bodily torments and still cannot endure speech. The perfect athlete, even weary, endures harsh words; bearing insult belongs to a great man. So the Apostle lists among his brave deeds: "Being reviled we bless, being persecuted we endure, being defamed we exhort; we have become as the refuse of the world, the offscouring of all until now." Job’s book especially holds his courage and endurance — and still he feels the toil of hard words from those who came to visit.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why harsh words weigh on Job more than bodily pain.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job warns that the God who afflicts him can afflict them, and grants for argument that he sinned, yet asks whether he should be reproached so.
comments.comment: "Know only that the Lord made me thus." What you see about me has not come from elsewhere than God. Fear: the one who brings this on me can bring it on you. "You speak against me; unashamed, you press upon me." Evil speech happens often; when the speaker does not blush, he says it to the face — not to refute or tell truth, but to reproach and insult. One must not insult those God is punishing, but mourn and fear. "Yes, in truth I have wandered; a wanderer lodges with me — to speak a word one ought not." By hypothesis he grants their view that he suffers for sins — was it then necessary to reproach him so? Even if he had done what he ought not, seeing scourges, ichor, worms, and lost goods, should they not have felt shame? Instead they tread further, without pity.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They leap on Job with reproach as if trampling him, but under the fortress of his circumstance he answers only with laughter and silence.
comments.comment: "Allow that you magnify yourselves against me and leap on me with reproach" — not moderate rebuke, but leaping as if trampling. "His fortress he raised against me": under the wall of circumstance he is a fortress he cannot flee until God judges to take it down. "Look, I laugh at reproach, and I will not speak" — that is, "conquer the evil in the good." At their reproach he is thought to laugh, not to speak.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture often calls the body skin, and Job spoke of his own body when he said that his skin would be raised.
comments.comment: But that in many of the divine teachings the body is called skin, it is possible to find. For the blessed Job says: 'For I know that he who is about to release me is ever-enduring; he will raise my skin upon the earth that draws these things' (Job 19:26), and Job clearly spoke these things about his own body. And again the same says such things about himself: 'You clothed me with skin and flesh, and you brought me together with bones and sinews' (Job 10:11). For it is a clear and most evident sign that the skin garments are the body, since Job also remembers the one who clothed, which was also said concerning the first-formed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what Job means by his 'skin'.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Even when the impious man's gifts seem to reach heaven and he seems fixed firm, he is destroyed like smoke and passes like a dream.
comments.comment: "If his gifts go up into heaven and his sacrifice touches the clouds" — even of the impious. When a heretic prays, when sacrifice rises by high-speaking, when he seems fixed firm, then he is destroyed utterly. "His prayer is reckoned to him as sin; the prayer itself is sin. "When he seems already fixed, then he is destroyed utterly." Like "the enemies of the Lord: when they are glorified and exalted, they fail as smoke." Those who see him — we of the church who see their errors — will say, "Where is he?" "Like a dream flown away, he will not be found." Such people dream and mold fantasies; they do not rest the mind on truth, and become a dream that cannot be found.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The teacher's deeds kindle his own punishment, and the gall of an asp in his belly is the bitter teaching he gives out.
comments.comment: "Let lesser ones destroy his sons" — sons and disciples of the teacher of these things. "Let his hands torch pains": the deeds kindle punishment; this impious man’s hands will spend him in last pains — spoken also of the lawless one’s sons. "Gall of an asp is in his belly:" teachings not sweet but asp gall — the wine of their doctrine. … Asp gall sits in the belly of the heterodox and of anyone impious in doctrines opposite the truth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wealth of the impious is the wealth in their words, which God makes them vomit up, and the pastures are souls under the good Shepherd.
comments.comment: "Wealth gathered unjustly will be vomited out." What wealth is that but the wealth in their words? The Good One will not let the fallen keep unjust wealth forever; he makes them vomit it. "An angel will drag him from his house" — from the badly built house that is a church of evildoers — by God’s energy and kindness. "May he not see the milking of pastures." The heterodox do not see that milking. Pastures are souls under the good Shepherd: "I am the door; if anyone enters through me he will be saved, and will go in and out and find pasture."
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Teachings against God are tough and without sweetness, so the one who wants alien enjoyments gains nothing from his toil.
comments.comment: "Like tough herb, unchewed, unswallowable:" words and doctrines against God are tough and dense, with nothing sweet. As that plant cannot be swallowed even when chewed hard, so the one who wants alien enjoyments carries off no profit from the toil. "For this his good things will not bloom; when he seems filled, he is afflicted. Belongings cannot buy him salvation. "Every necessity will come upon him; wrath of anger is sent" … hortatory so we stand off from alien things.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The iron is a most cutting word.
comments.comment: "He will not be saved from a hand of iron": not perceptible iron, but a most cutting word.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fire on sinners is invisible and burns within, as a fever burns the inwards though no flame is seen.
comments.comment: "Let an arrow go through his body." Fired arrows wound him. "Let unburnable fire eat him." We learn a mystery of the punishment laid up, to guard ourselves from it. Material fire here is seen and burnable; that fire on sinners is invisible, burns within, is intelligible and punishing. Take the image of extreme fever: you see no fire, yet it underlies and burns the inwards. So sin-fever burns a person out.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the 'unburnable fire' with the image of a fever.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'stranger' was the war-maker who dissolved their sanctuary.
comments.comment: "Let a stranger maltreat his house:" the war-maker against that people was a stranger, not a proselyte, dissolving the supposed sanctuary and the city they called holy.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The 'overseer' names God, and the overseer who understands and imitates the true Overseer becomes as God among humans.
comments.comment: "Let heaven uncover his lawless deeds" — terrors from God and heaven. Job had said he was struck by God and also wronged by humans; the construction is that all came because of sins. "Let earth rise up against him." "A possession of belongings from the overseer." Overseer here names God; good bishops strive to wear that image. As one who imitates a royal image well is honored, blessed is the overseer who understands the true Overseer, zealously imitates him, and becomes as God among humans — or who has an Overseer making him truly overseer in Christ Jesus.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job answers those who claim to know why he suffers.
comments.comment: "Looking into me, hold wonder." You claim to know why I suffer, as if God slept over sins, and dared call me a sinner justly arrived here.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: By asking why the impious prosper, Job seeks the causes that God gives for what happens to men.
comments.comment: And he does the same in other matters, asking again: 'Why do the impious live, having been prospered even in wealth, their seed according to the soul, and their cattle not having failed to calve?' In order that he might also instruct through these, he seeks the existing causes from God of the things happening to men, which are secondary and pleasant.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The wicked grow old in ever-increasing wealth, with seed according to soul and children, their works, done to be seen by humans.
comments.comment: "They have grown old in wealth" — not newly rich, always increasing. "Their seed according to soul:" the righteous sow to the spirit and reap eternal life; the soulish do not receive the Spirit — folly to them — so their seed is according to soul, the inferior. "Their children in eyes:" all they do is to be seen by humans; children are each one’s works. Heterodox children are not in heart and good reasonings but in eyes.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Such men fear nowhere and no scourge touches them, and they conceive wickedness, not the fear of God.
comments.comment: "Their houses prosper:" enter a heretic synagogue and see the crowd — houses prosper. "Fear nowhere": they do not fear God while speaking of God. "A scourge from the Lord is not upon them:" if you see such a speaker healthy, sensing, sometimes worldly-prosperous, that line is fulfilled. "Their ox did not miscarry:" they farm — but Sodom, Gomorrah, Egypt. The ox bears so their wicked earth is farmed. What they conceive they carry from wickedness, not fear of God: "he travailed injustice, conceived toil, and bore lawlessness."
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The eternal sheep are Christ's sheep.
comments.comment: "They remain like eternal sheep." Christ: "My sheep hear my voice, and I give them eternal life" — those are eternal sheep.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: They only seem to remain as eternal sheep.
comments.comment: [Those who teach otherwise, mimicking the] flock of Christ — appointing their own bishops, elders, deacons, teachers, people, and catechumens — they fulfill "they remain as eternal sheep." They are not eternal sheep; they only remain as if they were.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Their children play with the psaltery of the law and the harp of prophecy as toys, whereas ours hymn and glorify God.
comments.comment: "Their children play; taking up psaltery and harp." Ours take instruments to hymn and glorify God. Their senseless children play with them. When they take up Old Testament words they laugh at law and prophets — psaltery of the law, harp of prophecy — as toys. "They rejoice with a voice of a psalm:" they say psalms of Valentinus and odes of Basilides. "In a rest of Hades they slept" — not heaven’s rest. We pray to sleep in God’s rest in the holy heavens with Christ reigning.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The impious man, prospering, speaks to the Lord as if his prosperity came from nothing and he need not serve him.
comments.comment: From this audacity the impious man, prospering in finding what he desires, utters a voice like that in Job (Job 21:14-15): 'Depart from me, I do not wish to know your ways; what is sufficient, what shall we serve him?' For indeed they do not think the prosperity coming to them is due to anything, saying to the Lord: 'Depart; do not make your ways manifest to me; for I do not wish to know them; for what more is of us sufficient, that we may serve you?'
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words of the prosperous impious man in verses 14-15.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends' words are recorded to help the reader, and the true teacher of virtue is God, who lights the mind with his Word.
comments.comment: "Is it not the Lord who teaches understanding and knowledge?" What the Holy Spirit administers must be written so the reader benefits. If the three friends’ words were useless, Providence would not have recorded them in Job’s book. One may be helped by looking into the doctrines, and see that the charge fails at one point only: they accuse Job of suffering for his sins, not seeing many other causes of what happens to humans. The doctrine is sound: a true teacher of virtue cannot be merely human. "The one who teaches a human knowledge" is God. "Teach me your just deeds," says the Prophet, knowing God is the true and perfect teacher. God teaches by shining on the learner’s soul and lighting the mind with his true Word. Righteous men also teach us when they have received teaching grace.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God is so kind that he lets us speak as if judged with him, and promises to answer and persuade.
comments.comment: "He will enter with you into judgment." God accounts for the one under his care and convicts him — so philanthropic that, judging kindly, he lets us speak as if judged with him. So Isaiah: "Come, and let us reason, says the Lord." If you have something to convict my providence of neglect, speak; I will answer and persuade you as one worthy of condemnation.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means that God enters into judgment with man.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eliphaz assumes Job is wicked and accuses him of pledging brothers who owed nothing.
comments.comment: "Is your wickedness not much? Your sins are uncountable." Eliphaz assumes this of Job. Knowing him rich, he says Job took pledges from brothers as from debtors who were not debtors — "you pledged your brothers for nothing." …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Whoever strips a poor debtor without pity takes the clothing of a naked man.
comments.comment: If someone has one tunic and, demanding what is mine, I strip it without pity, I have taken the naked man’s clothing. Such things happen when we lend and chase debtors. Often a debtor is extremely poor and cannot repay; we shut our bowels, become merciless, and do not see that he feeds wife and children from a few obols — while we demand bitterly and sometimes hold surplus. So Eliphaz accuses Job of taking clothing from the naked.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Failing to do kindness is as blameworthy as injustice, so we must not send a widow away empty or maltreat orphans.
comments.comment: "You did not give water to the thirsty; you deprived the hungry of a morsel." Not only injustice but failure to do kindness is liable. These charges are truly blameworthy — but not true of Job, nor well said of him. In bitter demand sometimes a person has one morsel; even without a whole loaf we take it saying, "But you owe." "You sent widows away empty." If a widow enters our house, let us not send her empty; each fill her fold according to power. "You maltreated orphans." Maltreat no one; especially spare orphans. God commands fighting for helpless souls; poor, widows, and orphans need help more than others.
comments.selected_reason: Teaches that failing to show kindness is itself blameworthy.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The light of belongings, children and health has turned to the darkness of desolation, and the opposing energy covered him sleeping.
comments.comment: "Therefore snares have surrounded you" — the events into which his soul is trapped. "The light has turned out darkness for you:" once belongings, children, and health were light; now circumstances are darkness — desolation, open air, wanderer, fugitive, hearthless. "Water covered you sleeping:" the opposing energy covered you because you were not awake.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The high God sees all, humbles minds lifted by insolence, and judges even in a storm.
comments.comment: "Does not the one dwelling the heights oversee?" You think the high God does not see; he oversees all and brings down minds lifted by insolence. "Those carried by insolence he humbled." Likely because you insulted widows and orphans and pledged brothers for nothing, you suffer and are humbled. "You said, What has the Strong One known? Or will he judge according to the gloom?" God can judge even in a storm. "He traverses the circle of heaven" — providence goes around.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The righteous walk an eternal path and even when taken early are perfected in a little.
comments.comment: "Will you not keep an eternal path which righteous men have trodden?" Can you watch the path providence travels? The righteous walk it toward the coming age; even if steps look equal, the soul treads eternal paths. "Who were seized untimely:" often the righteous die early, yet "perfected in a little they fill long times," for virtue in the Lord is the soul. Their foundations are a flowing river — always advancing in goods.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The good houses are those of the ruling faculty.
comments.comment: "Who filled their houses with good things:" not these outer houses, but the houses of the ruling faculty — temperance, justice, courage, prudence, …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The blameless scorn the counsel of the impious.
comments.comment: "A blameless one sneered at them" — at the counsel of the impious who teach opposite the truth with wretched doctrines.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eliphaz, thinking he admonished Job, tells him to confess his sins.
comments.comment: "Fire will eat their remnant." "He took from his mouth an exposition:" … Confess your sins; take from God’s mouth an introduction with confession; take up his words from your heart. Eliphaz said this thinking he admonished Job.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Eliphaz's call to turn and confess is said unjustly of Job, who did not sin, but justly of us.
comments.comment: "If you turn and humble yourself before the Lord." "As a rock of a winter-torrent of Ophir:" from the gold-place your word will come varied and beautiful. "The Almighty will be a helper from enemies" if you subject yourself and confess. "He will render you pure as fired silver." Then free speech before the Lord, sins put away. "Upon your ways there will be light; he will restore a way of life of righteousness." Said toward Job unjustly — he did not sin — but toward us, justly.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job wished to go to court with God and learn His answer, not to charge Him with injustice, and in the end he obtained it.
comments.comment: "His hand has become heavy upon my groan." If the vote of punishments could be brought at once, he could find him. Would that he could go to court, petition, and learn what God would say to what Job would say. See how he obtained what he prayed — it comes last in the book. He wanted to know the answer, and whether punishment would continue; he said this not as condemning injustice.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The impious feed young men to work insults.
comments.comment: bread sweetened for younger ones — sweet to the impious to feed young men so as to work insults through them.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Though Job said he would appear righteous, he knew that no star is pure before God, as Paul did not justify himself.
comments.comment: For even if he said, 'I know that I will appear righteous,' yet he knew and is persuaded that, as a tester before God, 'there is no star pure in his sight' (Job 25:5) and he himself makes it clear. Such is what the blessed Paul says, writing: 'I do not know myself' (1 Corinthians 4:4). Then, not giving credit to himself, he proceeds: 'but not in this am I justified, but He who judges me is the Lord' (1 Cor 4:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The earth hangs on nothing because it is established on liquid, which has no hard and solid foundation.
comments.comment: What is said here is equal to what is said: 'He who made the earth stand upon the water,' and by Job: 'hanging the earth upon nothing' (Job 26:7); for if it is established in the sea, it does not have a hard and solid foundation, but in the waters it has the hanging. And every water has a ground beneath it. Since the sea has a ground beneath it, it must certainly have something underlying it. But nothing else is found except the liquid. For this reason, he says the earth is established upon the seas.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how the earth can be 'hung upon nothing' and yet stand on the seas.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Job swears by the Lord who let the devil test him.
comments.comment: I swear by the living Lord who judged me to suffer these things, who handed me to these circumstances, who gave the devil authority to examine and torment me so. "The Lord lives, who has thus judged me, and the Almighty who has embittered my soul."
comments.selected_reason: Shows what Job means when he swears by the living Lord.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil received authority to test Job through his goods, his body and his friends, hoping he would speak against Providence.
comments.comment: "The Lord lives, who has thus judged me." The devil received authority and tested Job night and day — first through outward things, later through the body, then through friends. When the wife did not conquer him, three friends came — not enemies with plotting doctrines, but true words badly and out of season. Through them the devil planned to make Job speak against Providence, turn impious under toil, and grow weary under pain.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job will not grant that his accusers understand his suffering, and he clings to righteousness with a clear conscience.
comments.comment: "May it not be for me to declare you righteous until I die." If I assent that you have understood why I suffer, I have declared you righteous till death. "I will not put away my guilelessness." I will not leave righteousness; I always remember to cling to it. "I am not conscious to myself of having done out-of-place things" — great freedom of speech for former life and for the time of trial.
comments.selected_reason: Explains why Job will not call his accusers righteous.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Knowledge holds things alike; understanding discerns.
comments.comment: "What place is there of knowledge?" Knowledge encompasses things that hold alike in contemplation; understanding is discernment.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nothing equals wisdom, neither silver, gold nor precious stones, nor even the inward holy mysteries of God.
comments.comment: "Silver will not stand as an exchange for it." Nothing equals wisdom — not silver or gold taken simply, not precious onyx or sapphire, not heights or gabis (some say the heaped lip of a measure). "Draw wisdom above the innermost things" — beyond India’s precious stones, or above the hyper-secret inward holy mysteries of God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom is more excellent than precious stones, so nothing precious, not even the topaz of Ethiopia, equals it.
comments.comment: 'Your mouth's law is more precious to me than ten thousands of gold and silver' (Psalm 119:72), and 'Take instruction and do not forsake knowledge, which is tested above silver' (Prov 8:10); for wisdom is more excellent than precious stones, and every precious thing is not of equal value to it. Therefore it is also said to companions concerning it to Job: 'The topaz of Ethiopia shall not be equaled to it' (Job 28:19).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Wisdom escapes every human.
comments.comment: "It has escaped every human" — even prophet or apostle.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job's paths were the virtues, poured out so that even infants were fed.
comments.comment: "When my paths were poured with butter." Job’s paths were virtues; temperance, justice, and courage poured so that even infants were fed from them. "My mountains were poured with milk" — high and great thoughts he climbed.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the images of paths poured with butter and mountains with milk.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job went out to benefit the city, and others laid hand on mouth, sensing their works unworthy beside his.
comments.comment: "When I went out upright in a city": busy with teaching and benefit, loving the common good, not self-love. "Putting a finger upon mouth" may signal silence; or, since hand stands for works, they put their little work on the mouth, sensing they were unworthy to speak while Job, with greater works, was present.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Hearers blessed Job and could not look into the sparkle of his thoughts, as Moses was cautious to look on God.
comments.comment: "Those who heard blessed me; their tongue was glued to their larynx." Before torment he was so great that hearers blessed him and wondered how he grasped such things and could help them. As Moses was cautious to look face-to-face before God for excess brightness, so Job’s excess of wisdom made hearers unable to look into the sparkle of his thoughts; eyes turned aside, not following the deepest mind. Aquila and Symmachus: "witnessed about me"; others: "an eye seeing turned aside" — I cannot speak against. "I saved a poor one from a hand of a powerful one."
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job was an eye to the blind in guiding minds and a guide in ethics, and he was a father protecting the helpless.
comments.comment: I was an eye to the blind and a guide. Regarding the intellect, he opened blind minds; he benefited those perfected in soul and became an eye to them. To those who have fallen, he granted feet—the very foundations of the soul—and through his word, he became a guide who leads others. Thus, the eye pertains to noetic guidance, while the guide pertains to ethical guidance. … I was a father to the helpless. In these words, the character of one who aids the helpless and the weak is made clear. … I traced out a justice I did not previously know. Observe his protection: it extends not merely to usefulness, nor even to food and clothing, but even to the dangers of foreign warfare.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: We ought to help the poor oppressed by the powerful, and to judge fairly when called to settle brothers' affairs.
comments.comment: [According to the] letter: as far as our power goes, we ought to help the poor oppressed by the powerful. "And a foot to a lame one:" he granted feet of the soul even to those lamed in their bases, and by the word he himself became their foot. "A judgment which I did not know, I tracked out:" he teaches how to judge when called to settle brothers affairs.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job crushed the mills of the unrighteous, as Christ crushed the mills of opposing forces.
comments.comment: I crushed the mills of the unrighteous. Consider the difficulty of the task; he says that he corrected the matter even when it had already been foreseen. Truly, when Christ came, he crushed the mills of opposing forces. The Lord crushed the mills of the lions, as it is written in the prophet: … 'For he wounds, but he also binds up; he has torn, but his hands will heal.'
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job speaks not from pride but because he must tell of God's providence and explain what his present state is.
comments.comment: And I said, 'My age has grown old, like a phoenix stem.' Observe how much time has passed before he says these things; he does not speak out of pride or a sense of greatness, but is compelled to speak of God's providence, explaining why he departed from it and what his current state is.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job holds the mocking young in no esteem.
comments.comment: Now even the least have mocked me; they admonish me in ways that render their own fathers powerless. He does not yield to this powerlessness, but understands them clearly, just as the prophet said: 'Every adulterer is made powerless before him,' for he held such people in no esteem.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job was not without fellow-feeling, yet he gave thanks when his children died.
comments.comment: Was Job's heart made of adamant? Were his inward parts fashioned from stone? Ten children fell to him in a brief moment of time, crushed by a single blow in the house of celebration, at the hour of enjoyment, when the devil brought the building down upon them. He saw a table mingled with blood; he saw children born at different times but reaching the end of life together. He did not wail, he did not tear his hair, he did not utter any ignoble sound, but he spoke that famous thanksgiving celebrated by all: "The Lord gave, and the Lord has taken away; as it seemed good to the Lord, so it has happened; blessed be the name of the Lord" (Job 1:21). Was the man without fellow-feeling? How could that be, when he says of himself, "I wept for everyone who was afflicted" (Job 30:25)? But was he lying when he said this? Indeed, the truth bears witness for him that along with his other virtues he was also truthful. For it says, "A man blameless, righteous, God-fearing, truthful" (Job 1:1).
comments.selected_reason: Shows from Job's life that he felt for others yet gave thanks to God.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea

comments.capsule: Job could not literally have cared for orphans from the womb, so his good practice began with the word fulfilled in him.
comments.comment: Job says: “And even if I have eaten my morsel alone and have not shared with the orphan, except as a father guided them from the womb of my mother” (Job 31:17-18); for how was he able to provide for and care for orphans from the womb of a mother? Thus, therefore, I take it: a praiseworthy practice is a continuous progression; then the practice takes its beginning when the word is fulfilled. I am able, therefore, to say this: he says that I have done good things not after the evil things, but the word having been fulfilled in me, it began from the praiseworthy things; …
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The friends fell silent because Job was righteous against them, and Job spoke when it was time and was silent after silencing them.
comments.comment: "And Job ceased with words." The three friends were quiet still to speak against him, for he was righteous opposite them. He did not simply cease; the heart understanding divine things did not cease. "There is a time for every matter under heaven, a time to be silent and a time to speak." When it was time to answer the three, he spoke; after silencing them, he was silent — said in praise: Job ceased.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Elihu held back out of fear, yet wisdom is not only for elders, and if time makes wise, much more does God.
comments.comment: Elihu: "I was quiet, fearing to announce my own knowledge." He knows how humans suffer, why they fall into circumstances in this life alone, how the unjust prosper. I saw those doing injustice, and my feet were almost shaken. If I look only in this life, my steps were nearly poured out. "Not the long-timed ones are wise:" not only elders; youth can hear something noble. If time makes wise, much more God.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Wisdom comes with time only to the one who desires and pursues it, so an old man is not wise by necessity.
comments.comment: Furthermore, those who think that learnings are by nature are rebuked by this; for nothing that belongs to human essence by nature and necessity is perfected by time. No mortal, as a living being, adds to himself by time; but the wise man is attained by time. "For when I was a child, I spoke as a child, I thought as a child, I reasoned as a child; when I have become a man, I laid aside the things of a child" (1 Cor 13:11). To this, someone might oppose the "not those of many years are wise, nor the elders know judgment" (Job 32:9), contrary to what was said by Job to those who think otherwise. Yet both can be understood as following one another; for the blessed Job says that he who begins wisdom and hastens to take it up will not take it up as it happens, but will take it up in much time. But neither would Elihu say contrary to this; for if someone did not desire wisdom, but had progressed in age, he would already be wise; for the old man is not wise by necessity.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The soul that loves learning conceives a word as a mother carries a child, and speaking brings it rest when it is ready.
comments.comment: "The spirit of the belly destroys me." As a pregnant person comes to birth-pains until the formed child is born, so the love-of-learning soul conceives a word, forms and stamps it in order, and when ready does not hand over a miscarriage but something brought to term. "My belly is like a wineskin of new wine boiling, bound" … "I will speak so that I may rest having opened the lips:" full of words before an understanding hearer, speaking rests.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the image of a belly full of words like new wine.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Moths eat those who take human faces.
comments.comment: "I do not know how to wonder at a face; if not, moths will eat me" — moths eat those who take human faces.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The Holy Spirit is a co-creator with the Creator God, as Job says that a divine spirit made him.
comments.comment: Again, the Holy Spirit shone forth without effort and as if spontaneously, being a co-creator and equal-worker with the Creator God who established it from the beginning, as it is fitting for us to know, from which these things were declared: Job says, 'A divine spirit made me; and the breath of the Almighty teaches me' (Job 33:4).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The sinner should approach the high priest, Christ, who is the propitiation for our sins, and righteousness adds nothing to God.
comments.comment: "If you have sinned, what will you do?" Look up to heaven and clouds and understand the sin. Approach the high priest so he may bring sacrifice: "If anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous, and he is the propitiation for our sins." If many lawless deeds, what can you do? Dissolve them — for the incurable we cannot heal, Christ came from heaven: "Blessed are those whose lawless deeds are forgiven and whose sins are covered." "Since you are righteous, what will you give him?" What can righteousness add to God?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: This age is night, and light is kept for the righteous.
comments.comment: "The one arranging night watches" is God. This whole age is night and darkness; light is kept for you. What you see now you see through a mirror; "in your light we will see light." Because it is night, many wars and wild beasts go about.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: A sinner is not marked off from senseless cattle.
comments.comment: "The one marking me off from four-footed ones of earth." If you are a sinner you are not marked off: "a human in honor did not understand; he was compared to senseless cattle; "do not become as horse and mule, which have no understanding."
comments.selected_reason: Explains what it means to be marked off from the beasts of the earth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Because the earth's support is beyond us, we should limit our thought, and the 'pillars' are the power that holds it together.
comments.comment: For this reason, set a boundary to your thought, lest the word of Job overtake you for your meddling as you peer into things incomprehensible, and you too be asked by him, “On what are its rings fastened?” (Job 38:6). But if you ever hear in the Psalms, “I have made firm its pillars” (Psalm 74:3 (LXX)), consider the power that holds it together to be called pillars. For what does “He founded it upon the seas” (Psalm 23:2 (LXX)) indicate, except that the nature of water is poured around the earth on every side? How then, since water is flowing and naturally falls downward, does it remain suspended and never flow away? But do you not consider that the earth hanging by itself, being heavier in nature, presents the same or even greater difficulty for reasoning?
comments.selected_reason: Explains the question 'on what are its rings fastened?' as a warning against over-curious thought about the earth.
comments.author: Basil of Caesarea
comments.work: Homilies on the Six Days of Creation

comments.capsule: God marked out the land when it lay hidden in the deeps and set it apart by bars and gates on the waters.
comments.comment: [Of the earth:] For He marked it out; that is, when of old it lay hidden in the deeps, invisible and unformed (Genesis 1:2), He made it visible and finished. He marked it out, for, as the books of Moses attest, He said: “Let the water be gathered into one gathering, and let the dry land appear” (Genesis 1:9). So it appeared out of the waters; and though it was under water and wholly unworked, He set it apart by itself, placing bars and gates on the deeps (compare Job 38:10) and separating it thoroughly from the waters.
comments.selected_reason: Explains how God set bars and gates on the waters when the dry land appeared.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God takes pride in making man from earth, since to make a rational creature of clay goes beyond all wonder.
comments.comment: Then how is it that God takes pride in the making of man? For He says somewhere to the blessed Job, “Did you take clay of the earth and form a living creature, and set it on the earth endowed with speech?” (Job 38:14). For to make a rational living creature out of earth would, I think, go beyond all wonder.
comments.author: Cyril of Alexandria

comments.capsule: God gives Job freedom of speech as a prize for enduring, and no one can answer God while the loin is loose.
comments.comment: "Gird as a man your loin." God already gives a prize — freedom of speech: I will ask you; you answer me. Had Job not conquered and endured, he would not have heard that. Let no one answer God before becoming a man and girding the loin; while the loin is loose, one cannot reasonably answer the Lord. The perfect contests wait after this life, yet grace already pledges the athletes. When Job cast away goods and glorified the Giver, put away children and gave thanks, understood worms from the body and was not conquered — God spoke through whirlwind and clouds as preface and pledge. Hearing earlier words he stays silent, not yet knowing Moses later pattern — Moses spoke and God answered with a voice. God then gives freedom to speak. So great is God kindness that he takes a face not of judge only but of one judged with the human: "Come, and let us reason, says the Lord; "My people, what did I do to you; answer me."
comments.selected_reason: Explains why God invites Job to gird his loin like a man and answer.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Nothing happens unless God judges it, and Job's endurance was hidden until his trials made it shine.
comments.comment: "Do not reject my judgment." Remember the saying. Whenever God judges us to lose a child, a ruler, health — nothing happens unless God judges. "Not even a sparrow falls into a snare without the Father will in the heavens." So to the sufferer: do not reject my judgment; do not deny that I judged about you. "Do you think I have spoken oracle to you otherwise than so that you may appear righteous?" You were righteous but not apparent; endurance and courage were hidden till toils made them shine. In times of trial hear God present saying this — and do not appear unjust or impious.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the words 'do not reject my judgment' for anyone who suffers.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The same hardships are lashes to the sinner but contests to the righteous, as happened to Job.
comments.comment: For many are the lashes of the sinner; and it has been said to us in other places that the same circumstances are lashes to the sinners, but contests to the righteous. Never do the burdensome and evil things come upon the pious as a scourge, but as a testing, just as it happened to Job, that the righteous might be revealed (Job 40:8).
comments.selected_reason: Distinguishes the scourge of the sinner from the testing of the righteous, as in Job.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The one afflicted in everything who endures to the end is proven righteous, as Job was.
comments.comment: … for the heart of everyone who endures in obscurity is tested, and he who is afflicted in everything is not distressed, but enduring until the end, he is proven righteous; such as Job, to whom God said: 'If perhaps I may prove you, you shall be more righteous than I' (Job 40:8).
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Since Job conquered the insolent one who campaigned against him, he is told to take courage and humble every proud one.
comments.comment: "Take up height and power; be crowned; put on glory and honor. Send angels in wrath; humble every insolent one; quench a proud one." The insolent one campaigned against you — Send your hand; touch all he has; then he will bless me to my face — but you conquered. Take courage; humble every insolent one and his angels; quench the proud; strike the impious at once. "Fill their faces with dishonor" by conviction in you.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The wild beasts are opposing powers, over which the human has authority.
comments.comment: "Look — wild beasts are beside you; he eats grass equal to oxen." Wild beasts are opposing powers; the Prophet prayed, "Do not hand over to the wild beasts the soul that confesses you." You have received authority over them, O human.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The beasts stand beside Job and every victor.
comments.comment: … "But look — wild beasts are beside you." Beside you, Job; beside every one who keeps the memory; beside everyone who has won.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The beasts beside Job are the opposing powers, made manifest because they lacked strength against his virtue.
comments.comment: Regarding Job, it is said: 'Behold, beasts eat grass beside you like oxen' (Job 40:15), not that the immediate beasts were driven wild in nature by Job, but that the disorder of opposing powers was being made manifest because they lacked strength against the greatness of the saint's virtue. And many things are found in the Scripture where animals are mystically led.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: The dragon's first force against a man begins in the loin, and against a woman at the navel of the belly.
comments.comment: "His power is upon the navel of the belly" — the first force set against the man, and the starting point of fornication. The same note marks the female so the campaign is not only against those who carry seed. Fittingly Scripture names the loin for the male and the navel of the belly for the woman: strength in the loin; power at the navel.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Through desire the dragon overpowers both male and female, the loin standing for the man and the navel for the woman.
comments.comment: For especially through this desire he is able both to overturn and to wrestle down human beings — the loin being understood, as of the man, and the navel of the belly decently as of the woman — so that it may be shown that through such desire he most of all overpowers both the male and the female (Job 40:16).
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Christ, like a fisherman, puts his flesh on the hook of his divinity as bait, so that the devil seizes it and is drawn up.
comments.comment: [Christ speaks:] I am a fisherman fishing for fish. For just as a fisherman puts a worm on the hook, extends the rod, and sometimes lets the hook sink down and sometimes pulls and drags it, so that by making the worm appear to flee he prepares the fish to rush upon it—so I too, placing my body on the hook of my divinity like a worm—for I am a worm and not a man (Psalm 22:6)—sometimes I pull death in as if in fear, and sometimes I let the hook sink down as if taking courage, so that the devil, like a fish leaping upon the worm—that is, coming against the flesh—may without knowing it fall upon the hook of the divinity, and having fallen may be dragged up, so that what was said by Job may be fulfilled in him: You will draw the dragon with a hook (Job 41:1).
comments.selected_reason: Shows how the early writers read the hook that draws up the dragon.
comments.author: Amphilochius of Iconium

comments.capsule: No fleet can kill the dragon's last extremities, but under divine oversight we can carry the whole beast and put it to death.
comments.comment: "Phoenician nations divide it." Because Canaanites — also called Phoenicians — are charged with great wickedness, each of that race takes a share from the dragon. "All the ships together cannot carry one hide of his tail": the dragon’s last extremities no fleet can kill. Humans sail in bodies as in boats and cannot lift even one hide of that tail by themselves; under divine oversight we can carry not only the hide but the whole beast and put it to death. Each kills the devil as far as lies in him, as the Apostle says: "May God crush Satan under your feet soon."
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Like an actor's mask, his clothing hides what he is.
comments.comment: "Who will uncover the face of his clothing?" Why not simply "his face"? What is the clothing doing here? Take actors who put on masks and hide what they are so they may seem something else.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dragon never shows his own face but borrows a face of virtue for each vice, and so deceives.
comments.comment:
[Of the actors:] Their own face stays hidden; what they are does not show, and what they seem is what the eye catches. The dragon is like that. He never shows his own face; he borrows a face to deceive people and uses that. This enemy keeps many masks, and for each vice he puts on a face of virtue.

Who can unmask the face he wore? Who can uncover it and stop the lie that a dragon sits inside? Some of his other disciples are the same: "They come to you in sheep’s clothing, but inwardly they are ravening wolves."
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The devil once deceived many by appearing as what he was not, until Christ exposed his illusion.
comments.comment: Long ago the enemy was great in his scheming against human beings, and by his illusions he deceived many, and the detection of his deceit was difficult—so that the Spirit says about him: “Who will uncover the face of his garment?” (Job 41:13) and so on. For he did not appear as what he was, but he produced an illusion of himself corresponding to whatever he was scheming. Therefore many were deceived by him. But when the Savior came, then all his illusion was exposed. For the things he did of old that went unrecognized are now known by the grace of Christ, and the things by which he once deceived human beings are now trampled underfoot by them. For faith is stronger than every assault of the devil and madness of demons.
comments.selected_reason: Explains what 'uncover the face of his garment' says about the devil's deceit before Christ.
comments.author: Athanasius of Alexandria

comments.capsule: His face cannot be found, for lifting it by word or thought uncovers something worse, and he is folded up everywhere.
comments.comment: He is a person, imitating the deceptive Protagonist; for he does not have a face that is entirely ordered. Thus he says in Job: 'Who will strip off his face-covering?' (Job 41:13). You cannot say that this is his face. If you lift his face by word or by thought, something worse is found. Furthermore, he is folded up everywhere; 'into the folding of his armor' no one can enter. And if you enter, it is folded up again.
comments.author: Didymus the Blind

comments.capsule: Nothing in the dragon is simple, for he is crafty and folded, and a holy person can expose the fold.
comments.comment: "Who would enter the folding of his breastplate?" He names a breastplate and a chest — the place of the ruling faculty. Nothing in him is simple; he is crafty and folded. A holy person can expose that fold; the holy breastplate is not folded that way. "Who will open the gates of his face?" He hides what is stored within. Who can open those gates and show the craft, the venom, the evils laid up there?
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The fear around the dragon's teeth is not the fear of God.
comments.comment: "Fear is round about his teeth." Of such teeth it is said, "You crushed the teeth of sinners," and "The Lord will crush the molars of the lions." That fear is not the fear of God; it is the fear around the dragon’s teeth.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Everything inside him is hard asp venom.
comments.comment: "His inwards are bronze asps" — the hidden doctrines and thoughts. Everything inside him is asp venom, and those asps are not soft but hard.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dragon's mouth is the place from which destroying words come, so we keep ourselves from their burning.
comments.comment: "From his mouth": the blasphemies and speeches of impious, atheist teachers. "From his mouth go out burning lamps, and fire-pans of fire are flung about." … The dragon’s mouth can be read tropically as the place from which destroying words come. When he has heard speech that, under a Christian mask, accuses the Craftsman — championing Marcion, Valentinus, or Basilides; speaking ill of the Maker of heaven and earth; denying that he is, or that he is of spiritual substance — then from such mouths go burning lamps and flung fire-pans. Knowing this, we keep ourselves so those lamps do not burn us and those pans do not touch us.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: An evil power exists, but God's weakness conquered it.
comments.comment: "In his neck power lodges." There is an evil power. But the weakness my Savior and Lord took on for me — the weakness of God — conquered …
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Scripture says 'glued', not 'united', for he is many.
comments.comment: "The fleshes of his body have been glued." Scripture could have said "united," but it did not. With him the one is many; things that seem one are glued, not truly united.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: The dragon's heart is turned to stone and cannot be hammered, while the one who is gold yields to the Word and receives the letters of God.
comments.comment: “His heart will not be shaken; it is fixed like a stone, and it stands like an anvil that cannot be hammered” (Job 41:15-16 (41:23-24)). His heart, he says, has turned to stone, and it cannot be beaten out; he is wholly hardened and brazen—not driven, not following reason, not yielding. He is hard, unmalleable, unyielding. And if anyone has drawn power from the devil, he too has the heart of this dragon, unmalleable and not to be driven. But if anyone is gold, following the word, he yields to the goldsmith’s art until he becomes a golden leaf and receives the impressions of the letters of God, in Christ Jesus …
comments.selected_reason: Explains the stone-like heart of the dragon and the contrast with the golden Word.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job received double as the prize of endurance, but Christ gives a hundredfold, and Job needed double virtue to earn it.
comments.comment: "The Lord gave Job double what he had before." The noble athlete who endured every trial receives the prize of endurance: everything double the former store. The Lord Jesus Christ gives not double but a hundredfold: "Whoever leaves father or mother, house, brothers, sisters for my sake or for the gospel will receive a hundredfold and inherit eternal life." Job would not have received double of the former things if he had not shown double virtue.
comments.selected_reason: Explains the double reward as the prize of Job's double virtue.
comments.author: Origen of Alexandria

comments.capsule: Job, after patience had won, recovered his body and double his goods, and he waited for his children to be restored.
comments.comment: And so that workman of God's victory, having blunted every dart of temptation with the breastplate and shield of patience, soon recovered the wholeness of his body from God, and possessed double what he had lost (Job 42:10). And if he had wished his children also to be restored, he could have been called father again. But he preferred to have them returned to him on that day; he postponed such great joy, confident in the Lord. He endured a voluntary childlessness for a time, so that he would not live without some patience.
comments.selected_reason: Explains Job's patience in the restoring of his goods and his children.
comments.author: Tertullian
